obligations.statement: Document title, LaTeX macros, theorem environments and typographic setup; no mathematical deliverable.
Purpose and source-disposition prose: coverage comes from the expanded unified manuscript; old mathematical code imposes no generality ceiling, and equivalent proof routes are permitted.

The scalar field $\K$ is either $\R$ or $\C$ unless specified otherwise. Hilbert inner products are conjugate-linear in the first variable and linear in the second. The continuous linear dual $X'$ is distinguished from the conjugate dual. The Banach transpose $T'$ acts on linear functionals; the Hilbert adjoint $T^*$ satisfies $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$. For an unbounded operator, its domain is part of its definition. Resolvents use $R(\lambda,A)=(\lambda I-A)^{-1}$; unitary groups use $U(t)=e^{itA}$. Any additional Fourier normalization is stated where it is used.

Prerequisites and scope: ordinary choice, linear algebra, general topology, measure/integration and real/complex analysis may be invoked in their precise forms. New functional-analytic assertions require proof or an identified proved result. Specialist sequels distinguished as not proved here are outside the actual proved-manuscript scope.

Working conventions: K is R or C; subspaces are scalar-linear unless a real underlying space is explicit, and completeness refers to the displayed norm. Scalar completeness and ordinary finite-dimensional Heine–Borel and extreme-value theorems are prerequisite facts, not additional manuscript deliverables.

Norm and seminorm. A norm on a vector space $E$ is a function $x\mapsto
orm{x}$ with $
orm{x}\geq0$, $
orm{x}=0$ exactly when $x=0$, $
orm{a x}=\abs{a}
orm{x}$, and $
orm{x+y}\leq
orm{x}+
orm{y}$. A seminorm satisfies the same conditions except that nonzero vectors may have value zero. A normed space carries the metric $d(x,y)=
orm{x-y}$ and its metric topology, the norm topology. Write $B(x,r)=\{y:
orm{y-x}<r\}$ and $\overline B(x,r)=\{y:
orm{y-x}\leq r\}$ for $r>0$.

Basic estimates and continuity. For a normed vector space over K = R or C: The induced distance is a metric. The norm is $1$-Lipschitz, addition and scalar multiplication are continuous, and translations and multiplication by a nonzero scalar are homeomorphisms. The closure of a linear subspace is a linear subspace. Every norm ball is convex, and a ball centered at zero is balanced: $\abs{a}\leq1$ implies $aB\subset B$.

For any real or complex vector space E and seminorm p, d(x,y)=p(x−y) is a pseudometric, N={x:p(x)=0} is a linear subspace, p(x+n)=p(x) for n∈N, and the formula ||x+N||=p(x) defines a genuine norm on the algebraic quotient E/N.

Banach space and absolute summability. A normed space is a Banach space if every Cauchy sequence converges in it. A series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n$ converges if its partial sums converge in norm; it is absolutely summable if $\sum_n\norm{x_n}<\infty$.

Series criterion for completeness. For a normed vector space over K = R or C: A normed space $E$ is Banach if and only if every absolutely summable series in $E$ converges. In a Banach space such a sum satisfies $\norm{\sum_n x_n}\leq\sum_n\norm{x_n}$.

Finite-dimensional norm equivalence. Let $E$ have finite dimension $n$ over $\K$. All norms on $E$ are equivalent; $E$ is complete, its closed bounded sets are compact, and it is locally compact. Every finite-dimensional subspace of any normed space is closed. These statements include $n=0$.

Every algebraic linear map from a finite-dimensional real or complex normed space to any normed space over the same scalar field is continuous. This is also included in the later bounded-operator estimates.

Canonical sequence spaces. For $1\leq p<\infty$, let $\ell^p=\{x=(x_j)_{j\geq1}:\sum_j\abs{x_j}^p<\infty\}$ with $\norm{x}_p=(\sum_j\abs{x_j}^p)^{1/p}$. Let $\ell^\infty$ be the bounded scalar sequences with $\norm{x}_\infty=\sup_j\abs{x_j}$, and let $c_0$ be its subspace of sequences tending to zero, with the inherited norm. The space $c_{00}$ consists of finitely supported sequences.

Discrete Holder and Minkowski inequalities. If $1\leq p,q\leq\infty$ and $1/p+1/q=1$, with $1/\infty=0$, then $\sum_j\abs{x_jy_j}\leq
orm{x}_p
orm{y}_q$ for every $x\in\ell^p$ and $y\in\ell^q$. For $1\leq p\leq\infty$ and every $x,y\in\ell^p$, $
orm{x+y}_p\leq
orm{x}_p+
orm{y}_p$.

Completeness of the canonical examples. All spaces are over K = R or C and C(K,K) consists of continuous scalar functions: The spaces $\ell^p$ for $1\leq p\leq\infty$ and $c_0$ are Banach. If $K$ is compact Hausdorff, then $C(K,\K)$ with $\norm{f}_\infty=\sup_{t\in K}\abs{f(t)}$ is Banach; for $K=\varnothing$ this is the zero space and the norm is zero.

Truncations $\sum_{j\leq n}x_j e_j$ converge to $x$ in $\ell^p$ for $p<\infty$ and in $c_0$, by the tail formulas for their norms. Hence $c_{00}$ is dense in each of these spaces. In $\ell^\infty$ its closure is exactly $c_0$; the constant sequence $1$ has distance $1$ from $c_{00}$.
Riesz's lemma. If $M$ is a proper closed subspace of a normed space $E$ and $0<\theta<1$, there exists $x\in E$ with $\norm{x}=1$ and $\dist(x,M)>\theta$.
Compact balls characterize finite dimension. A normed space has compact closed unit ball if and only if it is finite dimensional. It is locally compact if and only if it is finite dimensional.

A visible separated sequence. The coordinate vectors $(e_n)$ have norm $1$ in every $\ell^p$ and in $c_0$. For $m\ne n$, their distance is $2^{1/p}$ when $p<\infty$ and $1$ in the supremum norm. They supply a concrete bounded sequence with no norm-convergent subsequence. The space $c_{00}$ with any of these norms is incomplete: the finite truncations of $(2^{-j})_{j\geq1}$ are Cauchy but have no limit in $c_{00}$, since norm convergence forces the stated infinite-support coordinate limit.
Complete subspaces. A complete linear subspace $M$ of a normed space $E$ is closed in $E$. If $E$ is Banach, a linear subspace $M$ is complete with its inherited norm if and only if it is closed.

Distance quotient. Let $M\subset E$ be a linear subspace of a normed space. On the algebraic quotient $E/M$ put \[ \norm{x+M}_{E/M}=\inf_{m\in M}\norm{x-m}=\dist(x,M), \qquad q(x)=x+M. \] When $M$ is closed this is called the quotient norm.

Norm, topology, and factorization. Let E,F be normed spaces and M a linear subspace of E, with q(x)=x+M and quotient seminorm ||x+M||=inf_{m∈M}||x-m||: The formula is a well-defined seminorm, and is a norm exactly when $M$ is closed. In that case $q$ is linear, surjective, contractive, and open; more precisely $q(B_E(x,r))=B_{E/M}(q(x),r)$. A linear map $T:E\to F$ vanishing on $M$ factors uniquely as $\widetilde Tq$, and if $T$ is bounded then $\widetilde T$ is bounded with $\norm{\widetilde T}=\norm{T}$.

Let E be normed and M a nonclosed linear subspace, with quotient seminorm ||x+M||=dist(x,M). Its null subspace is closure(M)/M; quotienting by that null space gives a canonical linear isometry to E/closure(M). If M is dense and proper, E/M is algebraically nontrivial but its quotient seminorm is identically zero.
Completeness of a closed quotient. If $E$ is Banach and $M$ is closed, then $E/M$ with the quotient norm is Banach.

Isometric completion and its universal property. Every normed space $E$ has a Banach space $\widehat E$ and a linear isometry $i:E\to\widehat E$ with dense image. If $F$ is Banach, every bounded linear map $T:E\to F$ has a unique bounded extension $\widehat T:\widehat E\to F$ satisfying $\widehat Ti=T$ and $\norm{\widehat T}=\norm{T}$. Two completions are related by a unique surjective linear isometry agreeing with their embeddings of $E$.

Finite products. For normed spaces $E_1,\ldots,E_n$, the product carries the norms \[ 
orm{x}_p=\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n
orm{x_j}^p\Big)^{1/p}\quad(1\leq p<\infty), \qquad
orm{x}_\infty=\max_j
orm{x_j}. \] They give the same topology, coordinate projections and inclusions are bounded, and the product is Banach exactly when every factor is Banach. The empty product is the zero space.

Completeness and finite-support density. For an arbitrary family (H_j) indexed by any set I of real or complex Hilbert spaces, define the direct sum by suprema of finite sums of ||x_j||², norm squared the resulting sum and inner product sum_j <x_j,y_j>: This direct sum is Hilbert, each coordinate projection and inclusion is contractive, and finite-support vectors are dense. Every vector has at most countably many nonzero coordinates; the index set itself need not be countable.

Topological direct sum. Subspaces $M,N\subset E$ give a topological direct sum $E=M\oplus N$ if each $x\in E$ has a unique decomposition $x=m+n$ and the coordinate maps $x\mapsto m$, $x\mapsto n$ are bounded. A subspace with such a complement is called complemented. A bounded projection is a bounded linear map $P:E\to E$ satisfying $P^2=P$.

Projections and elementary complements. Let E be a normed space over R or C: A bounded projection gives the topological direct sum $E=\ran P\oplus\ker P$, and both subspaces are closed. Conversely a topological direct sum gives a bounded projection onto either summand. Every finite-dimensional subspace of a normed space is complemented. Every closed finite-codimensional subspace of a normed space is complemented.

If E is a Banach space and M,N are closed linear subspaces with E=M⊕N algebraically, then the decomposition maps x↦m and x↦n are bounded, so this is a topological direct sum. Algebraic splitting alone is insufficient to guarantee bounded coordinate maps in general.

Boundedness criterion for a linear map. For a linear map $T:E\to F$ between normed spaces, the following are equivalent: continuity everywhere; continuity at zero; existence of $C\geq0$ with $\norm{Tx}\leq C\norm{x}$ for every $x\in E$; and boundedness of $T$ on the closed unit ball. They are also equivalent to mapping bounded sets to bounded sets.

Norm estimates and finite-dimensional coordinates. For bounded linear maps between normed spaces over R or C, with ||T||=sup_{||x||≤1}||Tx||: The operator norm is a norm, $
orm{Tx}\leq
orm{T}
orm{x}$, and $
orm{ST}\leq
orm{S}
orm{T}$ whenever the composition is defined. Restriction to a subspace cannot increase the norm. Every linear map on a finite-dimensional domain is bounded; after bases are chosen its matrix acts by the usual coordinate multiplication, and changing the norms or bases gives equivalent operator norms in finite dimensions.
For every real or complex normed space E, ||id_E||=1 if E≠{0}, and ||id_E||=0 if E={0}. A continuous functional need not attain its norm on the closed unit ball (a concrete example is given later).
A complete target suffices. If $F$ is Banach and $E$ is any normed space, then $\Lin{E}{F}$ is Banach in the operator norm.

Neumann inversion. Let $E$ be Banach and $T\in\mathcal L(E)$ satisfy $
orm{T}<1$. Then $\id-T$ is invertible with bounded two-sided inverse \[ (\id-T)^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}T^n,\qquad 
orm{(\id-T)^{-1}}\leq rac1{1-
orm{T}}. \] For the partial sum through $n=N$, the norm error is at most $
orm{T}^{N+1}/(1-
orm{T})$.

Inverse difference and resolvent identities. Let E,F be normed spaces over R or C. For bounded invertible maps $A,B:E\to F$, \[ A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}. \] For $T\in\mathcal L(E)$ define $R(\lambda,T)=(\lambda\id-T)^{-1}$ when this bounded inverse exists. For any two such scalars, \[ R(\lambda,T)-R(\mu,T) =(\mu-\lambda)R(\lambda,T)R(\mu,T). \] The two resolvents commute.

Quantitative perturbation theorem. Let $E,F$ be Banach, and let $A:E	o F$ be a bounded bijection whose inverse is bounded. If $H:E	o F$ is bounded and $\eta=
orm{A^{-1}H}<1$, then $B=A+H$ is boundedly invertible and \[ B^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-A^{-1}H)^nA^{-1},\qquad 
orm{B^{-1}}\leq rac{
orm{A^{-1}}}{1-\eta},\qquad 
orm{B^{-1}-A^{-1}}\leq  rac{\eta
orm{A^{-1}}}{1-\eta}. \] Consequently the set of boundedly invertible maps in $\Lin{E}{F}$ is open and inversion is norm-continuous there.
The perturbation theorem assumes an initially bounded inverse; automatic boundedness of an inverse for a Banach-space bounded bijection is the distinct bounded-inverse theorem already inventoried.

Dual and dual norm. For a normed space $E$, its continuous linear dual is $E'=\Lin{E}{\K}$, with $\norm{f}=\sup_{\norm{x}\leq1}\abs{f(x)}$. Its algebraic dual $E^*_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is the space of all linear scalar-valued maps, with no continuity condition. The bidual is $E''=(E')'$.

Completeness and evaluation. Let E be a real or complex normed space and E′ its continuous scalar-linear dual. The dual of every normed space is Banach, whether or not the original space is complete. For $f\in E'$ and $x\in E$, $\abs{f(x)}\leq\norm{f}\norm{x}$.

In every infinite-dimensional real or complex normed space, choose linearly independent unit vectors u_n and extend them to a Hamel basis. Assign f(u_n)=n and zero on the remaining basis and extend scalar-linearly. This defines an algebraic linear functional unbounded on the unit sphere, hence discontinuous, so the algebraic and continuous duals differ.
Canonical evaluation map. The canonical map $J_E:E\to E''$ is $J_E(x)(f)=f(x)$ for $f\in E'$. A normed space is called reflexive if $J_E$ is surjective.

Evaluation is initially contractive. Let E be a real or complex normed space with J_E(x)(f)=f(x). For each $x$, $J_E(x)$ is a continuous linear functional on $E'$. The map $J_E$ is linear and $\norm{J_E x}\leq\norm{x}$.

Dependency commentary only: the initially contractive evaluation map is proved isometric using norming functionals in the later Hahn–Banach chapter; reflexivity was defined as surjectivity without assuming that theorem.

Annihilator and preannihilator. For $A\subset E$ and $B\subset E'$ put \[ A^\perp=\{f\in E':f(a)=0\ (a\in A)\},\qquad {}^\perp B=\{x\in E:f(x)=0\ (f\in B)\}. \] The notation denotes a dual pairing, not a Hilbert inner product. For $T\in\Lin{E}{F}$ its Banach transpose is $T':F'\to E'$, $T'f=f\circ T$.

Basic dual maps. Let E,F be real or complex normed spaces, M a linear subspace of E, with annihilators and preannihilators defined by vanishing of the continuous dual pairing and Banach transpose T′f=f∘T. Annihilators and preannihilators are closed linear subspaces; they depend only on the closed linear span of the set annihilated. Inclusion of sets reverses inclusion of annihilators. Restriction $E'\to M'$ is contractive for every subspace $M$. If $M$ is closed, the transpose of the quotient map identifies $(E/M)'$ isometrically with $M^\perp$. The transpose is bounded, $\norm{T'}\leq\norm{T}$, and $(ST)'=T'S'$.

Forward cross-references: restriction surjectivity, exact transpose norm, and concrete sequence/Lp/C(K) dual representations occur as separately stated results. Their continuous-dual pairings are scalar-linear in the vector variable; this is not an additional independent theorem.

Real sublinear function. On a real vector space, a finite real-valued function $p$ is sublinear if $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$ and $p(t x)=t p(x)$ for all $t\geq0$. In particular $p(0)=0$ and $-p(-x)\leq p(x)$. Neither positivity nor symmetry is required.

Real analytic Hahn--Banach. Let $E$ be a real vector space, $M\subset E$ a linear subspace, and $p:E\to\R$ sublinear. If $f:M\to\R$ is linear and $f(m)\leq p(m)$ for all $m\in M$, then there exists a real linear $F:E\to\R$ extending $f$ and satisfying $F(x)\leq p(x)$ for all $x\in E$.

Real and complex norm-preserving Hahn--Banach. Let $E$ be a normed space over $\K$, $M\subset E$ any linear subspace, and $f\in M'$. There exists $F\in E'$ with $F|_M=f$ and $\norm{F}=\norm{f}$. Neither completeness nor closedness of $M$ is required.
Proof-convention commentary: a real extension alone is not a complex-linear extension; complex reconstruction is part of the proof of the preceding norm-preserving extension theorem.

Norming and distance-separating functionals. Let E be a real or complex normed space. For each nonzero $x\in E$ there exists $f\in E'$ with $
orm{f}=1$ and $f(x)=
orm{x}$. For $x=0$ the functional $f=0$ suffices for the corresponding equality with norm at most $1$. If $M$ is a subspace and $x
otin\cl M$, there exists $f\in E'$ with $f|_M=0$, $
orm{f}=1$, and $f(x)=\dist(x,M)>0$.

Restriction as an isometric quotient. Let E be a real or complex normed space. For any subspace $M\subset E$, restriction $r:E'\to M'$ is a surjective contraction with kernel $M^\perp$, and each $g\in M'$ has an extension of exactly the same norm. It induces a surjective linear isometry $E'/M^\perp\longrightarrow M'$. If $M$ is closed, then $(E/M)'\cong M^\perp$ isometrically by composition with the quotient map.

A functional on $\ell^\infty$ outside $\ell^1$. Let $c\subset\ell^\infty$ be the subspace of convergent sequences. The limit functional $\lambda(x)=\lim_jx_j$ is linear and has norm $1$: its modulus is at most the supremum norm, and its value at the constant sequence $\mathbf1$ is $1$. Hahn--Banach extends it to $L\in(\ell^\infty)'$ with norm $1$. For every $j$, $L(e_j)=0$, while $L(\mathbf1)=1$. If $L(x)=\sum_j a_jx_j$ for some $a\in\ell^1$, testing $e_j$ would give $a_j=0$ for every $j$, contradicting the value at $\mathbf1$. For counting measure on $\N$, this is precisely a continuous functional on $L^\infty$ which no $L^1$ density represents. The construction works over both scalar fields.

In the separation chapter, order inequalities on complex spaces use real parts of continuous complex-linear functionals. A locally convex space is a TVS with a base of convex balanced zero neighborhoods; Hausdorffness is required where stated. The general normed and explicitly stated locally convex versions are both retained.

Minkowski functional. Let $U$ be an absorbing convex subset of a real vector space with $0\in U$. Its gauge is $p_U(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tU\}$. Absorbing means that the set inside this infimum is nonempty for every $x$.

Gauge and continuity. Let U be an absorbing convex subset containing zero in a real vector space, with p_U(x)=inf{t>0:x∈tU}. The gauge is finite, nonnegative, positively homogeneous, and subadditive. For the remaining assertions suppose that $U$ is an open convex neighborhood of zero in a topological vector space. Then $U=\{x:p_U(x)<1\}$, and every real linear functional $h$ dominated by $p_U$ is continuous. If in addition $U$ is balanced, its gauge is a continuous seminorm. In a normed space with $B(0,r)\subset U$, $p_U(x)\leq\norm{x}/r$.

Open convex separation. Let $A,B$ be nonempty disjoint convex subsets of a real topological vector space, and suppose $A$ is open. There are a nonzero continuous real linear functional $h$ and $\alpha\in\R$ with \[ h(a)<\alpha\leq h(b)\qquad(a\in A, b\in B). \] For a complex locally convex space one may write $h=\operatorname{Re}f$ for a continuous complex linear $f$. In particular, these conclusions hold in real or complex normed spaces.

Strong separation from closed convex sets. Let $C$ be a nonempty closed convex subset of a normed space $E$ and $x_0
otin C$. There exists $f\in E'$, $f
e0$, with \[ \sup_{c\in C}\operatorname{Re}f(c) <\operatorname{Re}f(x_0). \] More precisely, for any $0<r<\dist(x_0,C)$ the functional may be chosen so that the right side exceeds the supremum by at least $r
orm{f}$. If $C$ is closed convex and $D$ is compact convex, both nonempty and disjoint, there is a uniform positive gap between their functional values. The point and compact-set conclusions also hold in a Hausdorff locally convex space, without the norm-dependent quantitative formula.

Closedness alone for two disjoint convex sets does not supply the compact-set conclusion. For example in $\R^2$ the closed convex sets $\{(s,t):s>0, t\geq1/s\}$ and $\{(0,t):t\in\R\}$ are disjoint and have distance zero. A functional bounded above or below on the entire second set must have zero $t$ coefficient, and its values on the first set approach its value on the second; hence there is no uniform positive separating gap.

Polars and pairing topologies. For $A\subset E$, define $A^\circ=\{f\in E':\abs{f(a)}\leq1\text{ for all }a\in A\}$. For $B\subset E'$ define $ {}^\circ B=\{x\in E:\abs{f(x)}\leq1\text{ for all }f\in B\}$. The weak topology $\sigma(E,E')$ is the coarsest topology making all $f\in E'$ continuous. The weak-star topology $\sigma(E',E)$ is the coarsest topology making all evaluations $f\mapsto f(x)$ continuous. Their full development is in Chapter~\ref{fa2:p1:c12}. An absolutely convex set is convex and balanced over its scalar field.

Polar identities and the bipolar theorem. Let E be a real or complex normed space, A⊂E arbitrary, and A°={f∈E′: |f(a)|≤1 for all a∈A}, °B={x∈E: |f(x)|≤1 for all f∈B}. Polars reverse inclusions, the polar of a union is the intersection of the polars, and taking the closed absolutely convex hull does not change a polar. For $r>0$, $(rA)^\circ=r^{-1}A^\circ$, and the polar of the closed unit ball of $E$ is the closed unit ball of $E'$. Moreover, \[ {}^\circ(A^\circ)=\cl\operatorname{aconv}(A), \] where closure is in norm and the absolutely convex hull includes zero (also when $A$ is empty).

Double-annihilator closure in the stated pairing. Let E be a real or complex normed space with continuous scalar-linear dual E′ and annihilators with respect to evaluation. For a linear subspace $M\subset E$, $ {}^\perp(M^\perp)=\cl M$. For a linear subspace $N\subset E'$, \[ ({}^\perp N)^\perp =\cl^{\sigma(E',E)}N. \] The closure on the right in the second formula is weak-star closure, not in general norm closure.

For example take $E=\ell^1$, so $E'=\ell^\infty$, and $N=c_0$. Its preannihilator is zero by coordinate tests. Thus $c_0$ is weak-star dense in $\ell^\infty$ although it is a proper norm-closed subspace.

For every real or complex normed space E and every convex C⊂E, including C=∅, the weak closure σ(E,E′) of C equals its norm closure. In particular each norm-closed convex set is weakly closed, without completeness. This is the same canonical statement developed later in the weak-topology chapter.

On a real normed space E, an extended-real function φ:E→(−∞,+∞] is proper iff D(φ)={x:φ(x)<∞} is nonempty; −∞ is excluded. It is lower-semicontinuous iff every real sublevel is closed. Its epigraph epi φ={(x,t):t≥φ(x)} is closed iff φ is lower-semicontinuous, and epi φ is convex iff φ is convex.

Conjugate and biconjugate. Let E be a real normed space; proper extended-real functions take values in (−∞,+∞] and have a nonempty finite domain. For a proper $\varphi$ define \[ \varphi^*(f)=\sup_{x\in E}\{f(x)-\varphi(x)\}\quad(f\in E'), \qquad \varphi^{**}(x)=\sup_{f\in E'}\{f(x)-\varphi^*(f)\}. \] Terms with $\varphi(x)=+\infty$ or $\varphi^*(f)=+\infty$ contribute $-\infty$ to the respective supremum.

Fenchel inequality and Fenchel--Moreau. Let E be a real normed space, with φ*(f)=sup_x(f(x)−φ(x)) on E′ and φ**(x)=sup_f(f(x)−φ*(f)). For any proper function, Fenchel's inequality $f(x)\leq\varphi(x)+\varphi^*(f)$ holds whenever the sum has its usual extended-real meaning. If $\varphi$ is in addition convex and norm-lower-semicontinuous, then $\varphi^*$ is proper, convex and weak-star lower semicontinuous, and $\varphi^{**}(x)=\varphi(x)$ for every $x\in E$, including points where $\varphi(x)=+\infty$.

Norm and convex indicator. Let E be a real normed space with conjugation against E′ as above. For $\varphi(x)=\norm{x}$, its conjugate is $0$ on the closed dual unit ball and $+\infty$ outside it: the unit-ball case is the dual norm inequality, while a vector with $f(x)>\norm{x}$ can be scaled to make the defining supremum infinite. For a nonempty closed convex $C$, the convex indicator $I_C$, equal to $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty$ elsewhere, has conjugate $\sup_{x\in C}f(x)$, its support function. The identity $I_C^{**}=I_C$ is a precise separation statement. These conclusions are consequences of conjugation; no general optimization duality or unproved minimax principle has been invoked.

Nowhere dense and meagre sets. A subset of a topological space is nowhere dense if its closure has empty interior. It is meagre if it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets. A space is Baire if every countable intersection of open dense subsets is dense.

Baire's complete-metric theorem. Every complete metric space is Baire. In particular, a nonempty complete metric space which is a countable union of closed sets has at least one member with nonempty interior. No nonempty open subset of a complete metric space is meagre in the ambient space.
Proof commentary identifying completeness as the source of the common point in the Baire nested-ball argument.

Uniform boundedness principle. Let $E$ be Banach, $F$ normed, and $(T_i)_{i\in I}$ any family in $\Lin{E}{F}$. If for every $x\in E$, $\sup_{i\in I}\norm{T_i x}<\infty$, then $\sup_{i\in I}\norm{T_i}<\infty$. The target need not be complete and the index set need not be countable. For an empty family the nonnegative supremum is understood to be zero.
Weak boundedness detects norm boundedness. Scalar field K is R or C. For any normed space $E$, a set $A\subset E$ is norm bounded exactly when $\{f(x):x\in A\}$ is bounded for every $f\in E'$.

Continuity of an existing pointwise limit. Let $E$ be Banach, $F$ normed, and $T_n\in\Lin{E}{F}$. Suppose that for every $x\in E$ the sequence $T_nx$ has a limit $Tx$ in $F$. Then $T$ is bounded linear, $\sup_n
orm{T_n}<\infty$, and $
orm{T}\leq\liminf_n
orm{T_n}$.

Pointwise convergence is often called strong operator convergence. It does not imply norm convergence. On $\ell^2$, the rank-one maps $P_nx=x_ne_n$ have norm $1$ and satisfy $\norm{P_nx}=\abs{x_n}\to0$ for each $x$, while $\norm{P_n-0}=1$ for all $n$.

Extending convergence from a dense set. Let $E$ be normed, $F$ Banach, $D\subset E$ dense, and $T_n\in\Lin{E}{F}$ with $\sup_n\norm{T_n}\leq M<\infty$. If $(T_nd)$ converges for every $d\in D$, then there is a bounded linear $T:E\to F$ such that $T_nx\to Tx$ for every $x\in E$ and $\norm{T}\leq M$. The domain need not be complete. If a bounded $T:E\to F$ is already given and convergence to $Td$ holds on $D$, then convergence to $Tx$ holds on all $E$ without completeness of $F$.

An incomplete domain. On $c_{00}$ with the supremum norm let $T_nx=n x_n$. Then $\norm{T_n}=n$, by testing $e_n$, but for every finitely supported $x$, $T_nx=0$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus pointwise boundedness on an incomplete normed domain need not give uniform norm bounds. Also $S_nx=\sum_{j\leq n}x_j$ has norm $n$ and converges pointwise on this domain to $Sx=\sum_jx_j$. The limit is unbounded, since its value on $\sum_{j=1}^n e_j$, a unit vector in the supremum norm, is $n$. Thus even continuity of a pointwise limit can fail without completeness of the domain.

Boundedness on a dense set is insufficient. On the Banach space $c_0$, again take $T_nx=n x_n$, with norm $n$. For each $x\in c_{00}$ the family is pointwise bounded, and $c_{00}$ is dense in $c_0$. Nevertheless for $x_j=j^{-1/2}$ one has $x\in c_0$ and $T_nx=\sqrt n\to\infty$. This identifies exactly the missing hypothesis: uniform boundedness requires pointwise boundedness at every point of the Banach domain. The dense-convergence theorem requires an independent uniform operator bound and cannot obtain it from dense-set boundedness alone.

Open mapping theorem. Let $E,F$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:E\to F$ be bounded linear and surjective. Then $T$ maps open sets to open sets. In particular, there is $c>0$ such that \[ B_F(0,c)\subset T(B_E(0,1)). \] Consequently there is $C>0$ such that every $y\in F$ has at least one preimage $x$ with $\norm{x}\leq C\norm{y}$. This selection is not asserted to be linear or continuous.
Bounded inverse theorem. A bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces has bounded linear inverse. If $B_F(0,c)\subset T(B_E(0,1))$, then $\norm{T^{-1}}\leq1/c$.

Closed graph theorem. Let $E,F$ be Banach spaces and let $T:E	o F$ be an everywhere-defined linear map. Then $T$ is bounded if and only if its graph $G(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in E\}$ is closed in $E	imes F$ with the product norm $
orm{(x,y)}=
orm{x}+
orm{y}$. Equivalently, if $x_n	o x$ and $Tx_n	o y$, then $y=Tx$.

A closed linear operator on a proper domain in a normed space need not be bounded in the ambient norm. Even an everywhere-defined closed linear map between normed spaces need not be bounded when one of the Banach completeness hypotheses is missing; the following explicit ℓ1/supremum-norm example demonstrates the latter statement.

Failure of inverse and graph conclusions without completeness. Take the vector space $\ell^1$ once with its usual Banach norm and once with the supremum norm. The identity from the first space to the second is a bounded bijection. Its inverse is unbounded, since a vector with its first $n$ entries equal to $1$ has supremum norm $1$ and $\ell^1$ norm $n$. The supremum-norm space is incomplete: truncations of $(1/j)_{j\geq1}$ are Cauchy in that norm, but their coordinate limit is not in $\ell^1$. The unbounded inverse nevertheless has closed graph. Indeed, if $x_n\to x$ in supremum norm and $x_n\to y$ in $\ell^1$ norm, the second convergence also holds in supremum norm, so $x=y$. This gives an everywhere-defined closed unbounded linear map from an incomplete domain to a Banach target.

Comparison of two complete norms. Let a vector space $E$ have two Banach norms $
orm{\cdot}_1$ and $
orm{\cdot}_2$. If $
orm{x}_2\leq C
orm{x}_1$ for all $x$ and some finite $C$, then also $
orm{x}_1\leq D
orm{x}_2$ for some finite $D$; thus the norms are equivalent.

Closed range and distance to the kernel. For $T\in\Lin{E}{F}$ between Banach spaces, the range is closed if and only if there is $C>0$ such that \[ \dist(x,\ker T)\leq C
orm{Tx} \qquad(x\in E). \] For an injective $T$ this reduces to boundedness below: $
orm{x}\leq C
orm{Tx}$. In particular a bounded below map from a Banach space into a normed space has closed range and a bounded inverse on its range.
Qualification of the closed-range estimate: distance control modulo the kernel asserts no bounded linear choice of coset representatives and no complementary-kernel conclusion.

Right and left inverse criteria. Let $E,F$ be Banach and $T\in\Lin{E}{F}$. If $T$ is surjective, it has a bounded right inverse $S:F\to E$ with $TS=\id_F$ if and only if $\ker T$ is complemented in $E$. If $T$ is injective, it has a bounded left inverse $S:F\to E$ with $ST=\id_E$ if and only if its range is closed and complemented in $F$.

For a bounded linear surjection between Banach spaces whose target is finite-dimensional, there is a bounded linear right inverse. For a bounded linear injection between Banach spaces whose domain is finite-dimensional, there is a bounded linear left inverse. These follow from the finite-dimensional complement conclusions; arbitrary closed Banach subspaces need not be complemented.
Motivation/source references for TVSs; the following separately stated definitions and theorems impose local convexity only as required.

Scalar field K is R or C. A topological vector space, abbreviated TVS, is a vector space with jointly continuous addition and scalar multiplication. We require it to be Hausdorff unless explicitly stated otherwise. A set $A$ is balanced if $\lambda A\subset A$ for $|\lambda|\leq1$, absorbing if every vector belongs to some positive multiple of $A$, and bounded if for every zero neighborhood $U$ there is $s>0$ with $A\subset tU$ whenever $t\geq s$. A locally convex space, or LCS, has a zero-neighborhood base consisting of convex sets. An F-space is a complete metrizable TVS; a Fr\'echet space is a locally convex F-space. Completeness means convergence of every Cauchy net for the translation uniformity: for every zero neighborhood $U$, the differences of sufficiently late terms lie in $U$.

TVSs are Hausdorff unless explicitly stated otherwise; boundedness and equicontinuity use zero neighborhoods. Every TVS has a base of balanced zero neighborhoods. An LCS has a base of absolutely convex neighborhoods. Every zero neighborhood is absorbing. Compact sets and convergent sequences are bounded. Closures, finite unions, finite sums and scalar multiples of bounded sets are bounded. A linear map is continuous if and only if it is continuous at zero; continuous linear maps take bounded sets to bounded sets.

Every Hausdorff vector topology on a finite-dimensional vector space is its usual Euclidean topology. Finite-dimensional subspaces of Hausdorff TVSs are closed. A locally compact Hausdorff TVS is finite dimensional.

Scalar field K is R or C; a separating seminorm family means that every nonzero vector has positive value for some seminorm. A separating family $(p_i)$ of seminorms determines a Hausdorff locally convex topology with basic neighborhoods $\{x:p_{i_j}(x)<\eps,\ 1\leq j\leq m\}$. Every Hausdorff LCS is obtained in this way from its continuous seminorms. A linear $T:E\to F$ between LCSs is continuous exactly when for each continuous target seminorm $q$ there are continuous source seminorms $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ and $C>0$ such that \[ q(Tx)\leq C\max_jp_j(x)\quad(x\in E). \]

Scalar field K is R or C. A Hausdorff TVS is metrizable if and only if it has a countable local base. It then has a translation-invariant metric with balanced balls. For an LCS the balls can also be chosen convex. A Hausdorff LCS is normable if and only if it has a bounded zero neighborhood.

For a closed subspace $M$ of a Hausdorff TVS $E$, the quotient topology on $E/M$ is Hausdorff and makes the quotient map $q$ continuous, open and linear. A map out of the quotient is continuous exactly when its composition with $q$ is continuous. Local convexity, a countable local base, and completeness in the metrizable case pass to this quotient. Complete subspaces of Hausdorff TVSs are closed. In particular closed subspaces and closed quotients of Fr\'echet spaces are Fr\'echet.

On a nonatomic measure space and $0<p<1$, set $d(f,g)=\int|f-g|^p$. This is a complete translation-invariant metric on $L^p$. Its continuous linear dual is zero, so a nonzero such space cannot be locally convex or normable.

Topological Banach--Steinhaus. TVSs are Hausdorff unless explicitly stated otherwise. Let $\mathcal A$ be continuous linear maps from a TVS $E$ into a TVS $F$. If the set of $x$ with bounded orbit $\{Tx:T\in\mathcal A\}$ is nonmeagre in $E$, it is all of $E$, and $\mathcal A$ is equicontinuous: for every zero neighborhood $V$ in $F$ there is a zero neighborhood $U$ in $E$ with $T(U)\subset V$ for all $T\in\mathcal A$. In particular pointwise bounded families on an F-space are equicontinuous.

Open mapping and closed graph for F-spaces. F-spaces are complete metrizable Hausdorff real or complex topological vector spaces, without a local-convexity requirement. A continuous linear surjection between F-spaces is open. Consequently a linear map between F-spaces is continuous whenever its graph is closed. Local convexity is unnecessary.

TVSs are Hausdorff real or complex topological vector spaces. Let $B:E\times F\to G$ be separately continuous and bilinear, where $E$ is an F-space and $F,G$ are TVSs. Then $B$ is sequentially jointly continuous. If $F$ is metrizable, $B$ is jointly continuous.

An equivalent algebra norm. If a Banach space has an associative separately continuous bilinear multiplication, it admits an equivalent submultiplicative norm. If it has an identity and the algebra is nonzero, such a norm may be chosen with $\|1\|=1$. In the zero algebra the identity is zero and has norm zero; the submultiplicative renorming conclusion still holds.

Seminorm Hahn--Banach. Let $p$ be a seminorm on a real or complex vector space and let $f$ be a linear functional on a subspace with $|f|\leq p$. It extends to a linear $F$ on the whole space satisfying $|F|\leq p$. Every continuous linear functional on a subspace of an LCS extends continuously to the whole space. In a Hausdorff LCS the continuous dual separates points.

Compact--closed separation. TVSs are Hausdorff unless explicitly stated otherwise; LCS means locally convex TVS. Disjoint nonempty convex sets in a TVS can be separated by a nonzero continuous real linear functional if one is open. In an LCS, if $K$ is compact convex and $C$ is closed convex, disjoint and nonempty, there is a continuous real linear $f$ with $\max_K f<\inf_C f$. For complex spaces use real parts of continuous complex-linear functionals.

Dual-pair bipolar theorem. A separated dual pair consists of real or complex vector spaces with a bilinear scalar pairing separating points on both sides; σ denotes the weak topology of that pairing, and aconv includes zero. For a separated dual pair $(E,F)$ define $A^\circ=\{f\in F:|f(x)|\leq1\ (x\in A)\}$. Then \[ A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{aconv}(A)}^{\sigma(E,F)}. \] Double annihilators are the corresponding weak closures of linear spans. Two locally convex topologies with the same continuous dual have the same closed convex sets.

Alaoglu for neighborhood polars. E′ denotes the continuous scalar-linear dual of the real or complex TVS E, σ(E′,E) the evaluation topology, U°={f∈E′: |f(u)|≤1 for all u∈U}. If $U$ is a zero neighborhood in a TVS $E$, its polar $U^\circ\subset E'$ is compact for $\sigma(E',E)$. Every equicontinuous subset of $E'$ is contained in such a polar. In particular the closed dual unit ball of every normed space is weak-star compact, without requiring completeness of its predual.
Fréchet means complete metrizable locally convex Hausdorff real or complex TVS. The closed convex hull of a compact subset of a Fr\'echet space is compact.

Barycenters and continuous compact integrands. TVSs are over R or C; E′ is the continuous scalar-linear dual. Let $Q$ be compact Hausdorff, $\mu$ a regular probability measure, and $f:Q\to E$ continuous into a TVS whose dual separates points. If $C=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f(Q)$ is compact, there is a unique $b\in C$ satisfying $\ell(b)=\int_Q\ell(f)\,d\mu$ for every $\ell\in E'$. Every point of the compact closed convex hull of a compact set $K$ is the barycenter of a regular probability measure on $K$. In a Banach space $\|b\|\leq\int\|f\|\,d\mu$.

Weak holomorphy in Fr\'echet spaces. E′ is the continuous complex-linear dual; an entire weakly bounded map in the last clause is holomorphic on all C with bounded image under every dual functional. Let $E$ be a complex Fr\'echet space and $f:\Omega\to E$ a map on an open subset of $\C$. If $\ell\circ f$ is holomorphic for every $\ell\in E'$, then $f$ is continuous and holomorphic, has locally convergent Taylor series in every defining seminorm, and satisfies vector-valued Cauchy formulas. An entire weakly bounded map into any complex TVS with separating dual is constant.

Weak-topology working conventions: E is a real or complex normed space, E′ is its scalar-linear continuous dual, and compactness/convergence may require nets rather than sequences. The mathematical constructions are separately inventoried.

Weak topology of a dual pair. Let $X,Y$ be vector spaces with a bilinear pairing $\langle y,x\rangle$ separating points of $X$. The topology $\sigma(X,Y)$ is the coarsest topology making all maps $x\mapsto\langle y,x\rangle$, $y\in Y$, continuous. A basis of neighborhoods of $x_0$ consists of \[ \{x:|\langle y_j,x-x_0\rangle|<\eps, 1\leq j\leq m\}, \quad m<\infty,\quad\eps>0. \] Taking arbitrary unions of these finite intersections constructs the topology. For $X=E$, $Y=E'$ and $\langle f,x\rangle=f(x)$ this is the weak topology on $E$.

Hausdorffness and the continuous scalar tests. For a bilinear pairing of scalar vector spaces X,Y which separates points of X, with σ(X,Y) the initial topology for x↦<y,x>: The topology $\sigma(X,Y)$ is Hausdorff and locally convex, and addition and scalar multiplication are continuous. A linear functional on $X$ is continuous for $\sigma(X,Y)$ if and only if it belongs to the linear span of the pairing functionals. In particular the continuous linear functionals on $(E,\sigma(E,E'))$ are exactly $E'$.

Weak-star topology. Let E be a real or complex normed space and E′ its continuous scalar-linear dual. On $E'$ the weak-star topology $\sigma(E',E)$ is generated by $f\mapsto f(x)$ for $x\in E$. A basic neighborhood of $f_0$ is \[ \{f:|(f-f_0)(x_j)|<\eps, 1\leq j\leq m\}. \] The weak topology of the normed space $E'$ itself is $\sigma(E',E'')$. Thus \[ \sigma(E',E)\ \subset\ \sigma(E',E'')\ \subset\ \text{the norm topology on }E'. \] A specified predual means a normed space together with a specified identification of its dual with the space under study. It supplies the evaluation tests, and hence the particular weak-star topology.

When weak and weak-star agree. Let E be a real or complex normed space and J_E(x)(f)=f(x). The weak and weak-star topologies on $E'$ agree if and only if $J_E:E\to E''$ is surjective. Every weak-star continuous linear functional on $E'$ is evaluation at one $x\in E$.

Evaluation criterion for convergence. Let E,F be real or complex normed spaces with their continuous scalar-linear duals; σ denotes weak pairing topology. A net $(x_\alpha)$ converges to $x$ in $\sigma(E,E')$ if and only if $f(x_\alpha)\to f(x)$ for every $f\in E'$. A net $(f_\alpha)$ converges weak-star to $f$ if and only if $f_\alpha(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in E$. Norm convergence implies the corresponding weak convergence. Bounded linear maps are weak-to-weak continuous, and their transposes are weak-star to weak-star continuous.

Three different notions of convergence. The unit vectors $e_n$ of $\ell^2$ converge weakly to zero: Riesz represents each functional by $y\in\ell^2$ and its values on $e_n$ are $\overline{y_n}\to0$. Their norms are all $1$. In $\ell^\infty=(\ell^1)'$ let $u_n(k)=1$ for $k\geq n$ and $0$ for $k<n$. Then $u_n\to0$ in $\sigma(\ell^\infty,\ell^1)$ because $|\sum_{k\geq n}a_k|\leq\sum_{k\geq n}|a_k|\to0$. On the subspace of convergent scalar sequences the limit functional $L(a)=\lim_k a_k$ is continuous of norm $1$. Hahn--Banach extends it to $\ell^\infty$, and this extension has $L(u_n)=1$. Thus the same sequence does not converge weakly to zero in $\ell^\infty$. Finally in finite dimension all three topologies coincide: finitely many coordinate functionals control the norm, and the canonical bidual map is surjective by the finite-dimensional dimension formula.

Bounds for weakly convergent sequences. All duals are continuous scalar-linear duals over R or C. If a sequence $x_n$ converges weakly to $x$ in a normed space, then $\sup_n
orm{x_n}<\infty$ and $
orm x\leq\liminf_n
orm{x_n}$. If $E$ is Banach and $f_n	o f$ in $\sigma(E',E)$, then $\sup_n
orm{f_n}<\infty$ and $
orm f\leq\liminf_n
orm{f_n}$. Every weakly compact subset of a normed space is norm bounded.

The completeness and net qualifications. The Banach assumption for the weak-star sequence bound cannot simply be omitted. On $c_{00}$ with the $\ell^1$ norm, $f_n(x)=n x_n$ is continuous, has norm $n$, and converges pointwise to zero, because each $x$ has finite support. Also a convergent general net need not be bounded as a whole: its indices outside a chosen final segment may contain arbitrarily large values. The preceding sequence proof uses boundedness of every entire scalar sequence; it is not a statement that arbitrary weakly convergent nets are globally bounded.

Norm is weakly lower semicontinuous. Let E be a real or complex normed space; weak means σ(E,E′) and weak-star means σ(E′,E). Each closed norm ball is weakly closed; each closed dual norm ball is weak-star closed. More generally, a norm lower semicontinuous convex function $\Phi:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is weakly lower semicontinuous.

Weak and norm closures of a convex set. All spaces are normed over R or C and duals are continuous scalar-linear. For every convex subset $C$ of a normed space, $\cl^{\sigma(E,E')}C=\cl^{\norm\cdot}C$. In particular a norm closed linear subspace is weakly closed, and the weak topology induced on a subspace $M$ equals $\sigma(M,M')$ with its inherited norm.

Mazur's lemma with tail combinations. Let E be any real or complex normed space and x_n,x∈E. If $x_n\to x$ weakly, there are integers $m_n\geq n$ and real numbers $a_{n,j}\geq0$, $n\leq j\leq m_n$, with $\sum_{j=n}^{m_n}a_{n,j}=1$, such that $y_n=\sum_{j=n}^{m_n}a_{n,j}x_j$ converges to $x$ in norm.
Dual-ball compactness uses any real or complex normed predual, including incomplete ones; subsequence conclusions occur only after metrization. This is scope commentary for the following results.
Compact products of scalar disks. If $(D_i)_{i\in I}$ are closed bounded scalar disks centered at zero, their product is compact in its product topology.

Banach--Alaoglu. Let E be any real or complex normed space; its completeness is not assumed. The closed unit ball $B_{E'}=\{f\in E':\norm f\leq1\}$ is compact in $\sigma(E',E)$. Every closed dual ball of finite radius is weak-star compact.

Proof-dependency commentary: the scalar-product lemma supplies the compactness needed for Alaoglu; scalar boundedness makes the linear limit continuous even when E is incomplete. This introduces no additional result beyond those separately stated.

Weak-star metrization for a separable predual. Let E be a real or complex normed space, with E′ its continuous scalar-linear dual. If $E$ is separable, choose a sequence $(x_n)$ dense in its closed unit ball. On any norm-bounded subset $A\subset E'$, the metric \[ d(f,g)=\sum_{n\geq1}2^{-n}\min\{1,|(f-g)(x_n)|\} \] induces the relative weak-star topology. When $E=\{0\}$ the dual is a singleton, and the zero distance on that singleton is a metric.
Weak-star subsequences. Let E be a real or complex normed space. If $E$ is separable and $(f_n)$ is norm bounded in $E'$, some subsequence converges in $\sigma(E',E)$ to an element of $E'$.

The weak topology as an induced weak-star topology. Let E be any real or complex normed space, J_E(x)(f)=f(x), with continuous scalar-linear duals. The canonical isometry $J_E:E\to E''$ is a homeomorphism from $(E,\sigma(E,E'))$ onto its image with the topology induced by $\sigma(E'',E')$. In particular $x_\alpha\to x$ weakly if and only if $J_Ex_\alpha\to J_Ex$ weak-star in $E''$.

The dual ball detects predual separability. For any normed space $E$, if $B_{E'}$ is weak-star metrizable, then $E$ is separable. Hence $B_{E'}$ is weak-star metrizable if and only if $E$ is separable.

Nonmetrizable compactness and two separabilities. For an uncountable set $I$, the space $\ell^2(I)$ is nonseparable by its uncountable orthonormal system. Its dual unit ball is weak-star compact by Alaoglu and is not weak-star metrizable by the proposition. Thus the compactness proof cannot in general be read as a metric subsequence argument. Separability of $E$ and norm separability of $E'$ are different: $\ell^1$ is separable, but $(\ell^1)'=\ell^\infty$ is nonseparable. Indeed its uncountable family of $\{0,1\}$-valued sequences has pairwise distance $1$. Nevertheless the closed unit ball of $\ell^\infty$ is metrizable for its specified weak-star topology $\sigma(\ell^\infty,\ell^1)$.

For every infinite-dimensional real or complex Banach space E, the weak-star topology σ(E′,E) on its entire continuous dual is not first countable, hence is not metrizable. Completeness matters: on c00 the weak-star topology on its continuous dual is generated by the coordinate tests and is a metrizable subspace of the countable scalar product. The bounded-part metrization theorem therefore need not extend to the whole dual.

Reflexivity chapter conventions: reflexivity refers to surjectivity of the canonical isometric evaluation J_E, not to an arbitrary abstract isomorphism with E′′. The definition and counterexamples are separately inventoried.

Reflexive space. Let E be a real or complex normed space, J_E(x)(f)=f(x). A normed space $E$ is reflexive when $J_E:E\to E''$ is surjective. It is then automatically Banach, since it is isometric to the Banach space $E''$. In the compactness characterizations below we state the Banach hypothesis explicitly.

Goldstine's density theorem. B_E and B_{E′′} are closed unit balls, and J_E(x)(f)=f(x); scalar field R or C. For every normed space $E$, $J_E(B_E)$ is dense in $B_{E''}$ for $\sigma(E'',E')$ relative to that ball.

Reflexivity and the weakly compact ball. B_E denotes the closed unit ball and reflexivity means surjectivity of J_E(x)(f)=f(x); scalar field R or C. For a Banach space $E$, the following are equivalent: $E$ is reflexive; $B_E$ is weakly compact; and every norm bounded weakly closed subset of $E$ is weakly compact.

Reflexivity is preserved by Banach isomorphisms. If $T:E\to F$ is a bounded bijection of Banach spaces with bounded inverse, then $E$ is reflexive if and only if $F$ is. In particular equivalent Banach norms have the same reflexivity property.

Subspace, quotient and dual stability. Scalar field K is R or C; quotients carry the distance norm and reflexivity is canonical. Let $E$ be Banach and $M\subset E$ a closed linear subspace. If $E$ is reflexive, then $M$ and $E/M$ are reflexive. Also $E$ is reflexive if and only if $E'$ is reflexive.

A separable dual forces a separable space. Duals are continuous scalar-linear duals over R or C. If the continuous dual of a normed space $X$ is norm separable, then $X$ is separable. Consequently a separable reflexive Banach space has a norm-separable dual.

Weak subsequences in a reflexive Banach space. Weak convergence is convergence against every continuous scalar-linear functional; scalar field R or C. Every norm-bounded sequence in a reflexive Banach space has a weakly convergent subsequence. No separability assumption on the original space is needed.

Uniformly convex norm. Let E be a real or complex normed space. A normed space is uniformly convex if for each $0<\eps\leq2$ there is $\delta>0$ such that \[ 
orm x,
orm y\leq1,\quad
orm{x-y}\geq\eps \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left\| rac{x+y}{2}ight\|\leq1-\delta. \] The condition is vacuous when the indicated pairs do not exist. It implies strict convexity of the unit sphere.
Milman--Pettis. Every uniformly convex Banach space is reflexive.

Hilbert and $L^p$ uniform convexity. Hilbert and Lp spaces may be real or complex; no σ-finiteness or separability is assumed. Every Hilbert space is uniformly convex, with $\delta=1-\sqrt{1-\eps^2/4}$ for $0<\eps\leq2$. For every positive measure $\mu$ and $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(\mu,\K)$ is uniformly convex. The norms of $\ell^1$ and $\ell^\infty$ are not uniformly convex.
Weak convergence and convergence of norms. Scalar field K is R or C. In a uniformly convex normed space, if $x_n\to x$ weakly and $\limsup_n\norm{x_n}\leq\norm x$, then $x_n\to x$ in norm.

Reflexive and nonreflexive examples. All spaces and continuous duals are real or complex as indicated; reflexivity is surjectivity of the canonical bidual map. Every Hilbert space and every $L^p(\mu,\K)$ with $1<p<\infty$ and arbitrary positive $\mu$ is reflexive. The spaces $c_0$, $\ell^1$ and $\ell^\infty$ are not reflexive.

Attainment by weak compactness. Scalar field K is R or C; proper excludes −∞ and requires at least one finite value. Let $E$ be reflexive Banach, $C\subset E$ nonempty and weakly closed, and $\Phi:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ proper and weakly lower semicontinuous. Suppose its sublevel sets are norm bounded; it suffices that $\Phi(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\in C$, $\norm x\to\infty$, or that $C$ is bounded. Then $\Phi$ attains a finite minimum. In particular the conclusion applies when $C$ is norm closed and convex and $\Phi$ is the restriction of a norm lower semicontinuous convex function on $E$ with these bounded-sublevel hypotheses.

Norm attainment and best approximation. Scalar field K is R or C. Every continuous linear functional on a reflexive Banach space attains its norm on the closed unit ball. In a uniformly convex Banach space every nonempty closed convex set has a unique nearest point to each specified vector.
Motivation/source references for advanced weak compactness; completeness is not to be silently omitted in the stated convex-hull and bounded-dual theorems.

A countable test family on a separable subspace. Let $Y$ be a separable subspace of a normed space $E$. There is a sequence $(f_j)$ in $B_{E'}$ which separates points of $Y$. On every weakly compact subset of $Y$ the weak topology is metrizable. A weakly convergent sequence in $E$ is norm bounded.

Eberlein--\v Smulian. For a subset $A$ of a normed space $E$, the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item its weak closure is weakly compact; \item every sequence in $A$ has a subsequence weakly convergent in $E$; \item every sequence in $A$ has a weak cluster point in $E$. \end{enumerate} In particular, a weakly closed set is weakly compact if and only if it is weakly sequentially compact. On a weakly closed set these conditions are also equivalent to countable compactness for the weak topology. Thus defining relative countable compactness by countable compactness of the weak closure gives the same relative notion as condition 1.

Sequential density inside a weakly compact closure. Let $A$ be a relatively weakly compact subset of a normed space. Every point of its weak closure is the weak limit of a sequence of points of $A$. In particular a weakly compact set, with its weak topology, has this closure-by-sequences property. This does not assert it for arbitrary weakly star compact dual sets.

Krein's compact convex-hull theorem. If $K$ is weakly compact in a Banach space $E$, then $\overline{\operatorname{conv}}K$ and $\overline{\operatorname{aconv}}K$ are weakly compact. Here the closures may be taken in norm or weakly; the two closures of a convex set agree.

Weak sequential completeness and the Schur property. In $\ell^1$, weak convergence of sequences implies norm convergence. The space $\ell^1$ is weakly sequentially complete. The spaces $c_0$ and $C[0,1]$ are not weakly sequentially complete.

Compact dual sets over a separable TVS. TVSs are Hausdorff over R or C and the dual is continuous scalar-linear; weak-star means the evaluation topology. If $E$ is a separable TVS, every weakly star compact subset $K$ of its continuous dual is metrizable.

Metrizability of bounded weak topologies. For a normed space $E$, the weak topology on $B_E$ is metrizable if and only if $E'$ is norm separable. The weak star topology on $B_{E'}$ is metrizable if and only if $E$ is norm separable.

An incomplete compact-hull obstruction. In $c_{00}$ with the $\ell^1$ norm the set $K=\{0\}\cup\{e_n/n:n\ge1\}$ is norm compact. Its closed convex hull in $c_{00}$ is not weakly compact. Indeed the convex combinations $y_m=\sum_{n=1}^m2^{-n}e_n/n$ belong to it (use the remaining weight at zero). Their coordinates converge to $(2^{-n}/n)_n$, which has infinite support. No subsequence can converge weakly in $c_{00}$, since coordinate evaluations are continuous. Eberlein--\v Smulian therefore rules out weak compactness. They are also a norm Cauchy sequence without a limit in $c_{00}$, so the hull is not norm compact.

The bounded weak star topology. All duals are continuous scalar-linear over R or C; B_{E′} is the closed unit ball. Let $E$ be a normed space. The seminorms $p_{(x_n)}(f)=\sup_n|f(x_n)|$, where $x_n\to0$ in norm, define a Hausdorff locally convex topology $\beta$ on $E'$. It is the finest topology which induces the weak star topology on every norm bounded subset of $E'$. A set $C\subset E'$ is $\beta$-closed if and only if $C\cap rB_{E'}$ is weakly star closed for every $r>0$. If $E$ is Banach, the continuous linear functionals for $\beta$ are exactly the evaluations $f\mapsto f(x)$, $x\in E$.

Krein--\v Smulian. Let $E$ be Banach and $C\subset E'$ convex. Then $C$ is weakly star closed if and only if $C\cap rB_{E'}$ is weakly star closed for every $r>0$. A linear subspace $M\subset E'$ is weakly star closed if and only if $M\cap B_{E'}$ is weakly star closed. If $E$ is separable, a convex subset of $E'$ is weakly star closed if and only if it is weakly star sequentially closed.

Why completeness is indispensable. Let $E$ be an incomplete normed space, regard $E$ as a dense proper subspace of its completion $\widehat E$, and choose $z\in\widehat E\setminus E$. The hyperplane $M=\{f\in E':\widehat f(z)=0\}$ has weakly star closed intersection with every dual ball but is not weakly star closed in $E'$. Indeed, on each bounded ball evaluation at $z$ is the uniform limit of evaluations at points of $E$. If $M$ were weakly star closed, its nonzero defining linear functional would be a scalar multiple of an evaluation at some $x\in E$ (factor through a finite family of tests, or apply separation to the hyperplane). This would give $z\in E$ because $E'$ separates points of $\widehat E$, a contradiction.

Ekeland's variational principle. Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space and $F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and not identically infinite. If $F(x_0)\le\inf_XF+\alpha r$ with $\alpha,r>0$, there exists $\bar x$ such that $d(\bar x,x_0)\le r$, $F(\bar x)\le F(x_0)$, and \[ F(y)>F(\bar x)-\alpha d(y,\bar x)\qquad(y\ne\bar x). \]

Bishop--Phelps. Let $E$ be a real or complex Banach space and $C\subset E$ a nonempty closed convex set. If $f\in E'$ is bounded above in real part on $C$, then for every $\alpha>0$ there are $x\in C$ and $g\in E'$ with $\|g-f\|\le\alpha$ and $\operatorname{Re}g(y)\le\operatorname{Re}g(x)$ for every $y\in C$. The support points of $C$ are dense in its boundary. In particular, norm-attaining functionals are norm dense in $E'$.

Preserving a bounded separation. Let E be a real or complex Banach space. Suppose $C$ is nonempty, closed and convex, $A$ is bounded, $\|f\|=1$, and $\sup_C\operatorname{Re}f<\inf_A\operatorname{Re}f$. For every $\eps>0$ there are a support point $x\in C$ and $g\in E'$ such that $\|g\|=1$, $\|g-f\|<\eps$, and $\operatorname{Re}g(x)=\sup_C\operatorname{Re}g<\inf_A\operatorname{Re}g$.
James chapter proof-route and citation commentary; its independently stated convex-block lemma, witness lemma and attainment theorem remain mathematical obligations.

Let (f_n) be a norm-bounded sequence in the continuous dual of a real normed space E. Define L(f_n)={w∈E′:w(x)≤limsup_n f_n(x) for all x∈E} and V(f_n)={(g_n):g_n∈conv{f_j:j≥n} for every n}. Then L(f_n) is nonempty; every w∈L(f_n) satisfies liminf_n f_n(x)≤w(x)≤limsup_n f_n(x) for all x. If (g_n)∈V(f_n), then V(g_n)⊂V(f_n) and L(g_n)⊂L(f_n). Every increasingly indexed subsequence of (f_n) belongs to V(f_n).

James's convex-block lemma. For a bounded sequence h_n∈E′ in a real normed space define L(h_n)={w∈E′: ∀x∈E, w(x)≤limsup_n h_n(x)} and V(h_n)={(k_n): ∀n, k_n∈conv{h_j:j≥n}}. Let $A$ be a nonempty balanced subset of $B_E$ in a real normed space. Write $|h|_A=\sup_{x\in A}|h(x)|$. Suppose $0<\theta<1$, $f_n\in B_{E'}$, and \[ |f-w|_A\ge\theta \quad\bigl(f\in\operatorname{conv}\{f_n:n\ge1\},\ w\in L(f_n)\bigr). \] For any positive numbers $\beta_n$ with $\sum_n\beta_n=1$, there exist $g_n\in B_{E'}$ and $\theta\le a\le2$ such that, for every $w\in L(g_n)$, \[ \left|\sum_{j=1}^\infty\beta_j(g_j-w)\right|_A=a, \qquad \left|\sum_{j=1}^n\beta_j(g_j-w)\right|_A <a\left(1-\theta\sum_{j>n}\beta_j\right)\quad(n\ge1). \] All infinite sums here converge in the norm of $E'$.

A separable witness to failure of compactness. Here |f|_A=sup_{x∈A}|f(x)|, all balls are closed, and duals are continuous scalar-linear. Let $A\subset B_E$ be nonempty, norm separable and weakly closed in a Banach space. If $A$ is not weakly compact, there exist $0<\theta<1$ and $f_n\in B_{E'}$ such that $f_n(x)\to0$ for every $x\in A$ and $|f|_A\ge\theta$ for every $f\in\operatorname{conv}\{f_n\}$. This assertion holds over either scalar field.

James's weak compactness theorem. Let $A$ be a nonempty weakly closed subset of a real or complex Banach space $E$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is weakly compact; \item for every $f\in E'$, the finite supremum $\sup_{x\in A}|f(x)|$ is attained at a point of $A$; \item for every continuous real linear functional $u$ on the underlying real space, $\sup_A|u|$ is finite and attained; \item for every such $u$, $\sup_Au$ is finite and attained. \end{enumerate} Consequently $E$ is reflexive if and only if every member of $E'$ attains its norm on $B_E$.

\begin{remark}[What the closedness hypothesis does]
\label{fa2:p1:james-closedness}
In a nonzero finite-dimensional normed space, every scalar linear
functional attains its absolute supremum on the unit sphere, but this does not turn an
arbitrary norm closed bounded nonconvex subset of an infinite
dimensional space into a weakly closed set.  The theorem explicitly
requires weak closedness; for convex norm closed sets Hahn--Banach
supplies it.  In particular its commonly used convex form says that
a nonempty norm closed bounded convex set is weakly compact if
every continuous real linear functional attains its supremum there.
The completeness of $E$ is used when $J_YY$ is declared norm closed
in the witness lemma.  Removing it destroys that step, and the
attainment criterion is not being asserted for incomplete spaces.
\end{remark}
Basis chapter scope: E is a real or complex Banach space unless explicitly stated; Hamel, Schauder and orthogonal expansions are different notions.

Schauder basis and its algebraic coordinate maps. Let E be a real or complex Banach space, unless explicitly stated otherwise. A sequence of nonzero vectors $(e_n)_{n\geq1}$ is a Schauder basis of $E$ if for each $x\in E$ there is a unique scalar sequence $(a_n(x))$ with $x=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=1}^Na_n(x)e_n$ in norm. Write $e_n'(x)=a_n(x)$ and $P_Nx=\sum_{n=1}^Ne_n'(x)e_n$, with $P_0=0$. At this stage these maps are algebraic linear maps: uniqueness and addition of convergent series prove linearity, without any continuity assumption. A finite basis has the analogous finite expansion; for a list of length $d$ put $P_N=P_d=I$ when $N\geq d$. The empty basis is allowed for the zero space, with every $P_N=0$.

Continuity of Schauder coordinates. All spaces are real or complex; finite and empty bases use the conventions P_N=I after the last coordinate and P_N=0 in the zero space. If $(e_n)$ is a Schauder basis of a Banach space, all coordinate functionals $e_n'$ and partial-sum maps $P_N$ are bounded. The basis norm \[ \norm x_b=\sup_{N\geq0}\norm{P_Nx} \] is a complete norm equivalent to the original norm.

Partial-sum projections and basis bounds. Let E be a real or complex Banach space with a Schauder basis and coordinate functionals e_n′; P_Nx=Σ_{n≤N}e_n′(x)e_n and P_0=0, with finite and empty basis conventions. For a Schauder basis, $P_NP_M=P_{\min(N,M)}$, $P_Nx	o x$, and $K=\sup_N

e0$, $K\geq1$. For finitely supported scalars and $m\leq N$, \[ \left\|\sum_{n=1}^m a_ne_night\| \leq K\left\|\sum_{n=1}^N a_ne_night\|, \quad |e_n'(x)|

A useful basis criterion. Let $(e_n)$ be a sequence of nonzero vectors in a Banach space whose linear span is dense. It is a Schauder basis if and only if some $C<\infty$ satisfies \[ \left\|\sum_{n=1}^m a_ne_n\right\| \leq C\left\|\sum_{n=1}^N a_ne_n\right\| \quad(m\leq N) \] for every finite scalar family.

The standard bases. The sequence spaces are over R or C. The unit vectors form a Schauder basis of $c_0$ and of $\ell^p$ for $1\leq p<\infty$, with basis constant $1$. Their closed span in $\ell^\infty$ is only $c_0$, and $\ell^\infty$ has no countable Schauder basis at all.

A Hamel basis uses only finite expansions. The vector (1/n)∈ℓ² has no finite expansion in the unit vectors, so the unit orthonormal Schauder basis is not a Hamel basis. A countable complete orthonormal system is an unconditional Schauder basis; an uncountable complete orthonormal system gives convergent finite-subset nets rather than an ordered Schauder sequence. The coordinate-continuity theorem requires the displayed Banach hypothesis.

Unconditional series and basis. Series and bases are in a real or complex Banach space E unless specified otherwise. A series $\sum_n v_n$ is unconditionally convergent if the net $\sum_{n\in F}v_n$, over finite $F\subset\N$, converges in norm. A Schauder basis is unconditional if each of its expansions is unconditionally convergent. This is stronger than convergence in the specified natural order.

Tail, rearrangement and subseries criteria. For a series in a Banach space the following are equivalent: unconditional convergence; the condition \[ \forall\eps>0\ \exists N\ \forall F\subset\{N+1,N+2,\ldots\} \text{ finite},\quad\left\|\sum_{n\in F}v_n\right\|<\eps; \] convergence of every subseries; and convergence of every permuted series. All rearrangements then have the same sum. Absolutely norm-summable series are unconditional; the converse fails even in Hilbert space.

Coordinate subspace projections for an unconditional basis. Let E be a real or complex Banach space with unconditional Schauder basis (e_n) and continuous coordinate functionals e_n′. If $(e_n)$ is unconditional, for every $A\subset\N$ the map $P_Ax=\sum_{n\in A}e_n'(x)e_n$ is a bounded projection onto $\clspan\{e_n:n\in A\}$. There is one constant $C$ with $\norm{P_A}\leq C$ for every $A$. The standard bases of $c_0$ and $\ell^p$, $p<\infty$, are unconditional, as are countable complete Hilbert orthonormal systems.

Bounded projections and topological sums. For a closed subspace $M$ of a Banach space $E$, being the range of a bounded projection is equivalent to the existence of a closed subspace $N$ such that $E=M\oplus N$ algebraically. The projection is then the coordinate map $m+n\mapsto m$. Every closed Hilbert subspace is complemented, and every finite-dimensional or closed finite-codimensional Banach subspace is complemented.

Elementary failures of algebraic intuition. The dense proper subspace $c_{00}\subset\ell^2$ cannot be the range of a bounded projection, since that range would be closed. Even a projection onto a closed one-dimensional range can be unbounded if its complementary kernel is chosen only algebraically: extend the independent vectors $e_n$ to a Hamel basis of $\ell^2$, define an algebraic functional $f$ by $f(e_n)=n$ and arbitrary (say zero) values on the added basis elements, and put $Px=f(x)e_1$. Then $P^2=P$ because $f(e_1)=1$, but $\norm{Pe_n}=n$ while $\norm{e_n}=1$. Its range also has the usual bounded orthogonal projection; complementation concerns the existence of a bounded split, not boundedness of every algebraic split.

Basis truncations approximate uniformly on compact sets. Let E be a real or complex Banach space with a Schauder basis and partial-sum maps P_N. For a Schauder basis, $P_N\to I$ uniformly on every norm-compact subset of $E$. Consequently if $T:X\to E$ is compact, with $X$ normed, then $P_NT$ has finite rank and $\norm{P_NT-T}\to0$.
Motivation and source references for basic sequences, dual bases and the real James space; following separately stated assertions define mathematical scope.

Equivalent basic sequences and small perturbations. A basic sequence means a Schauder basis for its closed linear span; equivalent sequences have a bounded linear isomorphism of their closed spans carrying corresponding terms to each other. All spaces here are Banach over R or C. Basic sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are equivalent if and only if there are $0<c\leq C<\infty$ such that \[ c\Big\|\sum a_nx_n\Big\|\leq\Big\|\sum a_ny_n\Big\| \leq C\Big\|\sum a_nx_n\Big\| \] for all finitely supported scalar sequences. If $(x_n)$ has basis constant $K$ and the two sequences lie in one Banach space, the condition \[ 2K\sum_n\frac{\|y_n-x_n\|}{\|x_n\|}<1 \] suffices for equivalence. A Banach space with a basis has an equivalent basis contained in any prescribed dense subset.

Existence and weakly null selection. For every $M>1$, every infinite-dimensional Banach space contains a normalized basic sequence with basis constant at most $M$. Every weakly null sequence which does not tend to zero in norm has a basic subsequence.

Monotone and multiplier norms. Let E be a real or complex Banach space with Schauder basis (x_n), P_n its initial projections and x_n′ its coordinate functionals. For a basis $(x_n)$ the equivalent norm $\|x\|_b=\sup_n\|P_nx\|$ makes it monotone. For an unconditional basis, $\|x\|_u=\sup_{|a_n|\leq1}\|\sum a_nx_n'(x)x_n\|$ is finite, equivalent, and makes every coordinate multiplier of modulus at most one contractive. On a real space this is a lattice norm for the coordinate order. If $\|x_n\|=1$, coordinatewise multiplication makes the space, with this latter norm, a commutative Banach algebra without identity in infinite dimension.

A Banach space contains no subspace isomorphic to $c_0$ if and only if every weakly unconditionally Cauchy series is unconditionally norm convergent. Here weakly unconditionally Cauchy means $\sum_n|f(x_n)|<\infty$ for every $f\in E'$.
Orlicz--Pettis. If every subseries of $\sum x_n$ converges weakly in a Banach space, then the series converges unconditionally in norm.

Shrinking and boundedly complete bases. Let E be a real or complex Banach space with Schauder basis (x_n) and continuous coordinate functionals x_n′. For a basis $(x_n)$ of $E$ let $F=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{x_n'\}$ in $E'$. The coordinate functionals form a basic sequence. The basis is shrinking precisely when $F=E'$, equivalently $\|f|_{\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{x_j:j>n\}}\|\to0$ for every $f\in E'$. It is boundedly complete if every scalar sequence with bounded initial sums $\sum_{j\leq n}a_jx_j$ has a convergent series. The following hold: \begin{enumerate} \item $(x_n')$ is boundedly complete in $F$ if and only if $(x_n)$ is shrinking; \item $(x_n')$ is shrinking in $F$ if and only if $(x_n)$ is boundedly complete; \item $E$ is reflexive if and only if its basis is both shrinking and boundedly complete. \end{enumerate}

For a Banach space with an unconditional basis, that basis is shrinking if and only if no $\ell^1$ embeds, and boundedly complete if and only if no $c_0$ embeds. Consequently such a space is reflexive if and only if it contains neither $c_0$ nor $\ell^1$.

Function spaces are over R or C; dyadic hats are the usual normalized piecewise linear midpoint hats ordered by successive dyadic subdivision, and Haar functions are constant with opposite signs on the two halves of each dyadic interval. The dyadic hat functions, together with $1,t$, form the classical Schauder basis of $C[0,1]$. The Haar functions, ordered by successive dyadic subdivisions and preceded by $1$, form a basis of $L^p[0,1]$ for $1\leq p<\infty$. The former basis and the Haar basis in $L^1$ are conditional. The Haar basis is unconditional when $1<p<\infty$.
The closed subspace $c_0$ of $\ell^\infty$ is not complemented. Its canonical image is not complemented in $c_0''$, and $c_0$ is not isomorphic to the dual of any normed space.

For a real null sequence $a=(a_n)$ define \[ \|a\|_J=2^{-1/2}\sup_{m\geq2,\,p_1<\cdots<p_m} \left(\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}(a_{p_j}-a_{p_{j+1}})^2 +(a_{p_m}-a_{p_1})^2\right)^{1/2}. \] The real James space $J$ consists of the null sequences for which this is finite. The cyclic last difference is part of this particular norm; replacing it without analysis would lose the isometric statement below.

J denotes the real null sequences with cyclic-variation norm ||a||_J=2^(−1/2) sup_{m≥2,p_1<⋯<p_m}(Σ_{j<m}(a_{p_j}−a_{p_{j+1}})²+(a_{p_m}−a_{p_1})²)^(1/2). $J$ is a real Banach space. Its unit vectors form a normalized monotone shrinking basis. The canonical image $J_JJ$ has codimension one in $J''$, but $J$ and $J''$ are isometrically isomorphic by a different map. Consequently an abstract isometry onto the bidual does not imply reflexivity.
Equivalent norms preserve canonical reflexivity, but need not preserve strict convexity or uniform convexity of a particular norm. This distinction applies to real and complex Banach spaces.

Let E be a real or complex normed space. A norm is strictly convex, or rotund, if distinct unit vectors have a midpoint of norm less than one. The norm is locally uniformly convex at a unit vector $x$ if unit $y_n$ with $\|(x+y_n)/2\|\to1$ satisfy $y_n\to x$ in norm. It is uniformly convex if \[ \delta_E(\eps)=\inf\{1-\|(x+y)/2\|:\|x\|,\|y\|\leq1, \ \|x-y\|\geq\eps\}>0 \] for every $0<\eps\leq2$. For the zero space define $\delta_E(\eps)=1$ when $\eps>0$, and always put $\delta_E(0)=0$; the defining epsilon--delta implication is vacuous there. No real infimum of an empty set is being used. The Radon--Riesz property means that weak convergence together with convergence of norms implies norm convergence.

Let E be a real or complex normed space. Strict convexity is equivalent to each of the following: equality in the triangle inequality for two nonzero vectors requires one to be a positive real multiple of the other; every convex set has at most one nearest point to any given vector; each supporting hyperplane to the unit ball meets its sphere at at most one point. In a reflexive strictly convex Banach space every nonempty closed convex set has a unique nearest point.

Let all spaces be normed over R or C; sums have the ℓp norm, 1<p<∞, with nonnegative sums the supremum of finite subsums. Uniform convexity passes to subspaces and to quotients by closed subspaces. Locally uniform convexity implies Radon--Riesz. Finite $\ell^p$ sums, $1<p<\infty$, of uniformly convex spaces are uniformly convex; the same is true for arbitrary sums if their moduli have a common positive lower bound at every positive argument.

Clarkson inequalities. For any positive measure space and $f,g\in L^p$, the following hold. For $2\leq p<\infty$, \[ \|f+g\|_p^p+\|f-g\|_p^p \leq2^{p-1}(\|f\|_p^p+\|g\|_p^p). \] For $1<p\leq2$, writing $q=p/(p-1)$, \[ \|f+g\|_p^q+\|f-g\|_p^q \leq2(\|f\|_p^p+\|g\|_p^p)^{q/p}. \] Thus $L^p$ is uniformly convex for $1<p<\infty$.

Let E be a real or complex normed space. At a unit vector $x$ put $D(x)=\{f\in E':\|f\|=f(x)=1\}$, using the complex-linear dual and real equality when the field is complex. The norm is smooth at $x$ if $D(x)$ is a singleton. Define its modulus of smoothness by \[ \rho_E(t)=\max\left\{0,\sup_{\|x\|,\|y\|\leq1} \left(\frac{\|x+ty\|+\|x-ty\|}{2}-1\right)\right\}. \] The space is uniformly smooth if $\rho_E(t)/t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$. For nonzero spaces the same supremum can be taken over unit spheres, by convexity in each vector and rescaling. The explicit maximum makes $\rho_{\{0\}}=0$; the modulus identity in the next proof is used only for nonzero spaces, with the zero-space equivalences checked directly.

Let E be a real or complex normed space, smoothness at nonzero x meaning uniqueness of the norm-one functional f with f(x)=||x||; D(x)={f∈E′:||f||=f(x)=1} for unit x. Differentiation is over the underlying real space. The norm is smooth at $x\ne0$ if and only if it is real Gateaux differentiable there. At a unit $x$ the derivative is $h\mapsto\operatorname{Re}f_x(h)$ for the unique $f_x\in D(x)$. A strictly convex dual makes the primal smooth; a smooth dual makes the primal strictly convex. The converses hold in reflexive spaces.

Uniform duality. All spaces are normed over R or C, with scalar-linear continuous dual and real differentiation of the norm. Uniform smoothness means ρ_E(t)/t→0 as t↓0, with the zero-space modulus ρ=0; uniform convexity includes the zero space vacuously. A normed space is uniformly convex if and only if its dual is uniformly smooth, and uniformly smooth if and only if its dual is uniformly convex. Uniform smoothness is equivalent to uniform real Fr\'echet differentiability of the norm on the unit sphere. It implies reflexivity for Banach spaces. The norming map $x\mapsto f_x$ is then uniformly norm-to-norm continuous on the unit sphere.

Slices and minimizing sequences. Scalar field K is R or C; all duals are continuous scalar-linear. The following are equivalent for a normed space: \begin{enumerate} \item for each $f\in E'$ with $\|f\|=1$, the diameters of the slices $\{x:\|x\|\leq1,\operatorname{Re}f(x)>1-\delta\}$ tend to zero; \item every sequence of unit vectors with $\operatorname{Re}f(x_n)\to1$ for one norm-one $f$ is Cauchy; \item every minimizing sequence in a nonempty convex set, for distance to any fixed point, is Cauchy. \end{enumerate} This property, strong rotundity, implies strict convexity and Radon--Riesz. In a Banach space it makes all such minimizing sequences convergent. Reflexive strictly convex spaces with Radon--Riesz have this property; in particular reflexive locally uniformly convex spaces do.

Compact-convex chapter convention: Hausdorff locally convex real ambient space, complex spaces considered real, given locally convex topology for closures; fixed-point results explicitly use the indicated norm topology.

Extreme points and faces. Work in a Hausdorff locally convex real TVS E, or in the underlying real space of a complex one; closure and compactness refer to its specified locally convex topology. For a convex set $K$, a point $x\in K$ is extreme if $x=ty+(1-t)z$, $y,z\in K$, $0<t<1$, implies $y=z=x$. The set of these points is $\operatorname{Ext}K$. A nonempty convex subset $F\subset K$ is a face if every proper convex combination of points of $K$ lying in $F$ has both endpoints in $F$. A compact face is a face which is compact in the ambient topology.

Face operations and maximizing faces. Work in a Hausdorff locally convex real TVS E, or in the underlying real space of a complex one, with given topology. A singleton is a face exactly when its point is extreme. Nonempty intersections of faces are faces, and a face of a face of $K$ is a face of $K$. If $K$ is nonempty compact convex and $\ell$ a continuous real linear functional, then \[ F_\ell=\{x\in K:\ell(x)=\max_K\ell\} \] is a nonempty compact face.

Separation in the locally convex topology. Let E be a Hausdorff locally convex real TVS; complex spaces are regarded as real. Continuous real linear functionals separate distinct points of $E$. If $C$ is a nonempty closed convex subset and $x_0\notin C$, there is such a functional with $\ell(x_0)>\sup_{x\in C}\ell(x)$.

Extreme points in every compact face. Work in a Hausdorff locally convex real TVS E, or in the underlying real space of a complex one; compactness is in the given topology. Every nonempty compact convex set has an extreme point. More precisely, every nonempty compact face of it contains an extreme point of the original set.

Krein--Milman. If $K$ is a nonempty compact convex subset of a Hausdorff locally convex space, then \[ K=\cl\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{Ext}K). \] The closure is in the given locally convex topology, and the convex combinations are finite real convex combinations.

The topology of the closed convex hull matters. The closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is weakly compact by Chapter~\ref{fa2:p1:c14}; its extreme points are its unit sphere. Indeed a vector of norm less than one is the midpoint of two distinct ball vectors, while equality in the norm estimate for a unit vector written as a proper convex combination forces both endpoints to be that unit vector, by the strict convexity following from the parallelogram identity. Krein--Milman here asserts a weak closed convex hull equality. It does not assert that this ball is norm compact; Chapter~\ref{fa2:p1:c01} shows that it is not. For a general locally convex compact set it is the specified topology, rather than sequences in an unspecified norm, which enters the theorem.

Brouwer fixed-point theorem is invoked as the ordinary finite-dimensional prerequisite: every continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed space, including empty ambient interior, has a fixed point. The manuscript proves the later infinite-dimensional approximation and limiting results.
