Finite convex approximation of a compact set. Let $Q$ be a nonempty compact subset of a normed space and $\eps>0$. There are points $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in Q$ and a continuous map $P_\eps:Q\to\operatorname{conv}\{q_1,\ldots,q_m\}$ such that $\norm{P_\eps(x)-x}<\eps$ for every $x\in Q$.
Schauder on a compact convex set. A continuous self-map $T:C\to C$ of a nonempty compact convex subset of a real or complex normed space has a fixed point.
Compactness of the closed convex hull in a Banach space. If $Q$ is a compact subset of a Banach space, then $\cl\operatorname{conv}Q$ is compact in norm.

Compact-map fixed-point theorem. Let $D$ be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Banach space and let $T:D\to D$ be continuous with relatively compact image $T(D)$. Then $T$ has a fixed point. In particular this holds for a continuous compact self-map of a nonempty closed bounded convex set. The first assertion also holds in an arbitrary normed space if the compact closure of $T(D)$ is taken in that space.

Why the hull lemma states completeness. In $c_{00}$ with the $\ell^1$ norm, the set $Q=\{0\}\cup\{e_n/n:n\geq1\}$ is compact, since $e_n/n\to0$. The vectors $x_N=\sum_{n=1}^N2^{-n}e_n/n$ are finite convex combinations of points of $Q$ (put the unused coefficient at zero), and they are Cauchy in $\ell^1$. Their completion limit has infinitely many nonzero coordinates, so no subsequence converges in $c_{00}$. Consequently the closed convex hull in that incomplete space is not compact. This does not contradict the normed compact-map theorem, whose direct proof uses compactness of the image itself.

What contraction adds. If $D$ is a nonempty closed subset of a Banach space and $
orm{Tx-Ty}\leq q
orm{x-y}$ with $0\leq q<1$, then $T:D	o D$ has a unique fixed point and every iterate converges to it, with \[ 
orm{T^nx-x_*}\leq rac{q^n}{1-q}
orm{Tx-x}. \] Convexity and relative compactness of the image are not needed for this assertion. Schauder supplies existence under its own hypotheses and does not supply this uniqueness or iteration conclusion.

Schauder need not select a unique or attracting point. On the compact convex interval $[0,1]$, the identity map has every point fixed and satisfies Schauder's hypotheses. The map $T(x)=1-x$ also satisfies them and has the unique fixed point $1/2$, but its iterates oscillate between $x$ and $1-x$ unless $x=1/2$. Its Lipschitz constant is one, so the strict contraction hypothesis is absent. In contrast $T(x)=x/2$ is a contraction with the unique fixed point zero and all iterates converging geometrically. These examples separate existence, uniqueness and convergence without identifying any of them implicitly.
Motivation and source references for distinct convex-duality, representing-measure and invariance statements; their different stated topology hypotheses are retained.

Fenchel--Moreau in a locally convex space. If $\varphi:E\to(-\infty,\infty]$ is proper, convex and lower semicontinuous on a real Hausdorff LCS, then \[ \varphi(x)=\sup_{f\in E'}\{f(x)-\varphi^*(f)\},\qquad \varphi^*(f)=\sup_x\{f(x)-\varphi(x)\}. \]

Fenchel--Rockafellar. Let $\varphi,\psi:E\to(-\infty,\infty]$ be proper convex functions on a real Hausdorff LCS. Suppose $x_0$ is in both effective domains and $\varphi$ is continuous at $x_0$. Then \[ \inf_x(\varphi(x)+\psi(x)) =\sup_{f\in E'}[-\varphi^*(f)-\psi^*(-f)]. \] If the infimum is finite, the dual supremum is attained. No primal attainment is asserted.

Agnew--Morse invariant Hahn--Banach. Let $p$ be a finite real sublinear function on a real vector space, and let $\mathcal S$ be a commuting semigroup of linear maps with $p(Sx)\leq p(x)$. Let $Y$ be invariant under these maps and $f:Y\to\R$ linear, $f\leq p$, $f(Sy)=f(y)$. There is an extension $F\leq p$ to the whole space with $F(Sx)=F(x)$.

Banach limits. There is a positive norm-one real linear functional $L$ on $\ell^\infty$ extending the usual sequence limit and invariant under the left shift. It satisfies $\liminf x_n\leq L(x)\leq\limsup x_n$. It can be chosen to agree with every convergent Ces\`aro mean. It has no representation by an $\ell^1$ sequence.

Banach integration and extension of Lebesgue measure. The Lebesgue integral on bounded measurable functions on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ extends to a positive translation-invariant norm-one functional on all bounded functions on that circle. There is an extended nonnegative finitely additive function $\widehat m$ on every subset of $\mathbb R$, translation invariant and agreeing with Lebesgue measure on every Lebesgue measurable set. Countable additivity cannot be required.

The continuous dual of real $\ell^\infty(S)$ is isometrically the space of finitely additive signed set functions of bounded variation on the power set of $S$. The correspondence is $\mu(A)=L(1_A)$, and integration is first defined on finite simple functions and then by uniform approximation. Positive functionals correspond to positive finitely additive measures. The invariant extension theorem gives a translation-invariant finitely additive probability measure on the full power set of every abelian group.

Milman's converse and extreme-point lifting. If $K=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}A$ is compact in a Hausdorff LCS, then $\operatorname{Ext}K\subset\overline A$. If $T:K\to L$ is a continuous affine surjection between compact convex sets, every extreme point of $L$ is the image of an extreme point of $K$.

Two barycentric representation statements. Every point of a nonempty compact convex subset $K$ of a Hausdorff LCS is the barycenter of a regular probability measure on $\overline{\operatorname{Ext}K}$. If $K$ is metrizable, the measure can be chosen with mass one on $\operatorname{Ext}K$ itself. The latter set need not be closed.

Birkhoff--von Neumann, finite matrices. Every $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of permutation matrices. These are exactly the extreme points of the compact convex set of doubly stochastic matrices.

Bernstein representation with the endpoint explicit. Define Δ_h f(t)=f(t+h)−f(t). Let $f:[0,\infty)\to\R$ be finite and satisfy $(-1)^m\Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_m}f(t)\geq0$ for $t\geq0$, $h_j>0$, $m\geq0$. Then there is a unique finite positive measure $\nu$ on the compactified interval $[0,\infty]$ with \[ f(t)=\int e^{-t\lambda}\,d\nu(\lambda), \] where at $\lambda=\infty$ the integrand is zero for $t>0$ and one for $t=0$. The mass at infinity is $f(0)-\lim_{t\downarrow0}f(t)$. Thus the classical representation by a finite measure on $[0,\infty)$ holds at every $t\geq0$ exactly when $f$ is right-continuous at zero.

The function e_∞:[0,∞)→R equal to 1 at 0 and 0 at every positive point satisfies all alternating finite-difference inequalities but has no representation at every t≥0 by a finite positive measure on finite parameters [0,∞). Its correct compactified representing measure is an atom at ∞. Every function with the compactified Bernstein representation is smooth on (0,∞) and satisfies (−1)^m f^(m)(t)≥0 for every integer m≥0 and t>0.

The open-half-line Bernstein theorem. Alternating finite differences mean (−1)^m Δ_{h_1}⋯Δ_{h_m}f(t)≥0 for every m≥0, t>0 and h_j>0, with Δ_h f(t)=f(t+h)−f(t). For a finite function $f:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ the following are equivalent: all alternating finite differences are nonnegative; $f$ is smooth and $(-1)^mf^{(m)}\ge0$ for all $m$; and \[ f(t)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-t\lambda}\,d\nu(\lambda)\quad(t>0) \] for a unique positive measure $\nu$, with the displayed integrals finite. The measure may have infinite total mass but is finite on bounded intervals. It is finite exactly when $f(0+)<\infty$, in which case its mass is $f(0+)$.
Schauder--Tychonoff. A continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex subset of a Hausdorff LCS has a fixed point.

Compact images and compact-homotopy continuation. A continuous self-map $T$ of a nonempty closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space has a fixed point if $\overline{T(C)}$ is compact. More generally let $F:E\times[0,1]\to E$ be continuous, mapping bounded sets to relatively compact sets, where $E$ is Banach. Suppose $F(x,0)=0$ for every $x$, and that some $R>0$ satisfies \[ x=F(x,t),\quad 0\le t\le1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|x\|<R. \] Then $F(\cdot,1)$ has a fixed point. In particular, a compact continuous $T:E\to E$ has a fixed point whenever $\{x:x=tT(x)\text{ for some }0\le t\le1\}$ is bounded.

Markov--Kakutani. LCS means Hausdorff locally convex space over R or C, using real convex combinations. A commuting family of continuous affine self-maps of a nonempty compact convex subset of an LCS has a common fixed point.

A small cap of a separable weakly compact set. The LCS is Hausdorff over R or C; separable means separable for its original locally convex topology, weak means the continuous-dual topology, and p-diameter(A)=sup_{x,y∈A}p(x−y). If $K$ is nonempty separable weakly compact convex in an LCS and $p$ is a continuous seminorm, then for every $\eps>0$ there is a proper weakly closed convex $C\subset K$ with $p$-diameter of $K\setminus C$ less than $\eps$.

Ryll--Nardzewski. LCS means Hausdorff locally convex space over R or C; weak refers to the topology determined by its continuous dual and the closure in the noncontracting hypothesis is in the original topology. Let $K$ be nonempty weakly compact convex in an LCS. Let $\mathcal S$ be a semigroup of weakly continuous affine self-maps which is noncontracting in the original topology: for $x\ne y$, $0\notin\overline{\{Sx-Sy:S\in\mathcal S\}}$. Then the semigroup has a common fixed point.
Supplement chapter source-disposition and motivation: the following independent structural constructions and endpoint-sensitive examples complete source variants.

Classical differentiable and H\"older Banach spaces. Derivatives of scalar functions may be real or complex, and m is a nonnegative integer. Empty suprema in the arbitrary-metric-space Hölder definition are zero. On a compact interval $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, the space $C^m(I)$ is complete in $\sum_{j=0}^m\|f^{(j)}\|_\infty$. For $0<\alpha\le1$, $C^{m,\alpha}(I)$ is complete in that norm plus \[ [f^{(m)}]_\alpha =\sup_{s\ne t\in I}\frac{|f^{(m)}(s)-f^{(m)}(t)|}{|s-t|^\alpha}. \] The same assertion for $m=0$ holds on an arbitrary metric space when the uniform norm is required finite. Pointwise multiplication is continuous; the product of an $\alpha$-H\"older and a $\beta$-H\"older function on $I$ is $\min(\alpha,\beta)$-H\"older. If $m+\alpha<n+\beta$, with integer $m,n\ge0$ and $0<\alpha,\beta\le1$, then $C^{n,\beta}(I)\subset C^{m,\alpha}(I)$ continuously.

Metric completion. Every metric space $(X,d)$ has an isometric embedding $j$ into a complete metric space $\widehat X$ with dense image. Any two such completions have a unique surjective isometry intertwining their embeddings. Every uniformly continuous map from $X$ to a complete metric space extends uniquely to a uniformly continuous map on $\widehat X$; its Lipschitz constant, if prescribed, is preserved. Thus the linear completion above is also the metric completion; the underlying metric assertion does not require a vector space.

The integral space associated with a positive functional. Let $K$ be compact Hausdorff and $\ell$ a positive real functional on $C(K)$. Let $\mu$ be its finite regular representing measure. The completion of $C(K)/\{f:\ell(|f|)=0\}$ in the norm $\ell(|f|)$ is canonically $L^1(\mu)$, and the extension of $\ell$ is integration. In this completion the positive cone, absolute value, and arbitrary Lipschitz scalar functional calculus agree with their almost-everywhere function versions. An increasing sequence whose integrals are bounded converges in this norm to its pointwise supremum; subtraction of its first term reduces this assertion to a nonnegative sequence.

Tight functionals on bounded continuous functions. Let $X$ be any metric space and $L:C_b(X;\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ positive with $L(1)=1$. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K_\varepsilon\subset X$ such that \[ |L(f)|\le\sup_{K_\varepsilon}|f|+ \varepsilon\|f\|_\infty\qquad(f\in C_b(X)). \] Then there is a unique finite positive Borel measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $L(f)=\int f\,d\mu$. It is a tight probability and is inner regular by compact sets. No completeness, separability, or local compactness of $X$ is assumed.

The net tests used in duality. A subset of a topological space is closed if and only if it contains the limits of all its convergent nets. A map is continuous if and only if it preserves limits of all convergent nets. A space is compact if and only if every net has a convergent subnet. A convergent net in a TVS need not have bounded full range.

The weak topology is not determined by sequences. In every infinite dimensional normed space choose nested subspaces $E_n$ of dimension $n$ and put $S=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{x\in E_n:\|x\|=n\}$. Then $S$ is weakly sequentially closed but is not weakly closed. Indeed a weakly convergent sequence is norm bounded, so all its terms lie in a finite union of the displayed finite dimensional spheres. That union is norm compact, hence weakly compact and weakly closed; the limit lies in $S$. On the other hand any weak neighborhood of zero imposes only $m$ scalar tests. If $n>m$, their common kernel in $E_n$ contains a nonzero vector, which can be scaled to norm $n$. Thus the neighborhood meets $S$, while $0\notin S$. This does not contradict Eberlein--\v Smulian: that theorem characterizes compactness, not all closed sets by sequences. Compare \cite[Chapter 12, Theorem 1]{B08}.

Global weak-to-norm continuity is finite rank. A bounded linear map $T:E\to F$ between normed spaces is continuous from the weak topology of $E$ to the norm topology of $F$ if and only if it has finite rank.

A net in a real or complex TVS is Cauchy iff every zero neighborhood contains all sufficiently late differences. Any compatible translation-invariant metric gives exactly this condition; thus completeness for compatible invariant metrics is intrinsic to the vector topology. On a metrizable TVS, completeness for Cauchy sequences in a compatible invariant metric is equivalent to convergence of every Cauchy net. An arbitrary compatible metric need not preserve completeness.

Distance and the support function. Let $K$ be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real or complex normed space $E$. For $f\in E'$ put $\sigma_K(f)=\sup_{k\in K}\operatorname{Re}f(k)\in(-\infty,\infty]$, omitting $\operatorname{Re}$ in the real case. Then \[ \operatorname{dist}(x,K) =\sup_{\|f\|\le1} \{\operatorname{Re}f(x)-\sigma_K(f)\}. \] A term with $\sigma_K(f)=\infty$ has value $-\infty$. Neither a nearest point nor a maximizing functional is asserted.

Nonmeagre images and finite algebraic codimension. Let $T:E\to F$ be bounded linear, with $E$ Banach and $F$ normed. If the actual range $T(E)$ is nonmeagre in $F$, then $T$ is surjective and open; in particular $F$ is Banach. If both $E,F$ are Banach and the algebraic codimension of $T(E)$ in $F$ is finite, then $T(E)$ is closed. Finite codimension without the range-of-a-bounded-map hypothesis does not imply that a subspace is closed.

Strong and weak operator topologies. On $\mathcal L(E,F)$ the strong operator topology is defined by $T\mapsto\|Tx\|$ for $x\in E$, and the weak operator topology by $T\mapsto|g(Tx)|$ for $x\in E,g\in F'$. Both are Hausdorff locally convex, and $\mathrm{WOT}\subset\mathrm{SOT}\subset\text{norm topology}$. Their continuous linear duals coincide, consisting of finite sums $T\mapsto\sum_jg_j(Tx_j)$; hence they have the same closed convex sets. Composition with a fixed bounded operator is continuous for both topologies. If $S_\alpha\to S$ and $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly and $\sup_\alpha\|T_\alpha\|<\infty$, then $T_\alpha S_\alpha\to TS$ strongly. For sequences the boundedness condition follows from uniform boundedness when the intermediate space is Banach.

Composition and adjoints: the exact boundaries. On an infinite dimensional Hilbert space choose a unit vector $e$ and, for each finite dimensional subspace $M$, a unit vector $u_M\perp M$. Direct $(M,n)$ by inclusion and increasing positive integers and put \[ S_{M,n}x=n^{-1}\langle e,x\rangle u_M,\qquad T_{M,n}x=n\langle u_M,x\rangle e. \] Then $S_{M,n}\to0$ in norm and $T_{M,n}\to0$ strongly, since every fixed $x$ eventually belongs to $M$, but $T_{M,n}S_{M,n}x=\langle e,x\rangle e$. Thus joint SOT continuity of composition fails for general nets. For the unilateral shift $V$ on $\ell^2$, both $V^n$ and $V^{*n}$ tend weakly to zero (first test finite support vectors and then use their uniform norm bounds), but $V^{*n}V^n=I$. Joint WOT continuity fails even for sequences. Also $V^{*n}\to0$ strongly whereas $V^n$ does not, so adjunction is not SOT-continuous; it is WOT-continuous because its matrix coefficients are the conjugated transposed matrix coefficients of the original operator.

Arbitrary Banach sums. Let $(E_i)_{i\in I}$ be Banach spaces. For $1\le p<\infty$ the space \[ (\bigoplus_{i\in I}E_i)_p =\{x=(x_i):\sum_{i\in I}\|x_i\|^p<\infty\},\qquad \|x\|=(\sum_i\|x_i\|^p)^{1/p}, \] is Banach. An uncountable nonnegative sum means the supremum of its finite subsums. Also Banach are the bounded product with supremum norm and its closed subspace \[ (\bigoplus_{i\in I}E_i)_{c_0} =\{x:\text{for every }\eps>0,\ \{i:\|x_i\|\ge\eps\} \text{ is finite}\}. \] Coordinate inclusions and projections are contractions. Finite support vectors are dense in the $p$-sum and the $c_0$-sum, but in general not in the bounded product.

Closed sums and quantitative decompositions. Let $G,L$ be closed subspaces of a Banach space $E$. The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $G+L$ is closed; \item there is $C$ such that every $x\in G+L$ has a decomposition $x=g+l$ with $\|g\|+\|l\|\le C\|x\|$; \item there is $C$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(g,G\cap L)\le C\operatorname{dist}(g,L)$ for $g\in G$; \item there is $C$ such that, for every $x\in E$, \[ \operatorname{dist}(x,G\cap L) \le C\bigl(\operatorname{dist}(x,G)+\operatorname{dist}(x,L)\bigr). \] \end{enumerate} Moreover $G+L$ is closed if and only if $G^\perp+L^\perp$ is norm closed in $E'$. In that case $(G\cap L)^\perp=G^\perp+L^\perp$.

Positive extension from a majorizing subspace. In the C(K) clause K is compact Hausdorff, including the empty compact space. Let a real vector space $E$ be ordered by a convex cone, and let a subspace $Y$ majorize $E$: every $x\in E$ has an upper bound in $Y$. Every positive linear functional $f$ on $Y$ extends to a positive linear functional on $E$. In particular a positive functional on a subspace of $C(K,\mathbb R)$ containing the constants extends positively to $C(K,\mathbb R)$ and has norm $f(1)$.

A concrete failure of norm attainment. On $c_0$ put $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}x_n$. Then $\|f\|=1$, as shown by the vectors with their first $N$ coordinates one and all other coordinates zero. But for $x\in B_{c_0}$ choose $N$ with $|x_n|\le1/2$ for $n\ge N$. Then $|f(x)|\le\sum_{n<N}2^{-n}+\tfrac12\sum_{n\ge N}2^{-n}<1$. Thus the norm is a supremum which no unit-ball point attains, in both the real and the complex space.

Finite dimensional best approximation. Every point of a normed space has a nearest point in every nonempty closed subset of a finite dimensional subspace. In particular it has a nearest point in that subspace; strict convexity gives uniqueness for convex subsets whenever a nearest point exists.
Mazur--Ulam. A surjective isometry between real normed spaces is affine. Consequently a surjective isometry taking zero to zero is real linear. Completeness is not required.

Surjectivity and the scalar field. The map $t\mapsto(t,\sin t)$ from $\mathbb R$ into $(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is an isometry which is not affine. Complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$ is an onto real linear isometry but is not complex linear. Thus neither surjectivity nor the real scalar conclusion can simply be omitted or strengthened.

Sobczyk's separable extension theorem. Let $Y$ be a subspace of a separable normed space $E$. Every bounded map $T:Y\to c_0$ extends to a bounded map $S:E\to c_0$ with $\|S\|\le2\|T\|$. In particular every closed subspace isomorphic to $c_0$ in a separable Banach space is complemented. If the copy is isometric, a projection of norm at most $2$ exists.
Sequential completeness in the weak topologies. Reflexive Banach spaces are weakly sequentially complete. The dual of a Banach space is weakly star sequentially complete.
Polynomial approximation on an interval. Every continuous scalar function on a compact real interval is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Stone--Weierstrass. Let $K$ be compact Hausdorff. A real subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb R)$ which contains the constants and separates points is uniformly dense. A complex subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb C)$ with these properties is uniformly dense if it is also closed under complex conjugation.

The conjugation hypothesis. On the unit circle the polynomials in $z$ contain constants and separate points, but cannot uniformly approximate $\bar z$. Indeed the normalized circle integral of $zp(z)$ is zero for every such polynomial, whereas that of $z\bar z$ is one. Thus the complex conjugation hypothesis has mathematical content.

Extreme points of normalized convex functions. Let $\mathcal C$ consist of all nonnegative convex functions on $[0,1]$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=1$, allowing an endpoint jump at $1$. It is a compact convex set for pointwise convergence. Its extreme points are \[ e_r(x)=\frac{(x-r)_+}{1-r}\quad(0\le r<1),\qquad e_1(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<1,\\1&x=1.\end{cases} \] Every $f\in\mathcal C$ has a unique representation $f(x)=\int_{[0,1]}e_r(x)\,d\mu(r)$ by a probability measure.

Continuity points of a Baire first-class function. Let $X$ be a complete metric space and $f_n:X\to\mathbb R$ continuous with $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ at each point. The continuity points of $f$ form a dense $G_\delta$ subset of $X$.

A typical continuous function is nowhere differentiable. In $C[0,1]$ with its supremum norm, the functions with no finite derivative at any point of $(0,1)$, and no finite one-sided derivative at the endpoints, contain a dense $G_\delta$.

Universal embedding and Banach--Stone. Every normed space $E$ embeds linearly and isometrically into $C(B_{E'},w^*)$ by $x\mapsto(f\mapsto f(x))$. Let $K,L$ be compact Hausdorff spaces. Every surjective linear isometry $U:C(K,\mathbb K)\to C(L,\mathbb K)$ has the form \[ (Uf)(t)=h(t)f(\varphi(t)), \] where $\varphi:L\to K$ is a homeomorphism and $h\in C(L)$ satisfies $|h(t)|=1$. Conversely every such weighted composition is a surjective linear isometry. For real scalars the weight takes values in $\{-1,1\}$.

Bounded Borel functions do not exhaust the bidual. For compact Hausdorff $K$, bounded Borel functions embed linearly and isometrically in $C(K)''=M(K)'$ by $h\mapsto[\mu\mapsto\int_Kh\,d\mu]$. This embedding need not be onto, already for $K=[0,1]$.

Source-correction commentary: the cited textbook identification of the whole bidual C(K)′′ with bounded Borel functions is superseded by the preceding valid isometric embedding and explicit non-surjectivity example; it is not an additional requirement to establish the false identification. The first-dual regular-measure representation remains a separate theorem.

For open $\Omega\subset E$ and a map $F:\Omega\to F_0$ between Banach spaces, the Fr\'echet derivative at $x$ is a bounded linear map $DF(x)$ such that $\|F(x+h)-F(x)-DF(x)h\|=o(\|h\|)$. The derivative is unique, since the difference of two candidates vanishes on each vector after replacing $h$ by $th$ and letting $t\to0$. The notation $C^1$ means that this derivative exists everywhere and is continuous in operator norm.

Chain rule and the mean-value estimate. Maps are between real or complex Banach spaces, their domains are open, and derivatives are Fréchet derivatives (complex-linear when complex differentiability is asserted). The mean-value norm estimate uses real scalar differentiation on the segment. If $F$ is differentiable at $x$ and $G$ at $F(x)$, then $D(G\circ F)(x)=DG(F(x))DF(x)$. If the segment $[x,y]$ is contained in the domain and $\sup_{z\in[x,y]}\|DF(z)\|\le M$, then $\|F(y)-F(x)\|\le M\|y-x\|$.

Inverse and implicit function theorems. E,F_0,Y,Z are real or complex Banach spaces and Ω is open. Let $F:\Omega\subset E\to F_0$ be $C^1$ between Banach spaces. If $A=DF(x_0)$ is an isomorphism, $F$ has a $C^1$ local inverse near $x_0$, with derivative $D(F^{-1})(y)=DF(F^{-1}y)^{-1}$. Consequently, if $H$ is $C^1$ near $(x_0,y_0)$ in $E\times Y$, $H(x_0,y_0)=0$, and $D_yH(x_0,y_0):Y\to Z$ is an isomorphism, the nearby solutions of $H(x,y)=0$ are exactly $y=\phi(x)$ for a unique $C^1$ map, and \[ D\phi(x)=-D_yH(x,\phi(x))^{-1}D_xH(x,\phi(x)). \] If the initial map is $C^k$, so is the inverse or implicit map.

Directional derivatives do not suffice. The function $F(x,y)=x^3y/(x^6+y^2)$ off $(0,0)$, with $F(0,0)=0$, has every directional derivative zero at the origin, but $F(x,x^3)=1/2$ for $x\ne0$. It is not even continuous there, and therefore not Fr\'echet differentiable. The Banach inverse theorem above explicitly uses continuity in operator norm of the Fr\'echet derivative.

Asplund chapter scope: E is real normed, completeness is not required, and conjugates use the continuous real dual. The separately stated iteration, conjugate identities, geometric rate and conditional renorming theorem are retained.

Arithmetic and infimal-convolution means. Let E be a real normed space, not necessarily complete; conjugates are taken against its continuous real dual E′. Let $0\le\psi_0\le\varphi_0<\infty$ be convex functions on $E$ which vanish at zero. Define \[ \varphi_{n+1}(x)=\tfrac12(\varphi_n(x)+\psi_n(x)),\qquad \psi_{n+1}(x)=\tfrac12\inf_y [\varphi_n(x+y)+\psi_n(x-y)]. \] Then all iterates are finite convex functions vanishing at zero, $0\le\psi_n\le\psi_{n+1}\le\varphi_{n+1}\le\varphi_n$, and both sequences have the same convex limit $\theta$. Their continuous-dual conjugates satisfy \[ \varphi_n^*\uparrow\theta^*,\qquad \psi_{n+1}^*(f)=\tfrac12[\varphi_n^*(f)+\psi_n^*(f)]. \] At every $f$ for which $\psi_0^*(f)<\infty$, also $\psi_n^*(f)\downarrow\theta^*(f)$; in particular this holds on the whole dual when $D(\psi_0^*)=E'$. If $\varphi_0$ is continuous at some $x_0$, all iterates are continuous there, and \[ \varphi_{n+1}^*(f)=\tfrac12\inf_{g\in E'} [\varphi_n^*(f+g)+\psi_n^*(f-g)]. \] When its value is finite the last infimum is attained.

Squares of seminorms. Let E be a real vector space. A finite nonnegative convex function $q$ with $q(\lambda x)=\lambda^2q(x)$ for real $\lambda$ is the square of a seminorm, and every squared seminorm has these properties. For $0<t<1$, \[ q(x+y)\le q(x)/t+q(y)/(1-t),\qquad 4q(x)\le q(x+y)/t+q(x-y)/(1-t). \] A norm is strictly convex in the unit-sphere sense if and only if its square is a strictly convex function.

The factor four estimate and persistence of strictness. Let E be a real normed space, 0≤ψ_0≤φ_0<∞ convex and vanishing at zero; set φ_{n+1}(x)=(φ_n(x)+ψ_n(x))/2 and ψ_{n+1}(x)=1/2 inf_y[φ_n(x+y)+ψ_n(x−y)], with common limit θ. Suppose additionally that $\varphi_0,\psi_0$ are quadratically homogeneous and $\varphi_0\le(1+C)\psi_0$, $C\ge0$. All iterates and $\theta$ have the same homogeneity, and \[ \varphi_n\le(1+C4^{-n})\psi_n. \] If either initial function is strictly convex, then $\theta$ is strictly convex.

Asplund's simultaneous renorming theorem. Suppose a real normed space has two equivalent norms $p_1,p_2$ such that $p_1$ and the dual norm $p_2^*$ are strictly convex. The dual is taken for their common norm topology, which we use on $E$ in this application. It then has an equivalent norm $p$ for which both $p$ and $p^*$ are strictly convex. This is a conditional combination theorem; it does not assert the existence of the two initial norms on every Banach space.

Let E be a complex normed space with two equivalent complex norms p1,p2 such that p1 and the norm on the continuous complex-linear dual induced by p2 are strictly convex. Then E has an equivalent complex norm p for which both p and its continuous complex-linear dual norm p* are strictly convex. No completeness or reflexivity is assumed.

Infimal-convolution chapter scope: the first two theorems use a real reflexive Banach space, and the final closed-subspace cone theorem uses a real Banach space without reflexivity. Continuity qualification and full-cone qualification are distinct retained assertions.

Closure of conjugate domains. Let E be a real reflexive Banach space, D(q)={x:q(x)<∞}, and conjugates be taken against E′. Let $\varphi,\psi:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper convex lower semicontinuous functions with $D(\varphi)\cap D(\psi)\ne\varnothing$. Set \[ h(f)=(\varphi^*\mathbin\square\psi^*)(f) =\inf_{g\in E'}[\varphi^*(f-g)+\psi^*(g)]. \] Then $h$ is proper convex, never has value $-\infty$, \[ D(h)=D(\varphi^*)+D(\psi^*),\quad h^*=\varphi+\psi, \quad h^{**}=(\varphi+\psi)^*, \] where reflexivity identifies the dual of $E'$ with $E$. Consequently \[ \overline{D((\varphi+\psi)^*)} =\overline{D(\varphi^*)+D(\psi^*)}. \] The closures are norm closures in $E'$; convexity makes them also their weak closures. No exact equality of unclosed domains is asserted without an additional hypothesis.

Exact convolution under the full-cone condition. Let E be a real reflexive Banach space and φ,ψ:E→(−∞,+∞] be proper convex lower-semicontinuous functions with D(φ)∩D(ψ)≠∅. Put h(f)=inf_{g∈E′}[φ*(f−g)+ψ*(g)], with conjugation against E′. Under the preceding hypotheses assume \[ \bigcup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda (D(\varphi)-D(\psi))=E. \] For every norm bounded set $B\subset E'$ and every real $\alpha$, the set \[ \{g\in E':\text{some }f\in B\text{ satisfies } \varphi^*(f-g)+\psi^*(g)\le\alpha\} \] is norm bounded. The infimal convolution $h$ is lsc, and \[ (\varphi+\psi)^*(f) =\min_{g\in E'}[\varphi^*(f-g)+\psi^*(g)] \] whenever the left side is finite; at infinite values the equality holds with an infimum. In particular \[ D((\varphi+\psi)^*)=D(\varphi^*)+D(\psi^*). \] The corresponding primal--dual identity is \[ \inf_x[\varphi(x)+\psi(x)] =\sup_{g\in E'}[-\varphi^*(-g)-\psi^*(g)], \] with a finite maximizing value attained whenever the infimum is finite. No primal minimizer is asserted. If the primal infimum is $-\infty$, both sides are $-\infty$ in the extended-real sense.

Proof and hypothesis commentary: the reflexive full-cone theorem uses pointwise bounds from the cone, completeness for uniform boundedness, and reflexivity for weak subsequences. The earlier Fenchel–Rockafellar theorem has a different continuity qualification on an LCS; its result and the full-cone theorem with bounded split sublevels are both retained.

The Banach closed-subspace cone qualification. Let conjugation be against the continuous real dual, D(q)={x:q(x)<∞}, and h(f)=inf_{g∈E′}[φ*(f−g)+ψ*(g)]. Let $E$ be a real Banach space, and let $\varphi,\psi$ be proper convex norm-lsc functions with a common finite domain point. Suppose \[ L=\bigcup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda(D(\varphi)-D(\psi)) \] is a closed linear subspace of $E$. Then \[ (\varphi+\psi)^*(f) =\inf_{g\in E'}[\varphi^*(f-g)+\psi^*(g)], \] and every finite value has a minimizing split. Hence the exact domain identity and the primal--dual equality of the preceding theorem hold. No reflexivity hypothesis is needed in this form. When $L=E$ the uniform bounded-split sublevel assertion holds as well. For a proper subspace $L$, it concerns bounded representatives after restriction to $L$, rather than all ambient split functionals. Explicitly, D((φ+ψ)*)=D(φ*)+D(ψ*) and inf_x[φ(x)+ψ(x)]=sup_g[−φ*(−g)−ψ*(g)], with the supremum attained whenever the primal infimum is finite; if the primal infimum is −∞ both sides are −∞. No primal minimizer is asserted. When L=E, for every norm-bounded B⊂E′ and α∈R, {g:∃f∈B, φ*(f−g)+ψ*(g)≤α} is norm-bounded. For proper closed L the analogous bound applies to restricted splits in L′, which admit norm-preserving extensions, rather than to every ambient split.

Part II concerns Hilbert operators, algebras and spectral theory; chapter bibliographic framing. Real or complex Hilbert spaces use inner products conjugate-linear in the first variable and linear in the second; the continuous scalar-linear dual and conjugate-linear antidual are distinct.

For any real or complex Hilbert space H, nonempty closed convex C⊆H and x∈H there exists a unique nearest point p=P_C x, characterized by Re⟨x−p,v−p⟩≤0 for every v∈C. P_C is nonexpansive. For any closed linear M, H=M⊕M⊥ and P_M is linear, self-adjoint and contractive. For any linear subspace L, (L⊥)⊥=closure L.

Orthogonal projections on H form a complete lattice, with arbitrary meets projecting onto intersections of ranges and joins onto closed spans of ranges. P≤Q in operator order iff Ran P⊆Ran Q iff PQ=QP=P. Commuting projections have product equal to their meet. Any bounded self-adjoint sequence A_n≤A_(n+1)≤B converges strongly to its bounded self-adjoint supremum, without commutation assumptions.

Every continuous scalar-linear functional f on real or complex Hilbert H has a unique h∈H with f(x)=⟨h,x⟩ for all x and ‖f‖=‖h‖. Every bounded sesquilinear form a on H, conjugate-linear in its first variable, has a unique bounded linear A:H→H satisfying a(x,y)=⟨x,Ay⟩ and ‖A‖=‖a‖.

Every Hilbert space has a maximal orthonormal family (e_i)_(i∈I); for each x, x=Σ_i e_i⟨e_i,x⟩ and ‖x‖²=Σ_i|⟨e_i,x⟩|², where sums are nets over finite subsets, and each x has only countably many nonzero coefficients. Two Hilbert spaces are unitarily isomorphic iff their orthonormal bases have equal cardinalities, including finite/zero/nonseparable cases.

For each bounded linear T:H→K between real or complex Hilbert spaces there is a unique bounded linear T*:K→H with ⟨Tx,y⟩=⟨x,T*y⟩. One has ‖T*‖=‖T‖, ‖T*T‖=‖T‖², (ST)*=T*S*, T**=T, closure Ran T=(ker T*)⊥, closure Ran T*=(ker T)⊥. A closed M⊆H is T-invariant iff P_M T P_M=T P_M; M reduces T iff P_M T=T P_M iff M is invariant under T and T*.

For bounded T:H→K, Ran T is closed iff ∃c>0, ‖Tx‖≥c‖x‖ for all x⊥ker T, iff Ran T* is closed. Then Ran T=(ker T*)⊥ and Ran T*=(ker T)⊥. The reduced minimum modulus γ(T)=inf{‖Tx‖:x⊥ker T, ‖x‖=1} equals γ(T*), interpreting the empty infimum as +∞ when the complement is zero.

For a bounded sesquilinear form a on real or complex Hilbert H, conjugate-linear in the first variable and satisfying Re a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² for some α>0 and every v, every continuous conjugate-linear F admits a unique u∈H with a(v,u)=F(v) for every v, and ‖u‖≤‖F‖/α. If a is Hermitian, u uniquely minimizes (1/2)a(v,v)−Re F(v).

For bounded sesquilinear a with Re a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² (α>0) on real or complex Hilbert H, nonempty closed convex C, and continuous conjugate-linear F(v)=⟨v,f⟩, there is a unique u∈C with Re a(v−u,u)≥Re F(v−u) for every v∈C. For Hermitian a this is equivalent to minimizing (1/2)a(v,v)−Re F(v) on C. Right-hand-side solutions satisfy ‖u_f−u_g‖≤‖f−g‖/α.
A real or complex normed space has an inner product inducing its norm iff ‖x+y‖²+‖x−y‖²=2‖x‖²+2‖y‖² for all x,y.
Kakutani and de Figueiredo–Karlovitz characterizations are separate obligations stated/proved later at fa2:p2:kakutani and fa2:p2:radial-hilbert; this remark does not add a duplicate statement.

For real reflexive Banach X, let A:X→X′ be bounded on bounded sets, hemicontinuous (t↦⟨A(x+ty),z⟩ continuous for all x,y,z), and monotone (⟨Ax−Ay,x−y⟩≥0). If ⟨Ax,x⟩/‖x‖→+∞ as ‖x‖→∞, A is onto. If strictly monotone, Ax=f has exactly one solution for every f∈X′. In particular the continuous strictly monotone coercive variant applies.
Pre-Hilbert variants distinguish ambient completeness from completeness of the projection target; the same inner-product convention applies.
Every real or complex inner-product space E has a Hilbert completion H and linear inner-product-preserving dense embedding E→H. It is unique up to the unique unitary intertwining the embeddings.

In any real or complex inner-product space E without completeness assumed, every nonempty convex subset C complete in its induced metric has a unique nearest point p to each x∈E, characterized by Re⟨x−p,z−p⟩≤0 for all z∈C; the projection is nonexpansive. Any complete linear Y⊆E gives E=Y⊕Y⊥ with bounded orthogonal projection onto Y.

For any orthonormal family (e_i)_(i∈I) in a real or complex inner-product space E, p_F x=Σ_(i∈F)⟨e_i,x⟩e_i satisfies ‖x−p_Fx‖²=‖x‖²−Σ_(i∈F)|⟨e_i,x⟩|² for every finite F. Bessel and countability of nonzero coefficients hold. For each x, x∈closure span{e_i} iff the finite-subset net p_Fx→x iff Parseval equality holds at x. Thus span density iff Parseval holds for every x. Density implies zero orthogonal annihilator; the converse holds in Hilbert spaces but can fail in incomplete inner-product spaces.

In K⊕ℓ² with the induced inner product let E={(Σ_j a_j,a):a∈c₀₀} and M={(0,a):a∈c₀₀, Σ_j a_j=0}. E is incomplete; M is proper and closed in E but M⊥ in E is {0}. In the ambient Hilbert space closure M={0}⊕ℓ². Gram–Schmidt on (0,e_j−e_(j+1)) gives an orthonormal sequence whose closed span in E is M and whose annihilator is zero, so zero annihilator need not imply totality in pre-Hilbert spaces.

In any normed X, a bounded sequence x_n converges weakly to specified x iff f(x_n)→f(x) for every f in a subset whose norm-closed linear span is X′. A merely point-separating set of tests does not suffice.

For bounded linear T:D⊆X→Y between normed spaces, closedness of its linear domain D implies closedness of its graph; conversely a closed graph implies D closed if Y is complete. Neither implication assumes X complete. If X,Y are Banach, D is closed, and T:D→Y is a closed linear operator, then T is bounded for the norm induced from X.

On ℓ¹ the coordinate tests separate points and the bounded standard unit-vector sequence e_n tends to zero under each coordinate test, but it is not weakly null since the continuous sum functional has value one.

For X=ℓ², D=c₀₀ and Y=c₀₀ with its inherited ℓ² norm, the identity T:D→Y is bounded with closed graph in X×Y, although D is not closed in X. Completeness of the target in the converse domain-graph implication is necessary.

For real or complex Hilbert H₁,H₂, a bounded form a:H₁×H₂→K conjugate-linear first and linear second has a unique bounded linear S:H₁→H₂ with a(x,y)=⟨Sx,y⟩ and ‖S‖=‖a‖; equivalently a(x,y)=⟨x,S*y⟩. No coercivity/symmetry or equality of the Hilbert spaces is required, including zero spaces.

For bounded T on a complex Hilbert space, T=T* iff ⟨x,Tx⟩ is real for all x; the converse is false over real Hilbert spaces. Over either field, the product of bounded self-adjoint S,T is self-adjoint iff S,T commute. Bounded self-adjoint operators form a norm-closed set.
On R² the nonzero rotation J(s,t)=(−t,s) has ⟨x,Jx⟩=0 for every x, but J*=−J and J is not self-adjoint, disproving the real quadratic-value converse.

For a bounded sesquilinear form a on real or complex Hilbert H (conjugate-linear first, linear second), assume |a(v,v)|≥b‖v‖² for all v and some b>0. Every continuous conjugate-linear F has a unique u with a(v,u)=F(v) for all v and ‖u‖≤‖F‖/b. The solution operator from the continuous antidual is linear with norm ≤1/b. Energy minimization and Stampacchia retain their distinct real-part coercivity conditions.

For real or complex inner-product E and bounded self-adjoint T:E→E, assume the closure in E of the image of its unit ball is compact (not just total boundedness). There is a finite/countable orthonormal family (e_j) in E and nonzero real λ_j with Te_j=λ_j e_j and Tx=Σ_j λ_j e_j⟨e_j,x⟩ for all x∈E, the series converging in E norm to Tx. Each nonzero eigenspace is finite-dimensional; an infinite eigenvalue list tends to zero; the family is empty for T=0. No orthonormal basis of incomplete E is asserted.

For any finite list y₁,…,y_n in a real or complex inner-product space, G=(⟨y_i,y_j⟩) is positive semidefinite and positive definite iff the list is linearly independent. In that case, for Y=span{y_i}, b=(⟨y_i,x⟩), the nearest point to x is p=Σ_j(G⁻¹b)_j y_j and dist(x,Y)²=‖x‖²−b*G⁻¹b=det([[G,b],[b*,‖x‖²]])/det G. For dependent lists det G=0 and one uses an independent spanning sublist; the quotient is undefined. For the empty list det=1 and distance is ‖x‖. Ambient completeness is unnecessary.
In this chapter X is a real Banach space (complex convex order uses its underlying real space). For proper convex φ, ∂φ(x)={f∈X′:φ(y)≥φ(x)+f(y−x) for all y∈X} when φ(x)<∞, and ∂φ(x)=∅ otherwise.

For proper convex φ on real Banach X, each ∂φ(x) is closed convex, the graph of ∂φ is monotone, and f∈∂φ(x) iff φ(x)+φ*(f)=f(x). For q(x)=‖x‖²/2, ∂q(x)=Jx={f∈X′:‖f‖=‖x‖, f(x)=‖x‖²}. For x≠0 the norm subgradient is its norm-one norming functionals; at 0 it is the closed dual unit ball. For convex C, ∂I_C(x)=N_C(x)={f:f(y−x)≤0 for all y∈C} at x∈C. A differentiable convex function has its derivative as its unique subgradient. If φ is bounded above by M on closed B(x,R), it is locally Lipschitz and has subgradients on B(x,R); at x every subgradient obeys ‖f‖≤(M−φ(x))/R and φ′(x;v)=max_(f∈∂φ(x)) f(v). For lsc convex φ, Int D(∂φ)=Int D(φ). For proper convex φ,ψ with φ continuous at some point of D(φ)∩D(ψ), ∂(φ+ψ)(x)=∂φ(x)+∂ψ(x) at every x; without qualification the right side is always included in the left.
For φ(t)=−√t on t≥0 and +∞ otherwise on R, and ψ=I_{0}, ∂φ(0)=∅ while φ+ψ=I_{0} has every real scalar as a subgradient at zero. The unqualified subgradient sum inclusion can be strict.

If finite convex φ on real Banach X satisfies φ(x)≤k‖x‖+C globally, then φ is globally k-Lipschitz and D(φ*)⊆kB_(X′). If φ is continuous convex, C₀={φ≤0}, and φ(z)<0 for some z, then for every x∈C₀, N_(C₀)(x)={λf:f∈∂φ(x), λ≥0, λφ(x)=0}.
Every finite convex function on an open convex subset of Rⁿ is continuous, without assuming lower semicontinuity; it is locally bounded above on interior coordinate cubes and locally Lipschitz.

For real Banach X, if X′ is strictly convex, every Jx is a singleton and q(x)=‖x‖²/2 is Gâteaux differentiable with derivative Jx. J:X_norm→X′_(weak-star) is continuous and (Jx+Jy)(x+y)+(Jx−Jy)(x−y)=2(‖x‖²+‖y‖²). If X is additionally reflexive and strictly convex, J is bijective and J⁻¹ is the duality map of X′ under X″=X. Equivalently, X′ is uniformly convex iff J is everywhere single-valued and uniformly norm-continuous on every bounded subset of X. Under these conditions q is Fréchet C¹ with derivative J.

For real Banach X with uniformly convex dual X′ and proper lsc convex φ, each integer n≥1 defines the finite convex Fréchet C¹ envelope φ_n(x)=inf_y(φ(y)+n‖x−y‖²/2). Its derivative S_nx is the unique maximizer over f∈X′ of f(x)−φ*(f)−‖f‖²/(2n), and S_n:X→X′ is norm-continuous. φ_n(x) increases to φ(x), including φ(x)=+∞. No uniqueness of primal minimizers is required.

For uniformly convex Banach X and nonempty closed convex C⊆X, every nonempty bounded A⊆C has a unique center c_A∈C minimizing r_A(x)=sup_(a∈A)‖x−a‖; if diam A>0 its minimal radius is strictly less than diam A. Every bounded sequence a_n∈C has a unique asymptotic center c minimizing r(x)=limsup_n‖x−a_n‖. If c_n centers the tail {a_j:j≥n} and r_n is its radius function, then c_n→c in norm, r_n(c_n)→r(c), and r(c_n)→r(c). Every minimizing sequence for either problem converges in norm to its center. If a_n→a strongly then c=a; for Hilbert weak convergence a_n⇀a, r(x)²=‖x−a‖²+limsup_n‖a_n−a‖² and c=a.
For a nonexpansive T:C→C on nonempty closed convex C in uniformly convex Banach X, any bounded orbit a_n=Tⁿa has an asymptotic center c with Tc=c. The fixed-point set of T is closed and convex.
The proximal-map chapter uses a real Hilbert H, proper convex lsc φ:H→(−∞,+∞], finite domain D(φ), and norm closures throughout; bibliographic framing identifies required domain closures.

For real Hilbert H, proper convex lsc φ, λ>0 and f∈H, e_λ^φ(f)=inf_(v∈H)[φ(v)+‖f−v‖²/(2λ)] and its unique minimizer is P_λ^φf=prox_(λφ)f. For u∈D(φ), ∂φ(u)={w∈H:φ(v)≥φ(u)+(w,v−u) for every v}. The Hilbert conjugate is φ*(w)=sup_v[(w,v)−φ(v)].

For real Hilbert H, proper convex lsc φ, every f and λ>0 have finite e_λ^φ(f) and a unique minimizer u=P_λ^φf∈D(φ). Equivalently, (f−u,v−u)≤λ(φ(v)−φ(u)) for all v∈D(φ), equivalently (f−u)/λ∈∂φ(u). If u=P_λf,z=P_λg, then ‖u−z‖²≤(f−g,u−z) and ‖u−z‖≤‖f−g‖. If φ=I_K for nonempty closed convex K, P_λ^φ=P_K for every λ>0.

For real Hilbert H and proper convex lsc φ, φ* is proper convex lsc. For every f∈H and λ>0, u=P_λ^φ f and w=P_(1/λ)^(φ*)(f/λ) satisfy u+λw=f and φ(u)+φ*(w)=(u,w). The envelopes obey e_λ^φ(f)+e_(1/λ)^(φ*)(f/λ)=‖f‖²/(2λ). At λ=1 the two proximal minimizers sum to f and their minimum energies sum to ‖f‖²/2.
For every f in a real Hilbert H and proper convex lsc φ, P_λ^φ f converges in norm to P_(closure D(φ))f as λ↓0, without requiring D(φ) closed or f in its closure.
For proper convex lsc φ on real Hilbert H, let M=argmin_H φ. If M is nonempty, it is closed convex and P_λ^φf→P_Mf in norm as λ→∞ for every f. If M is empty, ‖P_λ^φf‖→∞.
For proper convex lsc φ on real Hilbert H and every f, (P_λ^φf)/λ→−P_(closure D(φ*))0 in norm as λ→∞.

All the real Hilbert proximal, primal–dual, energy and parameter-limit results hold for complex Hilbert spaces on their underlying real space, with real scalar product Re⟨x,y⟩, real convexity and real continuous functional subgradients; the conjugate uses Re⟨w,v⟩. No complex linearity of the nonlinear proximal map is asserted.
Additional Banach geometry problems use real spaces for order and monotonicity; complex sequence-ball and Clarkson variants are separately stated.

For convex K and a∈K, a is extreme iff K\{a} is convex. If a finite convex combination with strictly positive weights equals an extreme point, every entry equals that point. For compact convex K in a Hausdorff locally convex space, every nonempty closed extreme subset A contains an extreme point of K even if A is not convex. An extreme subset has the property that a proper convex combination of points of K lying in A forces both endpoints into A.

For real scalars, extreme points of closed unit balls are: for ℓ∞, exactly sequences with every coordinate ±1; for c, exactly convergent sequences of signs; for c₀, none; for ℓ¹, exactly ±e_n; for ℓᵖ, 1<p<∞, exactly norm-one vectors; for L¹(R), none. Over complex scalars replace signs by arbitrary modulus-one phases in the ℓ∞, c and ℓ¹ descriptions; the c₀, interior-exponent and nonatomic L¹ conclusions hold correspondingly.

For a convex cone P in real normed X and F=P−P, if every algebraic linear functional nonnegative on P is continuous, then F is closed and finite-codimensional. Conversely if X is Banach, P closed, and F closed finite-codimensional, every positive algebraic functional is continuous. In particular for a closed generating cone P in Banach X, ∃C such that every x=y−z with y,z∈P and ‖y‖,‖z‖≤C‖x‖.

For the nonnegative cone in real C[0,1], P−P=C[0,1] and every algebraic positive f is continuous with |f(u)|≤‖u‖∞ f(1). If the cone also requires both endpoint values zero, P−P={u:u(0)=u(1)=0} is closed codimension two and positivity still forces continuity. In X={u∈C¹[0,1]:u(0)=u(1)=0} with Banach C¹ norm, every u obeys |u(t)|≤C t(1−t) and u=(u+C t(1−t))−C t(1−t) is a positive decomposition, so P−P=X and positive functionals are continuous. With inherited sup norm instead, f(u)=u′(0) is positive but unbounded, as u_n(t)=t(1−t)e^(−nt) has derivative 1 at 0 and ‖u_n‖∞→0.

Let A:D(A)⊆X→X′ be a closed real linear operator on Banach X with q(y)=(Ay)(y)≥0. The condition inf_(y∈D(A))[q(y)−(Ay)(x)]>−∞ for every x∈D(A) is equivalent to existence of k≥0 with |(Ay)(x)|²≤k(‖x‖+‖Ax‖)² q(y) for all x,y∈D(A). If D(A)=X, for each α>0, ‖Ay‖²≤αq(y) for every y iff q(y)−(Ay)(x)≥−α‖x‖²/4 for all x,y. This estimate holds iff its same-α transpose version holds for A′|_X:X→X′ under canonical evaluation; symmetry is unnecessary.

Every weakly Cauchy sequence in ℓ¹ converges in norm. In L¹(0,1) there is a weakly null sequence of norm one. For any monotone A:B_X→X′ on the closed unit ball of a real normed X whose unit sphere S_X is nonempty, A(B_X) is contained in the weak-star closed convex hull of A(S_X).
The Rademacher functions r_n(t)=sign(sin(2ⁿπt)) on (0,1) have L¹ norm one, form an L² orthonormal sequence, and are weakly null in L¹(0,1).

For closed densely defined A:D(A)⊆X→Y between Banach spaces, weak-star closure Ran A′=(ker A)⊥ and weak-star closure D(A′)=Y′. The first closure can be norm closure if X is reflexive; the second if Y is reflexive. A maximal monotone real linear B:D(B)⊆X→X′ has closed graph and dense domain. Every everywhere-defined real linear monotone map X→X′ is maximal monotone and hence bounded.

For 1<p<∞, q=p/(p−1), and a positive measure admitting usual Lᵖ duality (in particular σ-finite), real or complex f,g∈Lᵖ satisfy, if p≥2, ‖f+g‖_p^p+‖f−g‖_p^p≤2(‖f‖_p^q+‖g‖_p^q)^(p/q)≤2^(p−1)(‖f‖_p^p+‖g‖_p^p); if 1<p≤2, ‖f+g‖_p^q+‖f−g‖_p^q≤2(‖f‖_p^p+‖g‖_p^p)^(q/p). Lᵖ is uniformly convex, with valid modulus 1−(1−(ε/2)^r)^(1/r), r=max(p,q), for 0≤ε≤2.

On any finite measure space, if bounded linear T:L¹→L¹ satisfies T(L∞)⊆L∞, its L∞ restriction is automatically bounded. With endpoint norms N₁,N∞, for 1<p<∞ and every f∈Lᵖ, ‖Tf‖_p≤N₁^(1/p)N∞^(1−1/p)‖f‖_p. Both real and complex operators and the zero-measure case are included.
The real geometric chapter supplies independent proofs of Hilbert norm characterizations; bibliographic/proof-route comments impose no additional intermediate-result obligations.

Fix a real three-dimensional vector space with auxiliary Euclidean coordinates. K is a centrally symmetric convex body containing 0 in its interior, and for every central plane L there is a linear projection P_L with P_LK⊆K, hence P_LK=K∩L. For boundary p, N(p)={f∈(R³)′:f(x)≤f(p) for all x∈K} is the supporting normal cone, including zero. Nonzero members have f(p)>0; normals exist by separation, and restriction to a central plane through p maps N(p) onto the section normal cone via extension g↦gP_L. If rB₂⊆K⊆RB₂, ‖P_L‖₂≤R/r uniformly. The normal-cone statements/bound are setup for the named geometry lemmas.

For centrally symmetric real three-dimensional convex body K with 0 interior and a K-preserving projection onto every central plane, the boundary has a unique supporting plane at every point. Each such central-plane projection is unique, and its kernel line depends continuously on the plane.

Under the same three-dimensional K hypotheses, fix p∈∂K and the central plane E parallel to its supporting plane. The sections of K by any two planes containing Rp are linearly equivalent by a map fixing p and preserving the coordinate along p in R³=E⊕Rp.
Every centrally symmetric real three-dimensional convex body K with 0 interior and a K-preserving linear projection onto every central plane is an ellipsoid.

For real normed X of dimension at least three, the norm comes from an inner product iff every two-dimensional linear subspace is the range of a linear projection of norm one. Completeness is not required; if X is complete the resulting inner-product space is Hilbert.

In dimension two, the identity is a norm-one projection onto the sole two-dimensional subspace of any normed space, while the unit ball need not be an ellipse; thus the dimension-at-least-three condition in Kakutani is necessary.
For any real normed space define the radial retraction onto its closed unit ball by R(x)=x/max(1,‖x‖).
For any real normed space, its radial retraction R is nonexpansive iff for every equal-norm pair ‖x‖=‖y‖>0 and every minimizer λ₀∈R of λ↦‖x−λy‖, one has |λ₀|≤1.
A real normed space of dimension at least three has nonexpansive radial retraction onto its closed unit ball iff its norm comes from an inner product.

Define Birkhoff orthogonality x⊥_B y by ‖x‖≤‖x+ty‖ for every real t. In every real normed space radial nonexpansion is equivalent to symmetry of this orthogonality. The norm ‖(s,t)‖=max(|s|,|t|,|s+t|) on R² has this symmetry and nonexpansive radial retraction, but is not an inner-product norm.
In this chapter X,Y,Z are Banach unless otherwise stated. The Banach adjoint is T′:Y′→X′, and canonical isometry J_X:X→X″ is (J_Xx)(x′)=x′(x).
For bounded linear T:X→Y, T′y′=y′∘T is bounded with ‖T′‖=‖T‖ and T″J_X=J_YT. For arbitrary normed X,Y, a linear S:Y′→X′ equals T′ for some bounded T:X→Y iff S is continuous from σ(Y′,Y) to σ(X′,X).

Compact operators K(X,Y) between Banach spaces form a norm-closed linear space and a two-sided operator ideal. T is compact iff its Banach adjoint T′ is compact. A compact operator sends each weakly convergent sequence to a norm-convergent sequence with the corresponding image limit; no entire weak-to-norm topological continuity is asserted.

Banach X has approximation property AP iff for every norm-compact K⊆X and ε>0 there is a bounded finite-rank F:X→X with sup_(x∈K)‖Fx−x‖<ε. A common bound on ‖F‖ is not required; it is the additional bounded approximation property.

Every compact K⊆Banach X lies in the closed absolutely convex hull C of a norm-null sequence, chosen so that K is compact for the Minkowski norm p_C as well. Every such C is compact. The space X_C=⋃_(n≥1)nC with p_C(x)=inf{t>0:x∈tC} is Banach; its inclusion i_C:X_C→X is injective compact and maps its closed unit ball onto C.

Banach X has AP iff for every Banach Y every compact T:Y→X is an operator-norm limit of bounded finite-rank Y→X operators. Every real or complex Hilbert space and every Banach space with Schauder basis has AP; basis partial-sum approximants have a common operator-norm bound. Existence of a Banach space without AP is a separate later construction.

For bounded T:X→Y between Banach spaces, these are equivalent: T is weakly compact; T″(X″)⊆J_Y(Y); T′:(Y′,σ(Y′,Y))→(X′,σ(X′,X″)) is continuous. Also T is weakly compact iff T′ is. Weakly compact operators form a norm-closed two-sided operator ideal.

For bounded T:X→Y between Banach spaces, T maps weakly compact subsets to norm-relatively-compact subsets iff it maps weakly convergent sequences to norm-convergent sequences. Every compact operator has this complete-continuity property. If X is reflexive this is equivalent to compactness. Without reflexivity the converse fails: identity on ℓ¹ is completely continuous but not compact (Schur property: every weakly convergent ℓ¹ sequence converges in norm).

For Banach X, these are equivalent: every weakly compact operator X→Y, for every Banach Y, is completely continuous; the same assertion with Y=c₀; for all weakly null x_n∈X and weakly null x_n′∈X′, x_n′(x_n)→0. This defines/characterizes the Dunford–Pettis property.
C(K) and L¹ Dunford–Pettis examples and their Vitali–Hahn–Saks bridge are separate later statements; this is a reference, not a duplicate obligation.
Let a unital algebra A⊆B(X) on complex Banach X have no nonzero proper common closed invariant subspace. For every nonzero compact K:X→X there is A∈A such that AK has eigenvalue one.

Any nonscalar bounded operator T on a complex Banach space commuting with a nonzero compact operator has a nonzero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace (invariant under every operator commuting with T), hence a nontrivial closed invariant subspace.
The Dunford–Pettis property of C(K) and L¹ is distinguished from weak compactness criteria for L¹ subsets; bibliographic and proof-route framing.

Let λ be finite positive on a sigma algebra Σ, and μ_n finite signed or complex countably additive measures with μ_n≪λ. If μ_n(A) converges for every A∈Σ then lim_(δ↓0) sup_n sup_(λ(A)<δ)|μ_n|(A)=0. The setwise limit is countably additive and absolutely continuous w.r.t. λ. In particular this applies to a weakly convergent sequence of finite regular measures on compact Hausdorff K with finite regular control λ=Σ_n 2^(−n)|μ_n|/(1+‖μ_n‖); weak-star convergence alone is insufficient.
On any positive measure space, if g_n⇀0 weakly in the Banach space L∞(μ), then ∫_A|g_n|dμ→0 for every measurable A with μ(A)<∞. Both real and complex scalars are included.

For every compact Hausdorff K, real or complex C(K) has the Dunford–Pettis property. For every positive measure space, real or complex L¹(μ) has the Dunford–Pettis property, without σ-finiteness or separability requirements.

Algebras in this chapter are complex. A unital Banach algebra is nonzero with ‖1‖=1. The resolvent convention is R(λ,A)=(λI−A)⁻¹; spectra of nonunital algebras are taken in the unitization. Scalar Cauchy and Runge results are underlying complex-analysis tools, not extra functional-analysis axioms.

For any complex Banach algebra A, its unitization A~=A⊕C has product (a,λ)(b,μ)=(ab+λb+μa,λμ), norm ‖a‖+|λ|, and is a unital Banach algebra with identity (0,1). Every closed two-sided ideal I has a Banach quotient A/I with well-defined submultiplicative multiplication and quotient norm.

For a bounded surjection T:X→Y between Banach spaces, every sufficiently small operator-norm perturbation is surjective; a complemented kernel or bounded linear right inverse is not assumed. Any boundary point λ of the spectrum of a bounded operator A has λI−A not surjective.

For compact Hausdorff K, the characters of complex C(K) are exactly point evaluations. For completely regular Hausdorff S, the character space Δ(C_b(S)) is its Gelfand compactification: evaluation gives a dense topological embedding S→Δ, every bounded continuous scalar function on S extends uniquely to Δ, and Δ has the Stone–Čech universal property of unique extension of continuous maps S→K into compact Hausdorff spaces. Characters of disk and polydisk algebras are evaluations at points of the closed disk/polydisk. For empty K or S the function algebra is zero and its character space empty, with the corresponding empty compactification interpretation.

For complex ℓᵖ(N), 1≤p<∞, the forward shift has spectrum the closed unit disk, empty point spectrum, and approximate point spectrum the unit circle. The backward shift has the same full spectrum and open unit disk as point spectrum. For every bounded operator T on complex Banach X, σ(T′)=σ(T); for a complex Hilbert adjoint, σ(T*)=conjugate σ(T).

For any a in a nonzero complex unital Banach algebra A with normalized identity, σ(a) is nonempty compact and contained in {|z|≤‖a‖}; R(λ,a)=(λ1−a)⁻¹ is analytic on the resolvent and satisfies R(λ,a)−R(μ,a)=(μ−λ)R(λ,a)R(μ,a). The spectral radius r(a)=lim_(n→∞)‖aⁿ‖^(1/n)=inf_(n≥1)‖aⁿ‖^(1/n). Every complex Banach division algebra is (isometrically) C.
For open U⊆C and Banach X, f:U→X is analytic in norm iff x′∘f is scalar analytic for every continuous scalar-linear x′∈X′.

For a in a nonzero complex unital Banach algebra and f holomorphic on an open neighborhood U of σ(a), choose a finite positively oriented contour cycle Γ⊆U\σ(a) with winding one near σ(a) and zero off U. The Riesz–Dunford value f(a)=(2πi)⁻¹∫_Γ f(z)R(z,a)dz is independent of cycle and chosen neighborhood. It gives a unital algebra homomorphism agreeing with polynomials and resolvents, with full spectral mapping σ(f(a))=f(σ(a)). Uniform convergence on a fixed contour gives norm convergence of values. Any bounded operator commuting with a commutes with every f(a).

For bounded T on complex Banach X and a spectral partition σ(T)=K₁ disjoint-union K₂ into compact sets, choose f=1 near K₁ and 0 near K₂. P=f(T) is a bounded projection commuting with T and X=PX⊕(I−P)X, with restricted spectra K₁,K₂ respectively (omit a zero summand). For isolated λ∈σ(T), λ is a pole of exact order m of the resolvent iff (T−λI)|_(PX), for the singleton Riesz projection, is nilpotent of exact order m; T−λI is invertible on the complementary summand.

If B⊆A is a closed unital complex Banach subalgebra with the same identity and a∈B, then σ_A(a)⊆σ_B(a), ∂σ_B(a)⊆∂σ_A(a), and their polynomial hulls agree. Each connected component of C\σ_A(a) is either wholly contained in σ_B(a) or disjoint from it. The spectrum of a in the closed algebra generated by 1,a equals the polynomial hull of σ_A(a).

For a commutative nonzero complex unital Banach algebra A, its characters are precisely quotient maps onto C coming from maximal ideals, each has norm one, and the character space Δ is compact Hausdorff in the weak-star topology. For all a, σ(a)={χ(a):χ∈Δ}; â(χ)=χ(a) is continuous and ‖â‖∞=r(a). The Gelfand transform A→C(Δ) is a contractive unital algebra homomorphism with kernel the intersection of maximal ideals.

For a nonzero complex unital Banach algebra A, any algebraic linear φ:A→C satisfying φ(1)=1 and φ(a)≠0 for every invertible a is a continuous character; continuity and multiplicativity are conclusions.

The identity component of the invertible group of a nonzero complex unital Banach algebra consists exactly of finite products of exponentials. If σ(a) lies in a domain admitting a holomorphic logarithm, a=e^b with b=(log)(a); holomorphic roots follow by calculus under the corresponding branch hypothesis. Every invertible operator on a complex Hilbert space is a product of two exponentials and its invertible group is norm-path-connected. No Kuiper contractibility assertion is included.

For a locally compact abelian group G with Haar measure, complex L¹(G) is a commutative Banach algebra under convolution; its nonzero characters are exactly f↦∫_G f(x)overline(γ(x))dx for continuous group homomorphisms γ:G→unit circle. In particular if Σ_(n∈Z)|a_n|<∞ and f(e^(it))=Σ_n a_n e^(int) never vanishes, then 1/f has an absolutely convergent Fourier series.
Riesz theory initially permits incomplete normed X, with compact closure taken in X itself; Banach assumptions are introduced only in subsequent statements requiring completeness/open mapping.

For compact K:X→X on any real or complex normed space (compact closure in X), A=I−K has finite-dimensional kernel and closed range. The ascending kernels and descending ranges of Aⁿ stabilize; for all sufficiently large r, X=ker Aʳ⊕Ran Aʳ and A restricts to a bounded isomorphism on Ran Aʳ. A is injective iff surjective; if bijective its inverse is bounded. Over C every nonzero spectral value of K is an eigenvalue of finite algebraic multiplicity, and zero is the only possible accumulation point of the nonzero spectrum.

Let (X_j,Y_j), j=1,2, be nondegenerate bilinear dual systems of normed spaces, without pairing boundedness assumed. Let bounded paired adjoints T:X₁→X₂,T′:Y₂→Y₁ and R:X₂→X₁,R′:Y₁→Y₂ have all four defects I−RT,I−TR,I−T′R′,I−R′T′ compact. Then T,T′ have finite-dimensional kernels and cokernels; Ran T={f∈X₂:[f,y]=0 for every y∈ker T′} and codim Ran T=dim ker T′, with the analogous T′ formulas. For left regularization, RTx=Rf has exactly the original Tx=f solutions for every f iff R is injective. For right regularization TRz=f, mapping z↦Rz covers all original solutions for every f iff R is surjective.

For every linear map of vector spaces T:X→Y, algebraic complements of ker T and Ran T yield a linear S:Y→X with TST=T and STS=S; I−ST and I−TS project onto ker T and a range complement. If these dimensions are finite, their difference ind T=dim ker T−codim Ran T is additive under products. Equivalently finite kernel and cokernel iff a linear inverse modulo finite-rank defects exists. Finite-rank perturbations preserve this algebraic index without topology; arbitrary algebraic-complement pseudoinverses are not asserted bounded.

For every continuous Φ:unit circle→GL_d(C), its Toeplitz operator on H²(unit circle;Cᵈ) is Fredholm with ind T_Φ=−wind(det Φ,0). A nonvanishing bounded measurable scalar symbol need not give a Fredholm Toeplitz operator: the unimodular a.e. boundary symbol of θ(z)=exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) is an explicit example, whose Toeplitz isometry has closed range of infinite codimension.

Let normed X,Y have a nondegenerate bilinear pairing [ , ]:X×Y→C, without assumed pairing boundedness. If compact K:X→X,L:Y→Y satisfy [Kx,y]=[x,Ly], then either both I−K,I−L are bijective, or their kernels have the same positive finite dimension. In all cases Ran(I−K)={f∈X:[f,y]=0 for every y∈ker(I−L)}, and the analogous Y formula holds. The sesquilinear version follows by conjugating one scalar structure.

For compact Hausdorff Q with finite regular measure μ and continuous real or complex kernel k∈C(Q×Q), Kf(x)=∫k(x,y)f(y)dμ(y) is compact C(Q)→C(Q). For bounded T on Banach X with ‖T‖<1, (I−T)⁻¹=Σ_(n≥0)Tⁿ in operator norm. For a continuous Volterra kernel on a≤y≤x≤b bounded in modulus by M, Vf(x)=∫_a^x k(x,y)f(y)dy satisfies ‖Vⁿ‖≤Mⁿ(b−a)ⁿ/n!; thus I−λV is invertible for every complex λ and on the infinite-dimensional function space σ(V)={0}.
A bounded T:X→Y between Banach spaces is Fredholm iff Ran T is closed and ker T and coker T=Y/Ran T are finite-dimensional; ind T=dim ker T−dim(Y/Ran T).

A bounded T:X→Y between Banach spaces is Fredholm iff it has a bounded parametrix S:Y→X with ST−I_X and TS−I_Y compact, equivalently with finite-rank defects. For X=Y this is equivalent to invertibility of its class in B(X)/K(X). On Hilbert spaces left semi-Fredholmness (a left parametrix modulo compact) iff closed range and finite-dimensional kernel; right semi-Fredholmness is the adjoint condition (closed range and finite-dimensional cokernel).

Products and direct sums of Fredholm operators are Fredholm with ind(ST)=ind S+ind T and ind(S⊕T)=ind S+ind T. The Fredholm set is norm-open, its index locally constant, and compact perturbations preserve Fredholmness and index. For Hilbert adjoints ind T*=−ind T. On Hilbert spaces the extended semi-Fredholm index (allowing ±∞) is locally constant on the semi-Fredholm set.
On a fixed complex Hilbert space, two Fredholm operators lie in the same norm-path component of the Fredholm operators iff their Fredholm indices agree.

For bounded T on infinite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert H, using the original scalar field for spectra and Fredholm indices, define σ_e(T)={λ:T−λI not Fredholm} and σ_w(T)=intersection_(compact K)σ(T+K). Then σ_w(T)=σ_e(T)∪{λ:T−λI Fredholm with nonzero index}; both sets are compact-perturbation invariant. For normal N, σ_w(N)=σ_e(N). Over C, σ_e(N) consists exactly of nonisolated spectral points and isolated eigenvalues of infinite multiplicity. Over R, real λ∈σ_e(N) iff λ∈σ(N_C) and either λ is nonisolated in the complexified spectrum or isolated there with ker_R(N−λI) infinite-dimensional. For real self-adjoint N its complexified spectrum is real, so the original isolated/nonisolated description holds in σ_R(N).

For bounded T on Banach X, λ∈σ_ap(T) iff there are unit vectors x_n with (T−λI)x_n→0; its complement is injectivity with closed range. Always ∂σ(T)⊆σ_ap(T). If A is Hilbert semi-Fredholm and ‖B‖<γ(A), then A+B is semi-Fredholm and neither its nullity nor its deficiency exceeds the corresponding dimension for A. Near any semi-Fredholm spectral λ of T, the nullity and deficiency of T−μI are constant on a sufficiently small punctured disk. A spectral boundary point is therefore either isolated or belongs to both left and right essential spectra.

For continuous complex symbol φ on the unit circle, T_φ=P_+ M_φ|_(H²). If φ is nowhere zero, T_φ is Fredholm, ind T_φ=−wind(φ,0), nullity=max(0,−wind φ), and cokernel dimension=max(0,wind φ). For every continuous φ, the Hankel map P_-M_φ|_(H²) is compact.
For an isolated spectral λ of a bounded operator T on a complex Hilbert space, T−λI is semi-Fredholm iff its Riesz projection has finite rank iff T−λI is Fredholm of index zero.

For bounded T:H→K and S:K→H between Hilbert spaces, if I_H−ST and I_K−TS are trace class, then T is Fredholm and ind T=tr(I_H−ST)−tr(I_K−TS). More generally if their mth powers are trace class for some integer m≥1, T is Fredholm and ind T=tr((I_H−ST)^m)−tr((I_K−TS)^m).

Let positive compact T on real or complex Hilbert H have decreasing eigenvalues μ_k repeated with multiplicity and zero-padded. For increasing closed V_n with dense union, P_n=P_(V_n), T_n=P_nT|_(V_n), and dim V_n≥k, their decreasing eigenvalues satisfy 0≤ν_k^(n)≤ν_k^(n+1)≤μ_k and ν_k^(n)→μ_k. More precisely |ν_k^(n)−μ_k|≤‖P_nTP_n−T‖→0, with zero padding. For R(x)=⟨x,Tx⟩/‖x‖² and finite integers 1≤k≤dim H, μ_k=max_(dim L=k) min_(0≠x∈L)R(x)=min_(dim M=k−1) sup_(0≠x∈M⊥)R(x). If T is injective, 1/μ_k=min_(dim L=k) sup_(0≠x∈L)1/R(x)=sup_(closed W, codim W=k−1) inf_(0≠x∈W)1/R(x), with the indicated attained min/max when stated; V_n need not be finite-dimensional.

For bounded T:E→F between Banach spaces, these right-sided conditions are equivalent: closed finite-codimensional Ran T and complemented ker T; TS=I_F+K for some bounded S and compact K; TU=I_F−P for some bounded U and finite-rank projection P. P may have rank exactly codim Ran T. Likewise the left-sided equivalents are: closed complemented range and finite-dimensional kernel; ST=I_E+K with bounded S and compact K; UT=I_E−Q with bounded U and finite-rank projection Q. Q may have rank exactly dim ker T. The complement conditions are essential.

For compact metric Q, finite positive Radon μ, continuous complex k on Q×Q, Kf(x)=∫_Q k(x,y)f(y)dμ(y), m=μ(Q), M=‖k‖∞. Define D_k(z)=Σ_(n≥0)(−z)ⁿ/n! ∫_(Qⁿ)det[k(t_i,t_j)]dμⁿ. Define B_k(x,y;z) by the analogous series whose determinant is the augmented kernel matrix with row indices x,t₁,…,t_n and column indices y,t₁,…,t_n. Empty determinant and integral equal one; the n=0 term of B_k is k(x,y). This continuous-kernel determinant is distinct from the trace-class determinant absent an actual trace-class hypothesis.

Under the continuous-kernel setup, D_k is entire scalar with D_k(0)=1, B_k is entire valued in C(Q×Q), and for every x,y,z: B_k(x,y;z)=D_k(z)k(x,y)+z∫ k(x,t)B_k(t,y;z)dμ(t)=D_k(z)k(x,y)+z∫ B_k(x,t;z)k(t,y)dμ(t), while D_k′(z)=−∫ B_k(t,t;z)dμ(t). I−zK is invertible iff D_k(z)≠0, and then (I−zK)⁻¹f(x)=f(x)+(z/D_k(z))∫ B_k(x,y;z)f(y)dμ(y). Exceptional parameters form a discrete set and are exactly reciprocals of nonzero eigenvalues of K.

For continuous kernels on the same compact metric Q with finite positive Radon μ, D_k varies continuously under uniform kernel convergence, locally uniformly in z. If h(x,y)=k(x,y)+ℓ(x,y)−∫k(x,t)ℓ(t,y)dμ(t), then D_h(1)=D_k(1)D_ℓ(1); the same holds after arbitrary scalar multiples of k,ℓ are substituted. If k_j is the continuous kernel of Kʲ and c_j=∫ k_j(t,t)dμ(t), then near zero log D_k(z)=−Σ_(j≥1)zʲc_j/j. If K on L²(μ) is trace class then c_j=tr Kʲ for every j≥1 and D_k(z)=det(I−zK) in the trace-class sense.

Under the continuous-kernel setup, let λ_j be the nonzero eigenvalues of K on L²(μ), repeated with algebraic multiplicity. Then D_k(z)=exp(−z∫k(t,t)dμ(t))∏_j(1−zλ_j)e^(zλ_j), locally uniformly in z. Every nonzero root has the algebraic multiplicity of its reciprocal eigenvalue. Nonzero eigenvalues and their algebraic multiplicities on C(Q) and L² agree, even without full support for μ; an unregularized product is not asserted without trace class.

Let Q=[a,b] with L=b−a>0, μ finite positive Radon of mass m, and continuous k satisfy |k|≤M and |k(x,y)−k(x,z)|≤H|y−z|^α for 0<α≤1. For every n≥2 and arbitrary x_i,y_j∈Q, |det[k(x_i,y_j)]|≤n^(n/2) M H^(n−1)(L/(n−1))^(α(n−1)). The same holds for Hölder regularity in the first variable. The coefficient d_n of zⁿ in D_k satisfies |d_n|≤(mⁿ/n!) n^(n/2) M H^(n−1)(L/(n−1))^(α(n−1)). The entire-function order of D_k is ≤1/(α+1/2), where order is limsup_(r→∞) log log max{e,max_(|z|≤r)|D_k(z)|}/log r.

For n−1 successive nonnegative gaps y_(j+1)−y_j of ordered points in an interval of length L, their sum is ≤L and their product is ≤(L/(n−1))^(n−1). The printed n^(−n) unit-interval bound for those gaps is false: n=2,y₁=0,y₂=1 gives product one. The corrected Hölder estimate retains the improved entire-function order and Fredholm resolvent identities.

For arbitrary possibly nonseparable Hilbert H,K, every compact operator H→K has separable range closure and countable nonzero singular part; its kernel may have arbitrary Hilbert dimension. Trace statements retain their stated ideal hypotheses; continuity of a kernel alone does not imply trace class.

A compact normal operator N on any complex Hilbert H decomposes H as the orthogonal Hilbert sum of ker N and its finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces. Distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal; nonzero eigenvalues are at most countable, with finitely many |λ|≥ε for each ε>0. Nx=Σ_(λ≠0)λP_λx in norm; finite spectral sums ordered by decreasing modulus converge in operator norm to N. Every omitted tail has norm exactly sup of omitted eigenvalue moduli, empty sup=0. Two complex compact normal operators are unitarily equivalent iff all eigenvalue multiplicities agree, including the arbitrary cardinal dimension of their kernels.

Every compact normal N on a real Hilbert space has an orthogonal Hilbert decomposition into its kernel, nonzero real eigenvalue lines, and two-dimensional reducing planes with matrix B(a,b)=[[a,−b],[b,a]], b>0. There are at most countably many nonzero blocks, finitely many of modulus ≥ε for each ε>0; line moduli are |λ| and plane moduli √(a²+b²). Finite block truncations converge in operator norm with exact tail norm equal to the supremum of omitted block moduli (empty supremum zero). Orthogonal equivalence is characterized by multiplicities of every real eigenvalue and every pair (a,b), b>0, and real Hilbert kernel dimension. For compact self-adjoint operators over R or C the eigenvector expansion has only real eigenvalues, with no nonreal real-plane blocks. Zero spaces/operators and finite spectra are included.
On R², N(x,y)=(−y,x) satisfies N*=−N, N*N=NN*=I and N²=−I, hence is compact normal, but has no nonzero real eigenvector. Its real spectral decomposition is the single rotation plane B(0,1).

For compact T:H→K on real or complex Hilbert spaces, there are decreasing positive singular values s_j→0 and orthonormal (v_j),(u_j), finite lists terminated and then zero-padded, with Tx=Σ_j s_j u_j⟨v_j,x⟩ in norm, T*u_j=s_jv_j, and (ker T)⊥=closure span{v_j}. For every n≥1, s_n(T)=inf_(rank F<n)‖T−F‖ and s_n(ATB)≤‖A‖‖B‖s_n(T) for compatible bounded A,B. For compact positive C with decreasing eigenvalues λ_n and finite n within the Hilbert dimension, λ_n=inf_(dim L=n−1) sup_(x⊥L,‖x‖=1)⟨x,Cx⟩=sup_(dim L=n) inf_(x∈L,‖x‖=1)⟨x,Cx⟩, using zero padding where appropriate; positive and negative eigenvalues of self-adjoint compact operators are treated separately.

For bounded T:H→K, the arbitrary-basis sum ‖T‖₂²=Σ_i‖Te_i‖² is independent of orthonormal basis. Its finiteness defines the Hilbert–Schmidt ideal S₂; such T are compact and ‖T‖₂²=Σ_j s_j(T)². S₂(H,K) is Hilbert with inner product tr(S*T). For σ-finite positive measure spaces (X,μ),(Y,ν), every k∈L²(ν×μ) defines T_k:L²(μ)→L²(ν) by (T_kf)(y)=∫k(y,x)f(x)dμ(x), with ‖T_k‖₂=‖k‖₂, and every Hilbert–Schmidt operator between these L² spaces has a unique such kernel up to a.e. equality. Nonseparable Hilbert spaces are allowed.

For compact T between Hilbert spaces, trace class means ‖T‖₁=Σ_j s_j(T)<∞. It is a complete two-sided ideal with ‖ATB‖₁≤‖A‖‖T‖₁‖B‖. For endomorphisms, tr T=Σ_i⟨e_i,Te_i⟩ is absolutely convergent and basis-independent, |tr T|≤‖T‖₁, and tr(AT)=tr(TA) for compatible bounded A. Trace-class maps are exactly products of two Hilbert–Schmidt maps (an intermediate Hilbert space may be used), and ‖AB‖₁≤‖A‖₂‖B‖₂.

For a compact complex Hilbert operator T, order its nonzero eigenvalues λ_j by decreasing modulus, repeated with algebraic multiplicity. For each n for which the list is defined, ∏_(j=1)^n|λ_j(T)|≤∏_(j=1)^n s_j(T); also Σ_j|λ_j(T)|≤Σ_j s_j(T). For every r≥0, ∏_j(1+r|λ_j|)≤∏_j(1+rs_j) whenever the latter product converges.
Every trace-class operator T on a complex Hilbert space satisfies tr T=Σ_j λ_j(T), with algebraic multiplicity and absolute convergence. Normality is not assumed.

For trace-class T on a complex Hilbert space, det(I+zT)=Σ_(n≥0)zⁿ tr(∧ⁿT)=∏_j(1+zλ_j(T)) is entire. It depends continuously on T in trace norm, locally uniformly in z; it vanishes exactly at parameters for which I+zT is not invertible. For all S,T∈S₁, det((I+S)(I+T))=det(I+S)det(I+T).

Let compact metric Q carry a finite positive measure μ with full support and let continuous Hermitian k on Q×Q have positive integral operator K on L²(μ). Then k(x,y)=Σ_j λ_j e_j(x)overline(e_j(y)), absolutely and uniformly on Q×Q, where λ_j>0 are nonzero eigenvalues and e_j normalized continuous eigenfunctions. K is trace class and tr K=∫_Q k(x,x)dμ(x). More generally this diagonal trace identity holds for any trace-class integral operator with continuous kernel on this space, without positivity or Hermitian symmetry. Real and complex Hermitian/symmetric variants are included.

Let nonempty compact Hausdorff Q and compact K:C(Q)→C(Q) preserve real functions and satisfy Kf>0 everywhere for every nonzero f≥0. Then r=r(K)>0 is an algebraically simple eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenfunction u. Every other eigenvalue has modulus <r; there is a positive eigenmeasure φ for K′ and r^(−n)Kⁿ→P in operator norm, with Pf=uφ(f)/φ(u), Ku=ru. If K1=1, then r=1,u=1 and normalized φ is the unique invariant probability measure.

Let (e_n) be an orthonormal basis in a real or complex Hilbert H and Σ_n‖y_n−e_n‖²<∞. The resulting bounded map B(Σ c_ne_n)=Σ c_ny_n is invertible if ker B=0; then (y_n) is a Riesz basis, with unique norm-convergent square-summable expansions. In particular Σ_n‖y_n−e_n‖²<1 alone suffices. Zero kernel excludes all nonzero square-summable infinite relations; finite linear independence alone is insufficient.

Let real Banach X have a closed convex cone P with nonempty interior and P≠X. If compact linear T satisfies T(P\{0})⊆int P, there are u₀∈int P and μ₀>0 with Tu₀=μ₀u₀. Every eigenvector in P\{0} is a positive multiple of u₀, with eigenvalue μ₀. μ₀ is algebraically simple, every other nonzero eigenvalue of the complexification has modulus <μ₀, and μ₀ is its complex spectral radius. No normality of P is assumed.

Order positivity on C(Q) is preservation of nonnegative real functions; it is distinct from Hilbert quadratic-form positivity. Strong positivity/cone results use their explicit order hypotheses, not merely a nonselfadjoint kernel called positive.
Regularity criteria chapter distinguishes sufficient trace-class conditions from trace identities assuming trace class, uses Lebesgue measure below, and supplies counterexamples to continuity alone.

Let k∈C([0,1]²) satisfy |k(x,y)−k(x′,y)|≤H|x−x′|^α for every x,x′,y and some 1/2<α≤1. Its Lebesgue L² integral operator K is trace class with ‖K‖₁≤‖k‖_(L²([0,1]²))+H/(1−2^(1/2−α)). The same holds for regularity in the second variable. In particular every C¹ and every smooth kernel is trace class. For nonzero eigenvalues λ_j counted with algebraic multiplicity, ∫₀¹k(t,t)dt=tr K=Σ_jλ_j and D_k(z)=∏_j(1−zλ_j). Both sum and product converge absolutely, the product locally uniformly in z. Affine changes of variables give corresponding statements on every compact interval.

On real or complex L²(0,1), Vf(x)=∫₀ˣf(t)dt is compact, Hilbert–Schmidt and quasinilpotent, but not trace class. Its singular values are ((n+1/2)π)⁻¹ for n≥0. Its ordinary trigonometric diagonal sum is 1/2 in either field, despite no nonzero eigenvalues. In complex L², the exponential basis has no unordered diagonal sum.

There exists a real continuous even f on the circle such that the continuous symmetric convolution kernel k(x,y)=f(x−y) defines a compact self-adjoint operator on L²(unit circle) that is not trace class. Thus continuity and symmetry do not replace Mercer positivity or the proved Hölder trace-class regularity. The proof constructs f by uniformly convergent disjoint Rudin–Shapiro frequency blocks, with divergent sum of absolute Fourier coefficients.
