Spectral chapter conventions: Hilbert spaces need not be separable unless explicitly required. The abstract C*-involution a↦a* is represented by the Hilbert adjoint; scalar regular measure representation is the separately proved Riesz–Markov theorem.

The C*-unitization norm. Here a C*-algebra has its given complete C*-norm and involution; the unitization has underlying vector space A⊕C, product (a,λ)(b,μ)=(ab+λb+μa,λμ), involution (a,λ)*=(a*,conj λ), and identity (0,1). The algebraic unitization of a nonunital nonzero C*-algebra becomes a C*-algebra with $\|(a,\lambda)\|=\|L_a+\lambda I\|_{\faB(\mathcal A)}$, where $L_ax=ax$. This is not in general the Banach-algebra sum norm. It contains $\mathcal A$ isometrically as a closed ideal.

Separable abelian von Neumann algebras. All *-algebras mentioned are unital operator *-algebras on the indicated real or complex Hilbert space; W*(N) denotes the von Neumann algebra generated by N,N* and I. Inner products are conjugate-linear first. A vector e is cyclic when the algebra orbit has dense linear span, and separating when Ae=0 implies A=0. Suppose $H$ is separable, over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Every maximal abelian unital WOT-closed *-algebra has a cyclic vector, and every abelian von Neumann algebra has a separating vector. For complex $H$, every such maximal algebra is unitarily the scalar multiplication algebra $L^\infty(\mu)$ on $L^2(\mu)$. For a bounded complex normal $N$, there is a finite scalar control measure $\mu$ on $\sigma(N)$ such that \[ W^*(N)=\{f(N):f\text{ bounded Borel}\}\cong L^\infty(\mu). \] Under this isomorphism $\sigma(L^\infty,L^1)$ equals WOT on the whole algebra. For real $H$, use the canonical Hilbert complexification $H_{\mathbb C}$, its conjugation $J$, and $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}=\mathcal A+i\mathcal A$. If $\tau$ is a measure-preserving involution, write \[ L^p_\tau(\mu)=\{g\in L^p(\mu;\mathbb C): g(\tau x)=\overline{g(x)}\text{ a.e.}\}, \qquad p=1,2,\infty, \] with their inherited real structures. Every real maximal abelian algebra has the orthogonal scalar model of all multipliers from $L^\infty_\tau(\mu)$ on $L^2_\tau(\mu)$, for a finite regular Borel measure on a compact metrizable space and an involutive measure-preserving homeomorphism $\tau$. For a bounded real normal $N$, take $X=\sigma_{\mathbb C}(N_{\mathbb C})$ and $\tau z=\bar z$. There is a finite $\tau$-invariant scalar control measure $\mu$ for the complex spectral PVM $E_{\mathbb C}$, meaning $E_{\mathbb C}(B)=0$ iff $\mu(B)=0$ for every Borel $B\subset X$, and \[ W^*_{\mathbb R}(N)= \{f(N_{\mathbb C})|_H:f\text{ bounded Borel}, f(\bar z)=\overline{f(z)}\} \cong L^\infty_\tau(\mu). \] Here the restrictions are real bounded operators. The real duality $L^\infty_\tau(\mu)=(L^1_\tau(\mu))'$ uses $(f,g)\mapsto\int fg\,d\mu\in\mathbb R$, and its weak-star topology equals real WOT on the whole algebra. For real self-adjoint $N$, $\tau$ is the identity on its spectrum and this is the usual real scalar calculus. All these finite-control-measure assertions are restricted to separable $H$; zero spaces and zero measures are included.

Separable spectral multiplicity and the commutant. A bounded normal operator on a separable Hilbert space is classified, up to unitary equivalence, by a finite measure class $[\mu]$ on $\mathbb C$ and a measurable multiplicity function $m:\mathbb C\to\{1,2,\ldots,\infty\}$, modulo $\mu$-null sets. It has the model $M_z$ on $\int^\oplus\mathbb C^{m(z)}d\mu(z)$, supported on its spectrum. Its commutant is exactly the essentially bounded measurable fields $z\mapsto B(z)\in\faB(\mathbb C^{m(z)})$ acting fiberwise. This classification statement is separable; the arbitrary-Hilbert cyclic-sum theorem remains valid without this restriction.

Commutative C*-representation and permanence. For the C*-algebras in the statement, Δ is the compact character space and the Gelfand transform is a↦(χ↦χ(a)); C*-subalgebras share the ambient identity. The normal-element calculus uses the unital algebra generated by 1,a,a*. The Gelfand transform of a commutative unital C*-algebra is an isometric *-isomorphism onto $C(\Delta)$. A unital C*-subalgebra has the same spectra as its ambient C*-algebra. For normal $a$, continuous functions on $\sigma(a)$ have a unique isometric unital *-calculus, generated by $z\mapsto a$, with full spectral mapping.

Closed ideals and automatic norm control. Ideals are closed two-sided linear ideals in the given C*-norm. An approximate identity of positive contractions means a net e_i∈I with 0≤e_i, ||e_i||≤1, and e_i a→a, a e_i→a for every a∈I. No separability or unit is required unless stated. Every closed two-sided ideal $I$ in a C*-algebra is *-invariant and has an approximate identity of positive contractions. The quotient with its quotient norm is a C*-algebra. Every *-homomorphism of C*-algebras is contractive, isometric when injective, and has closed range.

States and GNS. Let A be a unital C*-algebra, positivity of a scalar-linear functional meaning nonnegative values on positive elements, and inner products conjugate-linear in the first variable. The zero algebra has no normalized state; its sum-of-states representation on the zero space is faithful vacuously. Every positive functional $\varphi$ on a unital C*-algebra satisfies $|\varphi(b^*a)|^2\leq\varphi(a^*a)\varphi(b^*b)$ and $\|\varphi\|=\varphi(1)$. A state is a positive functional with value one at the identity. Each state has a cyclic representation $\pi_\varphi:\mathcal A\to\faB(H_\varphi)$ with unit cyclic vector $\xi_\varphi$ and $\varphi(a)=\faip{\xi_\varphi}{\pi_\varphi(a)\xi_\varphi}$, unique up to a unitary carrying the cyclic vector to the cyclic vector. The direct sum of the GNS representations of all states is faithful.

Projection-valued measure. H is a real or complex Hilbert space, B(H) denotes bounded scalar-linear operators, and measurable scalar functions use the corresponding scalar field. Inner products are conjugate-linear first. A PVM on a measurable space $(S,\Sigma)$ is a map $E:\Sigma\to\faB(H)$ with $E(S)=I$, each $E(B)$ an orthogonal projection, $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$, and $E(\bigcup_n B_n)x=\sum_nE(B_n)x$ for disjoint $B_n$, with norm convergence for every $x$. Put $\mu_{xy}(B)=\faip{x}{E(B)y}$ and $\mu_x=\mu_{xx}$. For bounded measurable $f$, uniformly approximating it by simple functions defines $f(E)$, a contractive *-homomorphism with \[ \faip{x}{f(E)y}=\int f\,d\mu_{xy},\qquad \|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu_x. \]

Representations give PVMs. H is a Hilbert space and C(S) and B(H) use the same real or complex scalar field; no separability is imposed. The PVM is regular when every scalar measure <x,E(·)y> is regular. If $S$ is compact Hausdorff and $\pi:C(S)\to\faB(H)$ is a unital *-representation, there is a unique regular Borel PVM $E$ such that $\pi(f)=\int f\,dE$ for continuous $f$. The representation extends to all bounded Borel functions as a *-homomorphism.

Bounded normal spectral theorem. H is complex and need not be separable; f in the calculus is any bounded Borel scalar function on σ(N), and E-null means a Borel set B with E(B)=0. Every bounded normal $N$ on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space has a unique regular Borel PVM on $\sigma(N)$ with $N=\int z\,dE(z)$. Its bounded Borel calculus is a *-homomorphism, $\|f(N)\|$ is the $E$-essential supremum of $|f|$, and $\sigma(f(N))$ is its $E$-essential range. If $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere and $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, then $f_n(N)\to f(N)$ strongly. A bounded operator commuting with both $N,N^*$ commutes with all its spectral projections.

Cyclic models, including nonseparable spaces. Let N be a bounded normal operator on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space H, with its regular spectral PVM E and μ_e(B)=<e,E(B)e>. A vector e is cyclic when closure(C*(I,N)e)=H. If $e$ is cyclic for $C^*(I,N)$, then $N$ is unitarily equivalent to $M_z$ on $L^2(\mu_e)$, with $e$ corresponding to $1$. In general $H$ is an orthogonal direct sum of cyclic reducing spaces, with no separability assumption; equivalently $N$ is multiplication by a bounded function on a disjoint union of finite-measure spaces. That union need not be sigma-finite and there need not be one finite scalar control measure on $\sigma(N)$ for the whole representation.

Polar decomposition. H,K are real or complex Hilbert spaces and B(H,K) consists of bounded scalar-linear maps; a partial isometry is isometric on the orthogonal complement of its kernel and zero on the kernel. Normality requires H=K. For $T\in\faB(H,K)$ let $|T|=(T^*T)^{1/2}$. There is a unique partial isometry $U:H\to K$ with initial space $(\ker T)^\perp$, final space $\overline{\faRan T}$ and $T=U|T|$. For normal $T$ it commutes with $|T|$ and $U$; for invertible $T$, $U$ is unitary. For a general operator it need not be unitary.

Fuglede--Putnam. Let N∈B(K) and M∈B(H) be bounded normal operators on real or complex Hilbert spaces, and T∈B(H,K). In the real case complex spectral functions are interpreted on canonical complexifications, and real spectral functions restrict to the fixed-real spaces. For bounded normal $N,M$ and bounded $T$ with $NT=TM$, one has $N^*T=TM^*$. Consequently $T$ intertwines all corresponding Borel spectral functions. Similar bounded normal operators are unitarily equivalent.

Operator topologies and double commutant. H is a real or complex Hilbert space, B(H) its bounded scalar-linear operators, and A′ denotes the commutant {T:TA=AT for all A∈A}, A′′=(A′)′, distinct from a Banach transpose or dual. The strong operator topology (SOT) is pointwise norm convergence and the weak operator topology (WOT) is convergence of all matrix coefficients. On norm-bounded sets adjunction is WOT continuous and multiplication is separately SOT and WOT continuous. A unital *-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subset\faB(H)$ satisfies $\overline{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{SOT}} =\overline{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{WOT}}=\mathcal A''$. No separability assumption is required.

Mean ergodic theorem. Hilbert spaces may be real or complex and convergence of the discrete averages is as N→∞, of the semigroup averages as t→∞. If $T$ is a contraction on a Hilbert space, then $N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}T^k$ converges strongly to the orthogonal projection onto $\ker(I-T)$. For a strongly continuous contraction semigroup the same holds for $t^{-1}\int_0^tT(s)\,ds$ onto the common fixed-vector space.

Spectral families and normal corollaries. No separability assumption on H is imposed. Real operator spectra in complex assertions use the canonical Hilbert complexification H_C. Inner products are conjugate-linear first. For bounded normal $N$ on a complex Hilbert space, self-adjointness is equivalent to a real spectrum, and unitarity to spectrum contained in $\mathbb T$. Also $E(\{\lambda\})H=\ker(N-\lambda)$. For bounded normal $N$ on a real Hilbert space, $N$ is self-adjoint exactly when $\sigma(N_{\mathbb C})\subset\mathbb R$, and is orthogonal exactly when $\sigma(N_{\mathbb C})\subset\mathbb T$. For real $\lambda$, the real eigenspace identifies with the fixed-real part of $E_{\mathbb C}(\{\lambda\})H_{\mathbb C}$. For self-adjoint $A$ over either scalar field the spectral family $E_t=E(({-}\infty,t])$ is increasing and strongly right continuous, with limits zero and $I$ at the two infinities. If its spectrum lies in $[m,M]$, Riemann--Stieltjes sums for $\int_{m-0}^M t\,dE_t$ converge in operator norm to $A$; the corresponding scalar matrix coefficients are ordinary Riemann--Stieltjes integrals. The lower endpoint includes its atom.

AP chapter purpose and proof-route provenance: the nonautomatic AP statement is a structural existence counterexample. Its Walsh-block construction and rank-one series follow Enflo; no AP/BAP equivalence is assumed. Internal estimates of the proofs are not separate additional deliverables.

Recall that a Banach space $X$ has the approximation property (AP) if, for every compact $K\subset X$ and $\eps>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank $T:X\to X$ with $\sup_{x\in K}\|Tx-x\|<\eps$. No uniform bound on $\|T\|$ is imposed.

Trace obstruction. Let X be a real or complex Banach space; X′ is its continuous scalar-linear dual and AP is compact-uniform approximation of the identity by bounded finite-rank maps. Suppose $f_j\in X'$, $x_j\in X$, and \[ \sum_j\|f_j\|\|x_j\|<\infty,\qquad \sum_j f_j(x)x_j=0\quad(x\in X),\qquad \sum_j f_j(x_j)\ne0. \] Then $X$ does not have AP.

Let X be Banach over R or C. For a finite algebraic tensor u=Σ_j f_j⊗x_j∈X′⊗X set ν(u)=inf Σ_j||f_j||||x_j||, taking all finite representations of the tensor, tr(u)=Σ_j f_j(x_j), and û(x)=Σ_j f_j(x)x_j. The trace and bounded-operator norms are at most ν(u). If Σ_{m≥1}ν(v_m)<∞, the formal sum u_1+Σ_m v_m has a flattened rank-one representation Σ_j f_j⊗x_j with Σ_j||f_j||||x_j||<∞, whose trace and associated operator are limits of the finite partial sums. This asserts no injectivity of the completed tensor-to-operator map.

Fix $n\ge2$, $H_n=\{0,1\}^{2n}$, and $\chi_S(a)=(-1)^{\sum_{j\in S}a_j}$ for $S\subset\{1,\ldots,2n\}$. The characters are orthonormal for the uniform probability on $H_n$. Let $W_{n,r}$ be the set with $|S|=r$, and put $F_{n,r}=\sum_{|S|=r}\chi_S$. The two levels $r=n-1,n+1$ have the same cardinality $t(n)=\binom{2n}{n-1}$.

A small Walsh difference. For every integer n≥2 let H_n={0,1}^{2n} with uniform probability, χ_S(a)=(−1)^(Σ_{j∈S}a_j), F_{n,r}=Σ_{|S|=r}χ_S, and t(n)=binom(2n,n−1)=binom(2n,n+1). The norm is the supremum on H_n. For \[ h_n=t(n)^{-1}(F_{n,n-1}-F_{n,n+1}) \] one has $\|h_n\|_\infty=2/n$.

Fix n≥2, H_n={0,1}^{2n}, χ_S(a)=(−1)^(Σ_{j∈S}a_j), t(n)=binom(2n,n−1) and h_n=t(n)^(−1)(Σ_{|S|=n−1}χ_S−Σ_{|S|=n+1}χ_S). Let E_n⊂C(H_n;R) be the span of those two Walsh levels and G_n the finite group generated by translations of H_n and permutations of its 2n coordinates; its action on E_n is isometric. For every endomorphism S of E_n let τ_−(S),τ_+(S) be its average diagonal Walsh coefficients on the n−1 and n+1 levels. Then τ_−(S)−τ_+(S)=|G_n|^(−1)Σ_{U∈G_n}(U^(−1)SU h_n)(0). Averaging the conjugates kills off-diagonal coefficients and gives a constant diagonal coefficient on each level.

There exists an integer m_0 sufficiently large such that, for every m≥1, on taking a=6/5, n_m=floor(a^(m+m_0)), t_m=binom(2n_m,n_m−1), k_m=t_m², and a symbol set M_m arranged in k_m rows of t_m symbols, there are k_{m+1} subsets N_{m,j}⊂M_m, each of cardinality t_{m+1}, with: |N_{m,i}∩N_{m,j}|≤t_{m+1}/(2n_{m+1}) for i≠j; each N_{m,j} meets each row in at most one symbol; and Σ_{e∈M_m}|1/(k_m t_m)−r_m(e)/(k_{m+1}t_{m+1})|≤1/n_{m+1}, where r_m(e)=#{j:e∈N_{m,j}}. These are the incidence data of the concrete Walsh construction; the subsequent modular listing and asymptotic estimates prove their existence and do not constitute extra independent conclusions.

Using the preceding Walsh-incidence data, let K_m be the disjoint union of k_m copies of H_{n_m}, one for each row of M_m, and Y=(⊕_{m≥1}C(K_m;R))_{ℓ²}. For each symbol e∈M_m choose its distinct upper-level character χ_S with |S|=n_m+1 on its own row of K_m; on row j of K_{m+1} it is zero unless e∈N_{m,j}, and otherwise is a distinct lower-level character with |S|=n_{m+1}−1, according to an arbitrary fixed bijection for that row. All other components vanish. Let X be the closed real linear span in Y of all these countably many vectors. The space Y is reflexive Banach and X is separable, real, reflexive Banach. Each C(K_m;R) uses its supremum norm.

In the concrete real Walsh-incidence space X just defined, the symbol vectors e are linearly independent and every finite sum satisfies ||Σ_e c_e e||_X≥|c_e| ||e||_X for each participating symbol e. The coordinates f_e(Σ_d c_d d)=c_e extend continuously to X with ||f_e|| ||e||=1. Define finite algebraic tensors u_m=(k_m t_m)^(−1)Σ_{e∈M_m} f_e⊗e∈X′⊗X. Then tr(u_m)=1 and ν(u_m)≤1, where ν is the finite algebraic tensor projective norm defined above.

Summable adjacent differences. Use the real Banach space X, continuous coordinates f_e, integer parameters n_m,t_m,k_m and finite tensors u_m=(k_m t_m)^(−1)Σ_{e∈M_m}f_e⊗e from the Walsh-incidence construction stated immediately before this lemma; ν is the infimum of Σ||f_j||||x_j|| over finite algebraic tensor representations. One has $\nu(u_{m+1}-u_m)\le5/n_{m+1}$.
Nonautomatic approximation property. There exists a separable real reflexive Banach space without AP, and consequently without a Schauder basis. There also exists a complex Banach space without AP.

Scope qualification: the AP theorem is existential; it asserts neither AP inheritance by arbitrary subspaces nor arbitrary finite-rank approximation of a compact operator based solely on its domain and target names.
Extension/geometry chapter scope: variational results use real Banach spaces; Hilbert geometric assertions apply also to complex spaces by underlying-real restriction.

Br\o ndsted--Rockafellar approximation. All pairings are with the continuous real-linear dual X′; D(φ) is the finite effective domain, ∂φ=∂_0φ, and subdifferentials are empty off the finite domain. Let $X$ be a real Banach space and $\phi$ a proper lower semicontinuous convex function. Put \[ \partial_\varepsilon\phi(x)= \{f\in X':\phi(y)\geq\phi(x)+f(y-x)-\varepsilon \text{ for all }y\}. \] If $f_0\in\partial_\varepsilon\phi(x_0)$, $\varepsilon>0$, then for every $\lambda>0$ there are $x_1$ and $f_1\in\partial\phi(x_1)$ with \[ \|x_1-x_0\|\leq\varepsilon/\lambda, \qquad \|f_1-f_0\|\leq\lambda. \] Moreover $\partial_\varepsilon\phi(x)$ is nonempty for every $x\in D(\phi)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and \[ \overline{D(\partial\phi)}=\overline{D(\phi)},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{Ran}\partial\phi} =\overline{D(\phi^*)} \] in the respective norm topologies.

Kirszbraun--Valentine. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, $S\subset H_1$, and $f:S\to H_2$ have Lipschitz constant $L\geq0$. It extends to all of $H_1$ with that same constant. No dimension, separability, boundedness or closedness assumption on $S$ is needed.

Cotlar--Stein almost orthogonality. The Hilbert space may be real or complex, including zero. For an infinite family row sums are the suprema of finite nonnegative subsums, and the strong-sum clause uses the indicated net or sequence of finite partial sums; no convergence is deduced from row bounds alone. For a finite family of bounded operators $T_i$ on a Hilbert space put \[ A=\sup_i\sum_j\|T_i^*T_j\|^{1/2},\qquad B=\sup_i\sum_j\|T_iT_j^*\|^{1/2}. \] Then $\|\sum_iT_i\|\leq\sqrt{AB}$. For an infinite family the same bound holds for every finite partial sum if these row sums are uniformly bounded. If those sums converge strongly on a dense subspace, they therefore extend to a strong sum on the entire Hilbert space with that bound.

Normal structure and nonexpansive fixed points. Work in a real or complex normed space (using underlying real convexity if complex). Nonexpansive means ||Tx−Ty||≤||x−y||; weak compactness uses the continuous dual and no weak continuity of T is assumed. A bounded convex set has normal structure if every convex subset of positive diameter contains a point whose supremum distance from that subset is strictly smaller than its diameter. Every nonempty weakly compact convex set with normal structure has a fixed point for every nonexpansive self-map. In particular every nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a uniformly convex Banach space has this property (Browder--G\"ohde--Kirk).

Alternating convex projections and the subspace improvement. Let H be a real or complex Hilbert space and x_0∈H arbitrary; for closed convex C let P_C be nearest-point projection, and define x_{2n+1}=P_{C_1}x_{2n}, x_{2n+2}=P_{C_2}x_{2n+1}. If $C_1,C_2$ are nonempty closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space with nonempty intersection, the alternating projection iterates converge weakly to a point of the intersection. If both are closed linear subspaces, the iterates converge in norm to the orthogonal projection of the initial vector onto their intersection.
Disjoint-set alternating-projection results are additional to the intersection theorem; all complex Hilbert inequalities use real parts of inner products.

The minimum-displacement vector. Let $C_1,C_2$ be nonempty closed convex subsets of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Starting from any $u_0\in H$, set $u_{2n-1}=P_{C_1}u_{2n-2}$ and $u_{2n}=P_{C_2}u_{2n-1}$. Write \[ D=\overline{C_2-C_1},\qquad p=P_D0,\qquad \delta=\operatorname{dist}(C_1,C_2). \] Then $u_{2n}-u_{2n-1}\to p$ in norm. Neither a nonempty intersection, a bounded orbit, nor attainment of the distance is required. The closure in the definition of $D$ is essential.

Weak convergence to an attained nearest pair. Let H be a real or complex Hilbert space, C_1,C_2⊂H nonempty closed convex, u_0∈H arbitrary, u_{2n−1}=P_{C_1}u_{2n−2}, u_{2n}=P_{C_2}u_{2n−1}, D=closure(C_2−C_1), p=P_D(0), and δ=dist(C_1,C_2). In the preceding theorem, suppose $p\in C_2-C_1$. There are $a\in C_1,b\in C_2$ with $b-a=p$ such that $u_{2n-1}\rightharpoonup a$ and $u_{2n}\rightharpoonup b$. The pair may depend on $u_0$. In particular the assumption holds when one of the two sets is bounded.
Minimax and variational-inequality chapter source-disposition: compactness-based existence is distinguished from coercive uniqueness; the separately stated results retain their actual hypotheses.

Convex--concave minimax. Let $K,L$ be nonempty compact convex subsets of Hausdorff topological vector spaces. Suppose $F:K\times L\to\mathbb R$ is convex and lower semicontinuous in its first variable and concave and upper semicontinuous in its second. Then \[ \min_{x\in K}\max_{y\in L}F(x,y) =\max_{y\in L}\min_{x\in K}F(x,y). \] All four extrema are attained, and a minimizing $x_0$ and maximizing $y_0$ give a saddle pair $F(x_0,y)\leq F(x_0,y_0)\leq F(x,y_0)$. In particular this applies to closed bounded convex sets of reflexive Banach spaces with norm-lower/upper-semicontinuous convex/concave sections, using their weak topologies. It includes the continuous bilinear von Neumann theorem.

A bounded-section replacement for coercivity. Monotonicity means <Au−Av,u−v>≥0 for all u,v; coercivity means <Au,u>≥α||u||² for some α>0 and all u. Let $A$ be a bounded linear monotone operator on a real Hilbert space, $K$ a nonempty closed convex set, and $f\in H$. If there is $v_0\in K$ for which \[ \{u\in K:\langle Au-f,v_0-u\rangle\geq0\} \] is bounded, then there is $u\in K$ with $\langle Au-f,v-u\rangle\geq0$ for every $v\in K$. This condition holds when $K$ is bounded, or when $A$ is coercive. Without strict monotonicity uniqueness is not asserted.

A coercive form plus a convex potential. The real Hilbert space may be zero, and coercivity means <Au,u>≥α||u||² for some α>0. The potential has values in (−∞,+∞], never −∞ and finite somewhere. For the final clause K is nonempty closed convex and I_K is zero on K and +∞ elsewhere. For bounded linear coercive $A$ on a real Hilbert space and a proper lower semicontinuous convex $\phi$, there is a unique $u\in D(\phi)$ with \[ \langle Au,v-u\rangle+\phi(v)-\phi(u)\geq0 \quad(v\in D(\phi)). \] Taking $\phi=I_K-\langle f,\cdot\rangle$ recovers Stampacchia with a forcing term.

The weak Minty inequality on an arbitrary monotone domain. Dual pairings are evaluation, A is monotone when <Av−Aw,v−w>≥0 for every v,w∈D; the domain need not be convex or all of X. Segment hemicontinuity means continuity of scalar evaluations along K-segments, in particular the limiting evaluations needed at u+t(w−u). Let $X$ be a real reflexive Banach space, $K\subset X$ nonempty closed bounded convex, and $A:D\subset X\to X'$ monotone, with no assumption that $D$ is all of $X$ or that $K\subset D$. There is $u\in K$ such that $\langle Av,u-v\rangle\leq0$ for every $v\in D\cap K$. If $K\subset D$ and $A$ is hemicontinuous along its segments, this is equivalent to $\langle Au,v-u\rangle\geq0$ for all $v\in K$.

Two explicit sign counterexamples clarify the monotone existence theorem. On H=R with A(v)=v and K=[−1,1], there is no u∈K satisfying <Av,u−v>≥0 for every v∈K: v=1 and v=−1 force u≥1 and u≤−1. The correct weak Minty sign is <Av,u−v>≤0. Also for v_1=0,v_2=1,A(v)=v and signed coefficients (s_1,s_2)=(1,−1), F(s,s)=Σ_{i,j}s_i s_j<Av_j,v_i−v_j>=1>0. The nonpositive sign identity used for the theorem is asserted for probability coefficients s_i≥0, Σs_i=1; the inconsistent printed opposite/all-signed formulas are not required claims.

An unbounded linear operator is its domain/action pair (D(A),A). Products have $D(AB)=\{x\in D(B):Bx\in D(A)\}$; sums have
$D(A+B)=D(A)\cap D(B)$. Equality includes equality of domains.
The resolvent convention remains $R(\lambda,A)=(\lambda I-A)^{-1}$.

Graphs and Hilbert adjoints: Let $A:D(A)\subset H\to K$ be densely defined. Its adjoint has domain
\[
 D(A^*)=\{y\in K:\text{there is }z\in H\text{ with }
              \faip{Ax}{y}=\faip{x}{z}\ (x\in D(A))\},
 \qquad A^*y=z.
\]
It is closed. The operator $A$ is closable iff $D(A^*)$ is dense;
then $\overline A=A^{**}$, whose graph is the closure of the graph
of $A$. For a closed densely defined $A$,
$(\faRan A)^\perp=\ker A^*$ and
$(\faRan A^*)^\perp=\ker A$.

A typical Schrödinger potential: If $q=q_2+q_\infty$ is real with $q_2\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and
$q_\infty\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)$, then
$-d^2/dx^2+q$ on exactly $H^2(\mathbb R)$ is self-adjoint and
bounded below, and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ is a core.

One expression, different adjoints: On $L^2(0,1)$ let $S=-i\,d/dx$ with
$D(S)=H_0^1(0,1)$, where $H^1$ functions use their absolutely
continuous representatives. Then $D(S^*)=H^1(0,1)$ and $S^*=-i\,d/dx$.
The self-adjoint extensions are precisely
$S_\theta=-i\,d/dx$ on
$\{u\in H^1(0,1):u(1)=e^{i\theta}u(0)\}$,
$0\leq\theta<2\pi$.

Banach unbounded adjoints and closed range: Let $A:D(A)\subset X\to Y$ be densely defined and closed between
Banach spaces. Define $D(A')\subset Y'$ by boundedness of
$x\mapsto y'(Ax)$ in the $X$ norm, and $A'y'$ by its unique
continuous extension. Then $A'$ is closed, and
\[
 \faRan A\text{ closed}\iff\faRan A'\text{ norm closed}
 \iff\faRan A'=(\ker A)^\perp
 \iff\faRan A={}^{\perp}(\ker A').
\]
Closedness of $\faRan A$ is also equivalent to
$\operatorname{dist}(x,\ker A)\leq C\|Ax\|$ on $D(A)$.
Surjectivity of $A$ is equivalent to
$\|y'\|\leq C\|A'y'\|$ on $D(A')$;
surjectivity of $A'$ is equivalent to
$\|x\|\leq C\|Ax\|$ on $D(A)$.

Symmetry, deficiency spaces, and Cayley: A densely defined $S$ is symmetric if $S\subset S^*$; it is
self-adjoint if equality holds, including domains. It is essentially
self-adjoint if its closure is self-adjoint. For closed symmetric $S$,
\[
 \|(S-z)x\|^2=\|(S-\operatorname{Re}z)x\|^2
                    +|\operatorname{Im}z|^2\|x\|^2.
\]
It is self-adjoint iff $\faRan(S+i)=\faRan(S-i)=H$, equivalently
$N_+=\ker(S^*-i)=0=N_-=\ker(S^*+i)$.
Its Cayley isometry $V=(S-i)(S+i)^{-1}$ maps the closed space
$\faRan(S+i)=N_+^\perp$ onto $\faRan(S-i)=N_-^\perp$.
Self-adjoint operators correspond bijectively to unitary operators
$U$ with $\ker(I-U)=0$, by
\[
 U=(S-i)(S+i)^{-1},\quad
 S=i(I+U)(I-U)^{-1},\quad D(S)=\faRan(I-U).
\]

All closed symmetric extensions: For a closed symmetric $S$ one has the graph-orthogonal decomposition
$D(S^*)=D(S)\dotplus N_+\dotplus N_-$.
Every closed symmetric extension is, uniquely, a restriction $S_W$
of $S^*$ with
\[
 D(S_W)=D(S)\dotplus\{u+Wu:u\in L_+\},\quad
 S_W(x+u+Wu)=Sx+iu-iWu,
\]
where $W:L_+\to N_-$ is an isometry on a closed subspace
$L_+\subset N_+$. It is self-adjoint exactly when
$L_+=N_+$ and $W$ is onto $N_-$. In particular self-adjoint
extensions exist iff the two deficiency indices are equal, including
infinite cardinalities. Deficiency dimensions are constant in each
open half-plane.

Friedrichs extension: If a densely defined symmetric $S$ satisfies
$\faip{x}{Sx}\geq c\|x\|^2$, it has a self-adjoint extension with
the same lower bound, canonically associated with the closure of its
quadratic form. More generally a densely defined closed positive
sesquilinear form $q$ on $V\subset H$, with
$\|u\|_V^2=q(u,u)+\|u\|^2$, determines a unique nonnegative
self-adjoint $A$ by
\[
 D(A)=\{u\in V:\exists f\in H, q(v,u)=\faip{v}{f}\ (v\in V)\},
 \qquad Au=f.
\]

Relative symmetric perturbations: If $A=A^*$ and $B$ is symmetric on a domain containing $D(A)$, and
$\|Bx\|\leq a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ on $D(A)$ with $a<1$, then $A+B$
on exactly $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is essentially self-adjoint
on a core $D_0$ and the same estimate holds there, the closure of
$A+B$ on $D_0$ is self-adjoint on $D(\overline A)$.

Unbounded measurable spectral calculus: For a PVM $E$ and finite-valued measurable $f$ define
\[
 D(f(E))=\{x:\int|f|^2\,d\mu_x<\infty\},\quad
 f(E)x=\lim_n(f1_{\{|f|\leq n\}})(E)x.
\]
It is a closed densely defined normal operator, its adjoint is
$\bar f(E)$, and
\[
 D(f(E)g(E))=D(g(E))\cap D((fg)(E)),\qquad
 \overline{f(E)g(E)}=(fg)(E).
\]
Likewise the closure of $f(E)+g(E)$ on the intersection domain is
$(f+g)(E)$. A real-valued $f$ gives a self-adjoint operator.
Even when $f$ is bounded the domain of the product $f(E)g(E)$ need
not be the full domain of $(fg)(E)$.

Commutation in the unbounded calculus: Let $N$ be closed densely defined normal and $B$ bounded with
$BN\subset NB$ and $BN^*\subset N^*B$. Then $B$ commutes with
every spectral projection of $N$. For every finite-valued Borel $f$,
$B D(f(N))\subset D(f(N))$ and $Bf(N)\subset f(N)B$.

Unbounded normal spectral theorem: Every closed densely defined normal $N$, meaning $N^*N=NN^*$
including product domains, has a unique Borel PVM on $\mathbb C$
with $N=\int z\,dE(z)$ on exactly its square-integrability domain.
It is supported on $\sigma(N)$ and every open set meeting the spectrum
has nonzero spectral projection. No assumption that the resolvent
is nonempty is needed. In particular a self-adjoint operator has a
PVM on $\mathbb R$; a general normal operator is a direct sum of
bounded normal pieces and hence a multiplication operator, including
on nonseparable Hilbert spaces.

For 1<p<∞, q=p/(p−1), scalar field ℝ or ℂ, a measurable finite-a.e. multiplier a, use the scalar-linear dual pairing [f,g]=∫fg dμ and the maximal operator M_a from the preceding definition. Domains, transpose, kernels, and range: Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$ be any positive measure space, and let
$a:\Omega\to\mathbb K$, where $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$,
be measurable and finite almost everywhere.
On $X=L^p(\mu;\mathbb K)$ put
\[
 D(M_a)=\{f\in X:af\in X\},\qquad M_af=af,
 \qquad Z=\{a=0\}.
\]
Then $M_a$ is densely defined and closed. Under the isometric
identification $X'=L^q(\mu)$ of
Theorem~\ref{fa2:p4:lp-duality}, its Banach transpose has exactly
\[
 D(M_a')=\{g\in L^q:ag\in L^q\},\qquad M_a'g=ag.
\]
Write $L^r(E)=\{f\in L^r:f=0\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus E\}$.
Then
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \ker M_a&=L^p(Z),& (\ker M_a)^\perp&=L^q(\Omega\setminus Z),\\
 \ker M_a'&=L^q(Z),& (\ker M_a')_\perp&=L^p(\Omega\setminus Z),\\
 \overline{\operatorname{Ran}M_a}&=L^p(\Omega\setminus Z).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The unclosed range is exactly
\[
 \operatorname{Ran}M_a
 =\left\{h\in L^p:h1_Z=0,\quad
             1_{\Omega\setminus Z}\frac{h}{a}\in L^p\right\}.
\]
These statements require no semifiniteness or $\sigma$-finiteness.
On complex $L^2$, the Hilbert adjoint instead is $M_{\overline a}$
with its maximal domain; in particular real $a$ gives a self-adjoint
operator.

For 1<p<∞, q=p/(p−1), scalar field ℝ or ℂ, a measurable finite-a.e. multiplier a, use the scalar-linear dual pairing [f,g]=∫fg dμ and the maximal operator M_a from the preceding definition. The ordinary essential-bound tests: Assume now that $\mu$ is semifinite: every measurable set of positive
measure contains a measurable subset of finite positive measure.
Then
\[
 D(M_a)=L^p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in L^\infty.
\]
When this holds, $\|M_a\|=\|a\|_\infty$. Moreover,
$\operatorname{Ran}M_a$ is closed exactly when, for some $c>0$,
$|a|\ge c$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus Z$. The operator
is surjective exactly when
\[
                    |a|\ge c\quad\hbox{almost everywhere on }\Omega
                    \quad\hbox{for some }c>0.
\]
In that case its inverse is the bounded, everywhere-defined
multiplier $M_{1/a}$ into $D(M_a)$, and $M_a$ is injective.

For 1<p<∞, q=p/(p−1), scalar field ℝ or ℂ, a measurable finite-a.e. multiplier a, use the scalar-linear dual pairing [f,g]=∫fg dμ and the maximal operator M_a from the preceding definition. Spectrum, eigenvalues, and continuous multipliers: Let $\mu$ be semifinite and use complex $L^p$ for the spectrum.
For real $a$ on real $L^p$, ``spectrum'' means the spectrum of its
natural complexification on complex $L^p$: its domain is
$D(M_a;\mathbb R)+iD(M_a;\mathbb R)$, since multiplication by
real $a$ preserves real and imaginary parts and their integrability.
The bounded or unbounded maximal multiplier has
\[
 \sigma(M_a)=\operatorname{essran}_\mu a
 =\{\lambda\in\mathbb C:
      \mu(\{|a-\lambda|<\varepsilon\})>0
                         \text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}.
\]
For $\lambda$ outside that closed set,
\[
 R(\lambda,M_a)f=\frac{f}{\lambda-a},\qquad
 \|R(\lambda,M_a)\|
       =\operatorname*{ess\,sup}\frac1{|\lambda-a|}.
\]
The eigenspace at $\lambda$ is $L^p(\{a=\lambda\})$;
thus $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when that level set has
positive measure. If $a$ is real, the spectrum is real. If also
$a\in L^\infty$ and $L^p\ne0$, its essential infimum and
essential supremum both belong to the spectrum, the spectrum lies
between them, and $\sigma(M_a)=\{0\}$ exactly when $a=0$ almost
everywhere.

For a nonempty open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue
measure and continuous finite $a$, one has the exact formula
\[
                    \sigma(M_a)=\overline{a(\Omega)}.
\]
In particular the closure is necessary even for bounded continuous
multipliers.

For 1<p<∞, q=p/(p−1), scalar field ℝ or ℂ, a measurable finite-a.e. multiplier a, use the scalar-linear dual pairing [f,g]=∫fg dμ and the maximal operator M_a from the preceding definition. The nonatomic compactness test and the measure boundary: If $\mu$ is semifinite and nonatomic, multiplication is compact
as an everywhere-defined bounded operator on $L^p$ exactly when
$a=0$ almost everywhere. More strongly, for any nonzero multiplier
the image of the $L^p$ unit ball intersected with $D(M_a)$ is not
relatively compact. Atomlessness is necessary: on counting measure
on $\mathbb N$, the nonzero multiplier $a_n=1/n$ is compact.

Without semifiniteness, the first theorem remains valid, but the
ordinary essential-bound, essential-range and surjectivity tests
need not be valid. If $L^p=0$, the maximal multiplier is the
unique zero-space operator and its spectrum is empty.
Bibliographic and scope explanation for the Banach adjoint-sum assertion; no additional mathematical target beyond the independently inventoried theorem.

One-sided gaps and annihilators: For closed linear subspaces of a Banach space put
$\delta(M,N)=\sup_{x\in M,\|x\|\leq1}\operatorname{dist}(x,N)$.
Then $0\leq\delta(M,N)\leq1$,
$\delta(M,N)=\delta(N^\perp,M^\perp)$, and
\[
 \delta(M,L)\leq\delta(M,N)+\delta(N,L)
                              +\delta(M,N)\delta(N,L).
\]
If $N\subsetneqq M$, their one-sided gap $\delta(M,N)$ is one.

A linear maximal-monotonicity criterion: Let $X$ be real reflexive and suppose both $X$ and $X'$ are
strictly convex. Let $A:D(A)\subset X\to X'$ be closed,
densely defined, linear and monotone. Identify $X''$ with $X$.
Then $A$ is maximal monotone if and only if its Banach adjoint
is monotone on $D(A')$. In that case $A'$ is maximal monotone,
\[
 \ker A=\ker A',\qquad
 \overline{\operatorname{Ran}A}
                         =\overline{\operatorname{Ran}A'}.
\]
The range equality is an equality of norm closures, as in
\cite[Problem 16, B3]{B01}, not an unsupported equality of
unclosed ranges.

Adjoint of a relatively bounded sum: Let $A:D(A)\subset X\to Y$ and $B:D(B)\subset X\to Y$ be
closed densely defined operators between Banach spaces, with
$D(A)\subset D(B)$ and $D(A')\subset D(B')$. Suppose
\begin{align*}
 \|Bx\|&\leq k\|Ax\|+C\|x\| &&(x\in D(A)),\quad 0\leq k<1,\ C\geq0,\\
 \|B'y'\|&\leq k'\|A'y'\|+C'\|y'\|
                &&(y'\in D(A')),\quad 0\leq k'<1,\ C'\geq0.
\end{align*}
Then $A+B$ is closed on $D(A)$ and
\[
 (A+B)'=A'+B'\quad\hbox{on exactly }D(A').
\]
Equality includes the adjoint domain. Neither reflexivity nor
symmetry nor a self-adjoint realization is assumed.

The domain inclusion may otherwise be strict: On $\ell^2$ let $Ax=(nx_n)$ on $D(A)=\{x:(nx_n)\in\ell^2\}$
and let $B=-A$ on that same domain. Both are self-adjoint and
closed, but $A+B$ is zero on $D(A)$ and its adjoint is zero
on all of $\ell^2$. In contrast $A'+B'$ remains defined only
on the corresponding proper dual domain. Thus a bare formal
sum does not identify the adjoint domain; the strict relative
bound in the theorem is substantive. Identifying the Hilbert
antilinear Riesz map with the scalar-linear dual transports this
example to the Banach-adjoint notation used there.

In this chapter X is an arbitrary real or complex Banach space. A C₀ semigroup is a family of bounded linear operators T(t), t≥0, with T(0)=I, T(t+s)=T(t)T(s), and T(t)x→x in norm as t↓0 for every x. Its generator is Ax=lim_{h↓0}(T(h)x−x)/h on exactly the set of vectors for which this norm limit exists.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Growth, generator, and Laplace resolvent: Every $C_0$ semigroup has $\|T(t)\|\leq Me^{\omega t}$ for some
$M\geq1$, $\omega\in\mathbb R$. Its generator is closed and densely
defined, $T(t)D(A)\subset D(A)$, and
$\frac d{dt}T(t)x=AT(t)x=T(t)Ax$ on $D(A)$.
For $\operatorname{Re}\lambda>\omega$,
\[
 R(\lambda,A)x=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x\,dt,
 \quad
 R(\lambda,A)^m x=\frac1{(m-1)!}
 \int_0^\infty t^{m-1}e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x\,dt.
\]
Thus $\|R(\lambda,A)^m\|\leq M/(\operatorname{Re}\lambda-\omega)^m$.
The generator uniquely determines the semigroup.

Resolvent lines obstruct superexponential decay: Let $G$ generate a $C_0$ semigroup on a complex Hilbert space.
Suppose real $\xi_n\to-\infty$ satisfy
$\xi_n+i\mathbb R\subset\rho(G)$ and
$\sup_\tau\|R(\xi_n+i\tau,G)\|\leq d^{-1}$ with one $d>0$.
If $u\in C^1([0,\infty);H)\cap C([0,\infty);D(G))$ and
$\|u'(t)-Gu(t)\|\leq k\|u(t)\|$ for $k<d$, then either $u=0$
or $\int_0^\infty\|u(t)\|^2e^{bt}dt=\infty$ for some $b>0$.
This is a lower bound on possible decay, not a theorem asserting
exponential stability of arbitrary semigroups.

Self-adjoint spectral gaps: If $G$ is self-adjoint, bounded above, and its spectrum has gaps
$(\xi_n-d,\xi_n+d)$ with $\xi_n\to-\infty$, the preceding lower-decay
alternative applies to every trajectory with residual constant $k<d$.

Point spectrum and eventual compactness: For every complex Banach $C_0$ semigroup and every $t>0$,
$\sigma_p(T(t))\setminus\{0\}=e^{t\sigma_p(A)}$.
The full spectral mapping equality can fail: irrational rotations
on $L^2(\mathbb T)$ give a countable dense exponential image but
an entire unit-circle operator spectrum.
If $T(t_0)$ is compact for some $t_0>0$, full spectral mapping holds
for every $t>0$ after omitting zero. The generator spectrum then
consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity,
with only finitely many in each right half-plane. Its growth bound
equals its spectral bound (both may be $-\infty$).
For any real $a$ whose vertical line misses the generator spectrum,
the part with real part greater than $a$ gives a finite exponential
polynomial expansion of $T(t)$, with remainder bounded by $C_a e^{at}$.

Spectral bound need not be the growth bound: On $H=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}\mathbb C^n$ let $S_n$ be the nilpotent
forward shift and
$A_n=(-1+in)I+S_n$.
The direct-sum generator has domain
$\{x:\sum n^2\|x_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and spectrum exactly
$\{-1+in:n\geq1\}$, but its contraction semigroup has
$\|T(t)\|=1$ for every $t\geq0$. Thus its spectral bound is $-1$
and its growth bound is zero. Also the adjoint of a $C_0$ semigroup
need not be $C_0$ on a nonreflexive space: translations on $L^1(\mathbb R)$
have adjoint translations on $L^\infty$, where a step function moves
distance one in the essential supremum norm for every nonzero shift.

Linear maximal monotone operators: If $L:D(L)\subset H\to H$ is linear, monotone, and $I+L$ is onto,
then it is closed, densely defined, and $I+\lambda L$ is onto for
every $\lambda>0$. Its resolvents are contractions and
$L_\lambda=L(I+\lambda L)^{-1}$ is bounded with
$\|L_\lambda x\|\leq\|Lx\|$ on $D(L)$,
$L_\lambda x\to Lx$ there. Moreover $D(L^2)$ is graph dense in
$D(L)$ and $-L$ generates the contraction semigroup above.

Semigroups of normal operators: If every $T(t)$ in a $C_0$ semigroup on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space
is normal, its generator $A$ is normal, its spectrum lies in a
left half-plane, and $T(t)=e^{tA}$ in the unbounded measurable
calculus. Conversely every normal $A$ whose spectral real parts
are bounded above defines such a semigroup.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: General Hille--Yosida theorem: A densely defined closed $A$ generates a $C_0$ semigroup with
$\|T(t)\|\leq Me^{\omega t}$ iff $(\omega,\infty)\subset\rho(A)$
and
\[
 \|R(\lambda,A)^m\|\leq\frac{M}{(\lambda-\omega)^m}
 \qquad(\lambda>\omega,\ m=1,2,\ldots).
\]
All resolvent powers are required when $M>1$.
For $\omega=0$, the bounded Yosida approximants
$A_\lambda=\lambda AR(\lambda,A)=\lambda^2R(\lambda,A)-\lambda I$
satisfy $e^{tA_\lambda}x\to T(t)x$ uniformly on bounded time intervals.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Lumer--Phillips on Banach spaces: A densely defined operator $A$ generates a contraction $C_0$ semigroup
iff it is dissipative,
$\|(\lambda-A)x\|\geq\lambda\|x\|$ for every $\lambda>0$, $x\in D(A)$,
and $\faRan(\lambda_0-A)=X$ for some $\lambda_0>0$.
On a Hilbert space dissipativity is equivalent to
$\operatorname{Re}\faip{x}{Ax}\leq0$ on $D(A)$.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Classical and inhomogeneous evolution: If $A$ generates $T$ and $x\in D(A)$, $u(t)=T(t)x$ is the unique
classical solution of $u'=Au$, $u(0)=x$.
For $x\in D(A^k)$,
$u\in C^{k-j}([0,\infty);D(A^j))$ for $0\leq j\leq k$,
using graph norms. If $x\in D(A)$ and $f\in C^1([0,T];X)$, then
\[
 u(t)=T(t)x+\int_0^tT(t-s)f(s)\,ds
\]
is the unique classical solution of $u'=Au+f$.
For $x\in X$, $f\in L^1(0,T;X)$ the same formula defines its
continuous mild solution and depends continuously on the data.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Bounded and relatively bounded perturbations: If $A$ generates a semigroup bounded by $Me^{\omega t}$ and
$B\in\faB(X)$, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ generates a semigroup bounded
by $M e^{(\omega+M\|B\|)t}$.
On a Hilbert space, if $A$ generates contractions, $B$ is dissipative
on a domain containing $D(A)$, and
$\|Bx\|\leq a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ with $a<1$, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$
also generates contractions.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Strong resolvent approximation: Let $A_n,A$ generate contraction semigroups $T_n,T$ on $X$.
The following are equivalent: for some (then every) $\lambda>0$,
$R(\lambda,A_n)x\to R(\lambda,A)x$ for every $x$; and
$T_n(t)x\to T(t)x$ uniformly for $t$ in bounded intervals, for every $x$.
The same equivalence holds under a common growth bound $Me^{\omega t}$.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Chernoff products, implicit Euler, and Trotter: Let $F(h)$ be contractions with $F(0)=I$, and suppose on a core $D_0$
of a contraction generator $A$ that
$(F(h)x-x)/h\to Ax$. Then
$F(t/n)^nx\to T(t)x$ strongly, uniformly on bounded $t$ intervals.
In particular
$T(t)x=\lim_n(I-tA/n)^{-n}x$.
If $A,B$ generate contractions and the closure $C$ of $A+B$ on
$D(A)\cap D(B)$ generates contractions, then
\[
 (T_A(t/n)T_B(t/n))^nx\longrightarrow T_C(t)x.
\]
For bounded $A,B$, Strang's symmetric product
$(e^{tA/(2n)}e^{tB/n}e^{tA/(2n)})^n$ has operator-norm error
$O_T(n^{-2})$ on $0\leq t\leq T$.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Lax consistency and stability: Suppose bounded time steps $C_h$ satisfy
$\sup_{nh\leq T}\|C_h^n\|<\infty$ and, on a graph core of a
generator $A$, $h^{-1}(C_h-I)x\to Ax$. If the stability estimate
and consistency extend to the graph-domain orbit uniformly on its
compact time intervals, then $C_h^nx\to T(t)x$ as $h\downarrow0$ with $nh\to t$,
uniformly for bounded times. Conversely, convergence for every $x$
in this same sense implies asymptotic stability: for every finite
$T\geq0$ there exist $h_T>0$ and $M_T<\infty$ such that
$\|C_h^n\|\leq M_T$ whenever $0<h<h_T$ and $nh\leq T$.

On an arbitrary real or complex Banach space X, with the C₀ semigroup/generator conventions stated in this chapter: Adjoint semigroups and spectral inclusion: The adjoints $T(t)'$ form a weak-star continuous semigroup on $X'$.
If $X$ is reflexive, it is a $C_0$ semigroup with generator $A'$.
In general strong continuity on the entire dual can fail.
For every $C_0$ semigroup,
$e^{t\sigma(A)}\subset\sigma(T(t))\setminus\{0\}$;
equality need not hold without further hypotheses.

Stone: Every strongly continuous unitary group $U(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$,
has a unique self-adjoint $H$ with $U(t)=e^{itH}$.
Its derivative generator is $iH$, with exactly $D(H)$ as domain.
Conversely every self-adjoint $H$ gives such a group by its PVM.

Self-adjoint smoothing: For $L=L^*\geq0$, $T(t)=e^{-tL}$ is a self-adjoint contraction
semigroup. For every $t>0$, $T(t)H\subset\bigcap_{m\geq1}D(L^m)$ and
\[
 \|L^mT(t)\|\leq(m/(et))^m.
\]
Its trajectories are smooth away from zero and are the unique
continuous-at-zero classical solutions of $u'+Lu=0$ there.
If $L\geq cI$ with $c>0$, then $\|T(t)\|\leq e^{-ct}$.

Let $V\hookrightarrow H$ be a dense continuous injection of real
Hilbert spaces. Identifying $H$ with its dual gives
$V\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow V'$, with
$\langle h,v\rangle=\faip{h}{v}_H$.

Let 0<T<∞ and V↪H↪V′ be the dense continuous real Hilbert triple of paper.tex:15206–15209. The Hilbert-triple trace and energy identity: If $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and its distributional derivative belongs to
$L^2(0,T;V')$, then it has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$,
and
\[
 \|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2
 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle\,dr.
\]
The trace map into $C(H)$ is continuous for the sum of these two
$L^2$ norms. This is the corrected scope of notes/001/AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA.txt, item 6; the energy identity is for all s,t∈[0,T].

Let V↪H↪V′ be a dense continuous real Hilbert triple and [0,T] a finite time interval; the fixed initial datum is retained also for T=0. Nonautonomous parabolic forms: Suppose $a(t;u,v)$ is bilinear, $t\mapsto a(t;u,v)$ measurable for
fixed $u,v$, and for almost every $t$, simultaneously for all $u,v$,
\[
 |a(t;u,v)|\leq M\|u\|_V\|v\|_V,\qquad
 a(t;v,v)\geq\alpha\|v\|_V^2-C\|v\|_H^2,\quad\alpha>0.
\]
Assume additionally $t\mapsto A(t)v$ is strongly measurable in $V'$
for each $v$, where $\langle A(t)u,v\rangle=a(t;u,v)$;
this is automatic if $V$ is separable. For every $f\in L^2(0,T;V')$
and $u_0\in H$, there is a unique
\[
 u\in L^2(0,T;V)\cap C([0,T];H),\quad u'\in L^2(0,T;V')
\]
with $u'+A(t)u=f$ in $V'$ almost everywhere and $u(0)=u_0$.
Its norm in these spaces is bounded by a constant depending only on
the displayed parameters, the embedding and $T$, times
$\|u_0\|_H+\|f\|_{L^2(V')}$.
Bibliographic and proof-method discussion for the hyperbolic theorem; weak compactness and recovery of strong continuity describe the argument, not extra independent deliverables.

Nonautonomous symmetric hyperbolic equation: Let $V\hookrightarrow H$ be a dense continuous embedding of real
Hilbert spaces and identify $H$ with a dense subspace of $V'$ by
its inner product. Suppose $a(t;u,v)$, $0\le t\le T$, is a family
of symmetric bounded bilinear forms on $V$, that each scalar function
$t\mapsto a(t;u,v)$ is $C^1$, and that uniformly in $t$,
\[
 a(t;v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2-C\|v\|_H^2
 \qquad(\alpha>0, C\ge0).
\]
Write $\langle A(t)u,v\rangle=a(t;u,v)$.
For $u_0\in V$, $v_0\in H$ and $f\in L^2(0,T;H)$ there is a
unique solution
\[
 u\in C([0,T];V),\qquad u'\in C([0,T];H),\qquad
 u''\in L^2(0,T;V')
\]
of $u''+A(t)u=f$ a.e., with $u(0)=u_0$, $u'(0)=v_0$.
It satisfies the energy identity, for every $s,t$,
\begin{align*}
 &\|u'(t)\|_H^2+a(t;u(t),u(t))
   -\|u'(s)\|_H^2-a(s;u(s),u(s))\\
 &\hspace{1cm}=2\int_s^t(f(r),u'(r))_H\,dr
                +\int_s^t\partial_ra(r;u(r),u(r))\,dr.
\end{align*}
There is a constant $M_T$, depending only on the embedding and form
bounds, such that
\[
 \sup_t\big(\|u(t)\|_V^2+\|u'(t)\|_H^2\big)
 \le M_T\left(\|u_0\|_V^2+\|v_0\|_H^2+\|f\|_{L^2H}^2\right).
\]
The Hilbert spaces need not be separable.

This chapter separates abstract functional analysis from further
boundary-value and dynamical applications. It supplies the current
subcases of mixed source families rather than dropping them merely
because their principal curricular home is later. See
\cite{B01,B02,B03,B06,B08,B09}.

Hamburger moment problem: A real sequence $(m_n)_{n\geq0}$ is the sequence of moments of a finite
positive Borel measure on $\mathbb R$, all absolute moments finite,
iff every Hankel form
$\sum_{j,k=0}^Nm_{j+k}\overline{c_j}c_k$ is nonnegative.
It is equivalent to the existence of a self-adjoint $A$ and a vector
$e\in\bigcap_nD(A^n)$ with $m_n=\faip{e}{A^ne}$. The canonical polynomial Hilbert space here is the completion of complex polynomials modulo the null space of ⟨p,q⟩=∑_{j,k}m_{j+k}overline(p_j)q_k; on polynomial classes the densely defined symmetric multiplication operator is S[p]=[tp].

Fourier transform as a bounded spectral example: The unitary Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ with phase
$e^{-2\pi ix\xi}$ has spectrum exactly $\{1,-1,i,-i\}$ and the
orthogonal decomposition into these four eigenspaces. A bounded
diagonal operator on $\ell^p$, $1\leq p\leq\infty$, has spectrum
the closure of its diagonal entries.

A genuinely indeterminate Stieltjes sequence: For $-1\leq a\leq1$, the distinct positive measures
\[
 d\mu_a(x)=\frac{e^{-(\log x)^2}}{\sqrt\pi x}
            (1+a\sin(2\pi\log x))\,dx,\qquad x>0,
\]
have the same moments $m_n=e^{n^2/4}$ for every nonnegative integer
$n$. Thus positivity of both Hankel forms does not imply uniqueness.

A full one-dimensional compact-resolvent realization: Let $a<b$, $p\in C^1[a,b]$ real with $p\geq p_0>0$, and
$q\in C[a,b]$ real. On $H=L^2(a,b)$ the Dirichlet realization
\[
 Lu=-(pu')'+qu,\qquad D(L)=H^2(a,b)\cap H_0^1(a,b)
\]
is self-adjoint and bounded below, and has compact resolvent.
Its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis, its eigenvalues have
finite multiplicity and tend to $+\infty$, and its heat semigroup
is compact at every positive time. The periodic realization has
domain
$\{u\in H^2:u(a)=u(b),\ p(a)u'(a)=p(b)u'(b)\}$ and has the
same conclusions. These are operator domains and boundary conditions,
not merely formal differential expressions.

The operator acts on L²(𝕋), with normalized Haar measure. Periodic convolution as a compact spectral model: For $k\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ and normalized Haar measure,
$Kf=k*f$ is bounded, compact, normal, and diagonal in the Fourier basis
$e_n(x)=e^{inx}$, with eigenvalues $\widehat k(n)$.
It is compact, its spectrum is the closure of these eigenvalues,
and it is self-adjoint iff they are real, positive iff they are
nonnegative. It is Hilbert--Schmidt exactly when $k\in L^2$,
with $\|K\|_2=\|k\|_2$. Trace class requires exactly the extra
condition $\sum_n|\widehat k(n)|<\infty$, even for continuous $k$.

For a real sequence (m_n)_{n≥0}, with finite positive representing measures and all absolute moments finite as in the preceding Hamburger construction: Stieltjes existence: The sequence has a representing positive measure on $[0,\infty)$ iff
both $(m_{j+k})$ and $(m_{j+k+1})$ define nonnegative finite Hankel
forms. The representing operator can be chosen nonnegative.

For the positive Hankel sequence and polynomial Hilbert space of the Hamburger construction: The Jacobi realization: If all nonzero polynomial Hankel forms are strictly positive,
Gram--Schmidt gives real orthonormal polynomials $p_n$ with positive
leading coefficients and a three-term recurrence
\[
 tp_n=a_{n+1}p_{n+1}+b_np_n+a_np_{n-1},\qquad
 a_{n+1}>0,\ b_n\in\mathbb R,\ a_0p_{-1}=0.
\]
Under $p_n\leftrightarrow e_n$ the minimal multiplication operator
is the symmetric Jacobi matrix on finitely supported sequences.
Its deficiency indices are either $(0,0)$ or $(1,1)$.
If there is a nonzero null polynomial instead, the polynomial
Hilbert space is finite dimensional and the moment measure is a
uniquely determined finite atomic measure. The canonical polynomial Hilbert space here is the completion of complex polynomials modulo the null space of ⟨p,q⟩=∑_{j,k}m_{j+k}overline(p_j)q_k; on polynomial classes the densely defined symmetric multiplication operator is S[p]=[tp].

Hamburger determinacy and essential self-adjointness: For the polynomial Hilbert space and symmetric multiplication operator
$S$ just constructed, the representing Hamburger measure is unique
iff $S$ is essentially self-adjoint. In particular bounded even
moments, or more generally a common positive exponential moment
determined by the moment series, give uniqueness. Here the exponential sufficient condition means ∑_{n≥0}m_{2n}r^{2n}/(2n)!<∞ for some r>0; the bounded-even-moment subcase is m_{2n}≤C for all n. The canonical polynomial Hilbert space here is the completion of complex polynomials modulo the null space of ⟨p,q⟩=∑_{j,k}m_{j+k}overline(p_j)q_k; on polynomial classes the densely defined symmetric multiplication operator is S[p]=[tp].

Position, momentum, and uncertainty: On $L^2(\mathbb R)$ set
$Qf(x)=xf(x)$ with $D(Q)=\{f:xf\in L^2\}$ and
$Pf=-if'$ with $D(P)=H^1(\mathbb R)$, using distributional derivatives.
Both are self-adjoint and the Schwartz space is a core for each and
a common invariant core. For the Fourier convention
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi ix\xi}f(x)\,dx$,
$\mathcal FP\mathcal F^{-1}=M_{2\pi\xi}$.
Their unitary groups are
$U(a)f(x)=e^{iax}f(x)$ and $V(b)f(x)=f(x+b)$, with
$U(a)V(b)=e^{-iab}V(b)U(a)$.
For a unit $f\in D(Q)\cap D(P)$,
\[
 \|(Q-q)f\|\,\|(P-p)f\|\geq\tfrac12,
 \quad q=\faip{f}{Qf},\ p=\faip{f}{Pf}.
\]
No bounded canonical commutator: Bounded operators on a nonzero Banach space cannot satisfy $AB-BA=I$.

Scope explanation and forward reference to the full Stone–von Neumann theorem at 16456–16474 (inventoried separately), retaining regularity, nonzero central character and arbitrary multiplicity; no extra commutator-only uniqueness claim.

Koopman and abstract waves: If a measure-preserving invertible flow $\Phi_t$ has strongly
continuous pullbacks on $L^2$, then $U(t)f=f\circ\Phi_t$ is a
unitary group and Stone supplies its self-adjoint generator.
Strong continuity is an assumption to verify, not a consequence of
the group law alone. It holds for every continuous measure-preserving
flow on a compact Hausdorff space with finite regular measure,
including the smooth compact-manifold flows in the source.
On a probability space its fixed vectors are only constants iff
the flow is ergodic, and then its time averages tend in $L^2$ to
the integral of the initial function.
If $L=L^*\geq0$, the abstract wave equation has
the energy solution
\[
 u(t)=\cos(t\sqrt L)u_0+
      \frac{\sin(t\sqrt L)}{\sqrt L}v_0,
 \quad u_0\in D(\sqrt L),\ v_0\in H,
\]
where the second multiplier has value $t$ at zero. It belongs to
$C(\mathbb R;D(\sqrt L))\cap C^1(\mathbb R;H)$ and preserves
$\|\sqrt L u(t)\|^2+\|u'(t)\|^2$.
For $L\geq cI>0$ it is a unitary group on the Hilbert energy space
$D(\sqrt L)\oplus H$ with that energy norm.

The completed homogeneous wave energy space: For $L=L^*\geq0$ put $H_0=(\ker L)^\perp$ and complete
$D(\sqrt L)/\ker L$ in the norm $\|\sqrt L u\|$.
On the product of this displacement completion with $H_0$ the
abstract wave evolution is a strongly continuous unitary group,
without a positive spectral gap. Under the isometry
$(u,v)\mapsto(\sqrt L u,v)$ onto $H_0\oplus H_0$, it is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}\cos(t\sqrt L)&\sin(t\sqrt L)\\
 -\sin(t\sqrt L)&\cos(t\sqrt L)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Zero-frequency velocities may be included as a separate constant
component; in the original displacement space they give the
explicit drift $u_{\ker}(t)=u_{\ker}(0)+tv_{\ker}(0)$.

Heat and Poisson semigroups: On $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ the multipliers
$e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$ and $e^{-2\pi t|\xi|}$ give contraction
$C_0$ semigroups with generators respectively
$\Delta$ on $H^2(\mathbb R^d)$ and
$-\sqrt{-\Delta}$ on $H^1(\mathbb R^d)$.
They smooth instantly into every power domain.
The heat kernels
$g_t(x)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$ give contraction
$C_0$ semigroups by convolution also on $L^p$, $1\leq p<\infty$.
Their generator domain there is exactly
$\{f\in L^p:\Delta f\in L^p\text{ distributionally}\}$.

Legendre as a complete classical example: The polynomials
$P_n(x)=(2^nn!)^{-1}(d/dx)^n(x^2-1)^n$ are orthogonal on $[-1,1]$,
have squared $L^2$ norm $2/(2n+1)$, and
$\sqrt{(2n+1)/2}\,P_n$ form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(-1,1)$.

Nonlinear monotone resolvents and evolution: Let $A\subset H\times H$ be a possibly multivalued monotone graph
on a real Hilbert space, and assume $I+\lambda A$ is onto for every
$\lambda>0$. Its resolvent $J_\lambda=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}$ is
single valued, firmly nonexpansive, and
$A_\lambda=(I-J_\lambda)/\lambda$ is everywhere Lipschitz and
monotone, with $(J_\lambda x,A_\lambda x)\in A$.
For every $x\in\overline{D(A)}$ there is a contraction semigroup
trajectory $u(t)=S(t)x$ obtained from $u_\lambda'=-A_\lambda u_\lambda$.
For $x\in D(A)$ it is Lipschitz, satisfies
$u'(t)+Au(t)\ni0$ almost everywhere, and is unique in that class.
Moreover
$S(t)x=\lim_nJ_{t/n}^{\,n}x$, uniformly on bounded time intervals. The contraction semigroup is on the closed set closure(D(A)), with S(0)=I and strong continuity there.

On a real Hilbert space H and for every λ>0: Convex subgradients supply the hypothesis: For a proper norm-lower-semicontinuous convex
$\Phi:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, its subgradient
$a\in\partial\Phi(u)$ iff
$\Phi(v)\geq\Phi(u)+\faip{a}{v-u}$ for all $v$, is monotone and
has onto $I+\lambda\partial\Phi$ for every $\lambda>0$.
Its resolvent uniquely minimizes
$\Phi(v)+\|v-f\|^2/(2\lambda)$.

Weighted energy space and a confining compact resolvent: Let $p\in C(\mathbb R)$, $p\ge0$, and set
\[
 V=\{u\in H^1(\mathbb R):\sqrt p\,u\in L^2\},\qquad
 \|u\|_V^2=\|u'\|_2^2+\|u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt p\,u\|_2^2.
\]
This is a separable Hilbert space with $C_c^\infty$ dense.
Suppose $p(x)\ge\delta>0$ for $|x|\ge R$.
The form $a(v,u)=\int(\overline{v'}u'+p\overline vu)$
is coercive on $V$. For every $f\in L^2$ it gives a unique
$u=Tf\in V$, with $a(v,u)=\langle v,f\rangle$.
The operator $T$ on $L^2$ is bounded, positive, self-adjoint,
injective and has dense range. Its inverse $A=T^{-1}$ is the
positive self-adjoint realization of $-u''+pu$, with
\[
 D(A)=\{u\in V:-u''+pu\in L^2\text{ in distributions}\}.
\]
If $p(x)\to\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, $T$ is compact.
There is then an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_n$ and numbers
$0<\lambda_n\to\infty$ with $Ae_n=\lambda_ne_n$,
and $D(A)=\{\sum c_ne_n:\sum\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$.

Hermite basis and the harmonic oscillator: For $p(x)=x^2$, define
\[
 H_n(x)=(-1)^ne^{x^2}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}e^{-x^2},\qquad
 h_n(x)=\frac{e^{-x^2/2}H_n(x)}{(2^nn!\sqrt\pi)^{1/2}}.
\]
Then $(h_n)_{n\ge0}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb R)$,
$Ah_n=(2n+1)h_n$, and
\[
 D(A)=\left\{\sum c_nh_n:\sum(2n+1)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.
\]
The restriction of $-d^2/dx^2+x^2$ to $\mathcal S$ is
essentially self-adjoint, with this closure. Its resolvent is
compact. The sharp ground-state inequality is
$\|u'\|_2^2+\|xu\|_2^2\ge\|u\|_2^2$ on $V$;
equality holds exactly for Gaussian multiples.
Supplementary chapter example contrasting Stieltjes and Hamburger uniqueness criteria.

Friedrichs--Krein resolvent bounds: Let $S$ be densely defined, closed, symmetric and nonnegative on a
complex Hilbert space $H$. It has nonnegative self-adjoint extensions
$S_F,S_K$ such that for every $a>0$ and every nonnegative self-adjoint
extension $T$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal H\supset H$, isometrically
containing $H$ as a closed subspace,
\[
 (S_F+a)^{-1}\ \le\ P_H(T+a)^{-1}|_H\ \le\ (S_K+a)^{-1}.
\]
Order is quadratic-form order on bounded self-adjoint operators.
The inclusion $T\supset S$ refers to both the action and its original
domain in $H$. The construction does not require $S\ge cI$ with $c>0$.

Stieltjes existence and exact uniqueness criterion: Let $s_n$ be a real sequence and define $L(t^n)=s_n$ on the complex
polynomials. There is a finite positive measure $\mu$ on $[0,\infty)$
with all moments finite and $s_n=\int t^n\,d\mu$ if and only if
\[
 L(\overline p p)\ge0,\qquad L(t\overline p p)\ge0
 \quad\text{for every polynomial }p.
\]
In its polynomial Hilbert space, let $S$ be the closure of
multiplication by $t$ on the polynomial classes. The representing
measure is unique if and only if $S$ has exactly one nonnegative
self-adjoint extension in that Hilbert space, equivalently
$S_F=S_K$. This condition is not replaced by essential
self-adjointness, which corresponds to the stronger unrestricted
Hamburger uniqueness condition. Its canonical polynomial space is the completion of polynomials modulo the null space of ⟨p,q⟩=L(overline(p)q), and S is the graph closure of [p]↦[tp] on polynomial classes.

The Gaussian integrals below use angular Fourier frequency $p$;
it equals $2\pi$ times the frequency in the global Fourier convention.

Stone--von Neumann, with multiplicity: Let $d\ge1$, let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$W:\mathbb R^{2d}\to\mathcal U(H)$ be strongly continuous with
\[
 W(z)W(w)=e^{i\omega(z,w)/2}W(z+w),\qquad W(0)=I,
 \quad \omega((q,p),(q',p'))=p\cdot q'-p'\cdot q.
\]
There is a nonzero Hilbert space $M$ and a unitary
$H\simeq L^2(\mathbb R^d)\otimes M$ under which
\[
 W(q,p)=W_0(q,p)\otimes I_M,
 \qquad (W_0(q,p)f)(t)=e^{ip\cdot(t-q/2)}f(t-q).
\]
In particular an irreducible such representation is unitarily
equivalent to $W_0$, and $W_0$ is irreducible. A specified nonzero
constant in place of $1$ in the phase is reduced to this form by a
linear rescaling of one set of coordinates.

Scope limitation for the preceding Stone–von Neumann theorem: it covers finitely many coordinates, strongly continuous unitary Weyl relations and a fixed nonzero central character; it makes no uniqueness assertion after removing these hypotheses.

Weak continuity at zero already gives a $C_0$ semigroup: Let $T(t)$, $t\ge0$, be bounded linear operators on a Banach space,
with $T(0)=I$ and $T(t+s)=T(t)T(s)$. If
$\ell(T(t)x)\to\ell(x)$ as $t\downarrow0$ for every $x,\ell$,
then $T$ is strongly continuous. This is the weak-continuity
variant in \cite[Section 34.1]{B08}.

Stable dual-consistent schemes produce weak solutions: Let $G$ be a closed densely defined operator on a complex Hilbert
space $H$, and suppose $D(G^*)$ is dense. Let $C_h\in\mathcal B(H)$
for $h\downarrow0$, and write $G_h=(C_h-I)/h$. Suppose that for
each $T<\infty$ the powers $C_h^n$, $nh\le T$, are uniformly
bounded, and
$G_h^*w\to G^*w$ for every $w\in D(G^*)$.
For each $x\in H$, the step functions
$u_h(t)=C_h^{\lfloor t/h\rfloor}x$ have weakly convergent
subsequences in $L^2(0,T;H)$. Every such weak limit belongs to
$L^\infty(0,T;H)$ and satisfies
\[
 \int_0^T\big(\langle w'(t),u(t)\rangle+
                    \langle G^*w(t),u(t)\rangle\big)dt
       +\langle w(0),x\rangle=0
\]
for $w\in C^1([0,T];H)\cap C([0,T];D(G^*)_{\rm graph})$
with $w(T)=0$. No uniqueness or strong convergence is asserted
without additional hypotheses. This is the weak-existence
variant of \cite[Section 34.3, Theorem 9]{B08}.

Spectral mapping under eventual norm continuity: Let $T$ be a $C_0$ semigroup on a complex Banach space with generator
$A$. If $t\mapsto T(t)$ is operator-norm continuous for all
$t>t_0$ for some $t_0\ge0$, then for every $t>0$,
\[
 \sigma(T(t))\setminus\{0\}=\exp(t\sigma(A)).
\]
This is the norm-continuity variant of
\cite[Section 34.5, Theorem 12$'$]{B08}; eventual compactness is
a sufficient stronger hypothesis, not the hypothesis used here.

The full translation model and its exact multiplicity condition: Let $M$ be any complex Hilbert space. On $L^2(\mathbb R;M)$,
$V(t)f(s)=f(s+t)$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with
self-adjoint Stone operator $-i\,d/ds$, on the domain of functions
whose distributional derivative belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R;M)$.
Its angular Fourier model is multiplication by $e^{it\lambda}$,
with Stone operator multiplication by $\lambda$ on
$\{g:\lambda g\in L^2\}$.
A self-adjoint operator, or its unitary group, has this full
translation representation exactly when it has a spectral model
with Lebesgue measure and constant multiplicity $M$.
Absolute continuity and full topological support alone do not
assert that constant multiplicity.

Foundational scalar measure convention: measures are positive countably additive, functions identified a.e., assertions on completed measures understood on the completion. Tonelli for nonnegative measurable functions on sigma-finite products; Fubini for absolute integrability. Scalar monotone convergence, Fatou, dominated convergence and construction of Lebesgue measure are reused measure foundations, with cited D11 locations, rather than new vector/distribution theorems. Unless explicitly restricted, scalars are R or C and functionals scalar-linear. Integral duality is integral fg without conjugation; Hilbert products are conjugate-linear first.

Sequence duals [fa2:p4:sequence-duals]. Integration against a sequence gives surjective linear isometries $\ell^1\simeq(c_0)'$, $\ell^\infty\simeq(\ell^1)'$, and $\ell^q\simeq(\ell^p)'$ for $1<p<\infty$, $p^{-1}+q^{-1}=1$. Moreover $c'=\ell^1\oplus\mathbb K\lambda$, where $\lambda(x)=\lim x_n$; this is an algebraic decomposition with $L(x)=\sum a_nx_n+b\lambda(x)$ and $\pfnorm L=\sum|a_n|+|b|$.

Radon--Nikodym and the Hilbert route [fa2:p4:radon-nikodym]. If $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite and $
u$ is a finite signed or complex measure with $
u\ll\mu$, there is a unique $g\in L^1(\mu)$ such that $
u(A)=\int_Ag\,d\mu$ for every measurable $A$. More generally a $\sigma$-finite positive $
u\ll\mu$ has a nonnegative measurable density, possibly nonintegrable on the whole space.

Put 1/p+1/q=1. $L^p$ duality, including the measure boundary [fa2:p4:lp-duality]. For any positive measure $\mu$ and $1<p<\infty$, integration is an isometric linear bijection $L^q(\mu)\to L^p(\mu)'$. For $p=1$ the same assertion with ordinary $L^\infty$ holds when $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite. These assertions require neither separability nor finite total mass. The ordinary $p=1$ statement is not asserted for an arbitrary measure space.

Riesz--Markov, precise scalar-linear version [fa2:p4:riesz-markov]. Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff. Every positive functional on $C_c(X,\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique positive Radon measure. Every bounded functional on $C_0(X,\mathbb K)$ is integration against a unique finite signed or complex Radon measure $\nu$, and $\pfnorm L=|\nu|(X)$. Here Radon means compact-finite, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Finite Radon measures are compact-inner regular on all Borel sets. For compact $X$, $C_0(X)=C(X)$.

The bounded-variation bridge on an interval [fa2:p4:stieltjes-bridge]. For a finite scalar Borel measure $
u$ on $[a,b]$, define on $\mathbb R$ $F(t)=
u([a,b]\cap(-\infty,t])$. Then $F$ is right-continuous, has bounded variation, is zero for $t<a$, is constant for $t\ge b$, and $
u((s,t])=F(t)-F(s)$ after extending $
u$ by zero. Its total variation on $\mathbb R$ is $|
u|([a,b])$. Conversely every such normalized right-continuous BV function defines a unique finite measure. For continuous $f$ the functional $\int f\,d
u$ is the corresponding Riemann--Stieltjes functional, with both endpoint atoms retained by this extension convention.

The literal normalized Riemann--Stieltjes form [fa2:p4:riemann-stieltjes-endpoint]. Let $a<b$ and let $
u$ be a finite scalar measure on $[a,b]$. For standard tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums on this interval use \[ w(a)=0,\qquad w(t)=
u([a,t])\quad(a<t\le b). \] Then $w$ has bounded variation, $\operatorname{Var}_{[a,b]}w =|
u|([a,b])$, and for every $f\in C[a,b]$, \[ \int_a^bf\,dw=\int_{[a,b]}f\,d
u. \] Thus a continuous functional $L$ on $C[a,b]$ has this normalized representation with $\operatorname{Var}w=\|L\|$. An atom at $a$ produces the right jump $w(a+)-w(a)=
u(\{a\})$. Right continuity is imposed inside $(a,b)$, and is not required at the normalized left endpoint.

A weakly null $L^1$ sequence is uniformly integrable [fa2:p4:l1-gliding-hump]. On a $\sigma$-finite space, if $f_n\rightharpoonup0$ in $L^1$, then the integrals of $|f_n|$ are uniformly absolutely continuous on small-measure sets and uniformly small outside a suitable finite-measure set. The latter assertion is essential on an infinite-measure space.

Dunford--Pettis in scalar $L^1$ [fa2:p4:dunford-pettis-l1]. Let $\mu$ be $\sigma$-finite. A set $\mathcal A\subset L^1(\mu)$ has weakly compact closure if and only if it is bounded and \[ \sup_{f\in\mathcal A}\int_E|f|\longrightarrow0\quad(\mu(E)\to0), \qquad \inf_{\mu(F)<\infty}\sup_{f\in\mathcal A}\int_{X\setminus F}|f|=0. \]

Strong measurability and Bochner integrability [fa2:p4:bochner-definition]. A Banach-valued function is strongly measurable if it is an almost everywhere pointwise norm limit of measurable finite-valued simple functions. It is Bochner integrable if it is an $L^1$-norm limit of integrable simple functions. For $s=\sum_j1_{A_j}x_j$, on disjoint sets of finite measure, put $\int s=\sum_j\mu(A_j)x_j$.

Construction and convergence of the Bochner integral [fa2:p4:bochner, fa2:p4:dominated-convergence, fa2:p4:lp-completeness]. A strongly measurable $f$ is Bochner integrable exactly when $\int\pfnorm f<\infty$. Its integral is the unique continuous extension of simple integration, with $\pfnorm{\int f}\le\int\pfnorm f$. Bounded linear maps commute with the integral. If $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere in norm and $\pfnorm{f_n}\le g\in L^1$, then $\int\pfnorm{f_n-f}\to0$ and $\int f_n\to\int f$. For $1\le p\le\infty$ the strongly measurable $L^p(X;E)$ is Banach. For $E=\mathbb K$ this proves scalar $L^p$ completeness on every positive measure space: each strongly measurable scalar function has an ordinary measurable representative and conversely, so the almost-everywhere quotient is the usual scalar one.

Pettis measurability criterion and weak integrals [fa2:p4:pettis-measurability]. On a complete measure space, $f:X\to E$ is strongly measurable if and only if it is weakly measurable and essentially takes values in a separable subspace. A Bochner integral is also a weak integral: $\ell(\int f)=\int\ell(f)$ for every $\ell\in E'$. Weak integrability alone does not imply Bochner integrability.

The test-function LF topology [fa2:p4:test-lf]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For compact $K\subset\Omega$, let $\pfD_K$ be the smooth functions supported in $K$, with seminorms $p_m(\phi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_x|\partial^\alpha\phi(x)|$. Choose compact $K_j\subset\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}$ exhausting $\Omega$. On $\pfD(\Omega)=\bigcup_j\pfD_{K_j}$ take the finest locally convex topology making all inclusions continuous. Equivalently, its continuous seminorms are exactly the seminorms whose restrictions to every $\pfD_{K_j}$ are continuous. This is the strict LF topology. It is a topology defined by seminorms, not a definition by convergent sequences. A distribution is a continuous scalar-linear functional on this space, denoted $u\in\pfD'(\Omega)$.

For the strict LF test-function topology of an open Omega subset R^d defined at 17226–17239: Bounded sets, continuity, and distribution order [fa2:p4:test-bounded, fa2:p4:finite-order]. The subspace topology on $\pfD_K$ is its displayed Fr\'echet topology. A set in $\pfD(\Omega)$ is bounded if and only if it is contained in one $\pfD_K$ and all its $p_m$ are bounded. A linear functional $u$ is a distribution if and only if for every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there are $C_K<\infty$ and $m_K\in\mathbb N$ such that \[ |u(\phi)|\le C_Kp_{m_K}(\phi)\quad(\phi\in\pfD_K). \] A sequence tends to zero in $\pfD$ exactly when its supports lie in one compact set and every derivative tends uniformly to zero there.

Limits and calculus [fa2:p4:distribution-calculus]. Locally integrable functions and locally finite scalar Radon measures define distributions by integration. Set $\partial^\alpha u(\phi)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}u(\partial^\alpha\phi)$ and $(au)(\phi)=u(a\phi)$ for $a\in C^\infty(\Omega)$. These are distributions; the Leibniz rule holds. If $u_j(\phi)$ has a limit for every test function, the limit is a distribution. If $u_j\to u$ in this weak distribution sense and $a_j\to a$ in $C^\infty_{\rm loc}$, then $a_ju_j\to au$.

Smooth partitions of unity [fa2:p4:partition-unity]. Every open cover of an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ admits a countable locally finite subordinate smooth partition of unity, with compactly supported nonnegative members.

Localization, support, and gluing [fa2:p4:distribution-gluing]. Distributions on overlapping open sets that agree on all intersections glue uniquely to a distribution on their union. The support of $u$ is the complement of the union of open sets where it vanishes; $u$ vanishes on that union. A compactly supported distribution extends uniquely to a continuous functional on $C^\infty(\Omega)$ by $u(f)=u(\chi f)$ with $\chi=1$ near its support. Conversely every continuous functional on $C^\infty(\Omega)$ has compact support and defines such a distribution.

Point support and local continuous primitives [fa2:p4:point-support, fa2:p4:distribution-structure]. A distribution supported at $a$ is a finite linear combination of $\partial^\alpha\delta_a$. Every distribution is locally a finite sum of derivatives of continuous functions. If its support is compact and contained in an open $V\Subset\Omega$, these continuous functions can be chosen with compact support in $V$. Globally one obtains a locally finite sum of such derivatives.

Young inequalities and approximate identities [fa2:p4:young, fa2:p4:approximate-identity]. If $1\le p,q,r\le\infty$ and $1+1/r=1/p+1/q$, then $\pfnorm{f*g}_r\le\pfnorm f_p\pfnorm g_q$. For $1\le p<\infty$, translations are norm-continuous on $L^p$. If $\rho\in C_c^\infty$ is nonnegative with integral one and $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-d}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$. In particular $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $L^p$. For continuous $f$ the convergence is locally uniform, and is uniform globally when $f$ is uniformly continuous.

Distribution convolution [fa2:p4:distribution-convolution]. For $u\in\pfD'(\mathbb R^d)$ and $\phi\in\pfD$ put $(u*\phi)(x)=u_y(\phi(x-y))$. This is smooth and $\partial^\alpha(u*\phi)=(\partial^\alpha u)*\phi =u*(\partial^\alpha\phi)$. For distributions $u,v$ convolution is defined whenever the addition map is proper on $\pfsupp u\times\pfsupp v$; in particular one compact support suffices. It is commutative, derivatives commute with it, and $\pfsupp(u*v)\subset\pfsupp u+\pfsupp v$. Associativity holds when both inner convolutions exist by the pair-support condition and triple addition is proper, in particular when two factors have compact support. Finally $u*\rho_\varepsilon\to u$ in distributions.

Fourier normalization [fa2:p4:fourier-normalization]. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ use $\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$. The Schwartz space $\pfS$ has seminorms $\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$. Its continuous scalar-linear dual is $\pfS'$, the tempered distributions. Set $\widehat u(\phi)=u(\widehat\phi)$. Thus $\widehat{\partial_j u}=2\pi i\xi_j\widehat u$ and $\widehat{x_ju}=-(2\pi i)^{-1}\partial_j\widehat u$.

Fourier inversion and Plancherel [fa2:p4:fourier-inversion, fa2:p4:plancherel]. The Fourier transform is a continuous automorphism of $\pfS$, $\widehat{\widehat f}(x)=f(-x)$, and $f(x)=\int e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\widehat f(\xi)\,d\xi$. It extends uniquely to a unitary map on $L^2$ and to an automorphism of $\pfS'$. For $f\in L^1\cap L^2$ the $L^2$ extension agrees with the integral transform. Multiplication and differentiation obey the displayed normalization; convolution of Schwartz functions transforms to pointwise multiplication.

Here polynomial integral growth means: for some N>=0, integral (1+|x|)^(-N)|f(x)| dx<infinity. Tempered examples and compact support [fa2:p4:tempered-examples]. Every compactly supported distribution is tempered. A locally integrable function of at most polynomial growth in the integral sense defines a tempered distribution. In particular $\widehat1=\delta_0$, $\widehat{\delta_0}=1$, and polynomials transform to the corresponding delta derivatives. Not every distribution is tempered.

Paley--Wiener, smooth and distribution forms [fa2:p4:paley-wiener]. For a nonempty compact convex $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ put $H_K(\eta)=\sup_{x\in K}x\cdot\eta$. The Fourier--Laplace transform of $f\in C_c^\infty$ supported in $K$ is entire and satisfies, for every $N$, \[ |\widehat f(z)|\le C_N(1+|z|)^{-N}e^{2\pi H_K(\operatorname{Im}z)}. \] Conversely every entire function with these bounds is the transform of such an $f$. The transforms of distributions supported in $K$ are exactly the entire functions with a bound \[ |F(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^M e^{2\pi H_K(\operatorname{Im}z)} \] for some $C,M$. The exponent $M$ need not equal the least order of the distribution.

Let K be nonempty compact convex in R^d and H_K(eta)=sup_{x in K} x dot eta. More explicitly, for a nonzero polynomial P on C^d and entire G, if |P(z)G(z)|<=C(1+|z|)^M exp(2pi H_K(Im z)) for all z in C^d and some C,M, then |G(z)|<=C'(1+|z|)^(M') exp(2pi H_K(Im z)) for all z and some C',M'. Polynomial division preserves exponential type [fa2:p4:polynomial-division]. If $P$ is a nonzero polynomial and $G$ is entire, a Paley--Wiener polynomial-growth bound for $PG$ with convex type $K$ implies one for $G$ with the same $K$.

Compact-support solvability [fa2:p4:compact-pde-solvability]. Write $D_j=(2\pi i)^{-1}\partial_j$ and let $P\ne0$ be a polynomial. For compactly supported $v\in\pfD'(\mathbb R^d)$, the equation $P(D)u=v$ has a compactly supported distributional solution if and only if $\widehat v=PG$ for an entire $G$. Such a compactly supported solution is unique, and its support is contained in the convex hull of $\pfsupp v$.

Malgrange--Ehrenpreis for constant coefficients [fa2:p4:fundamental-solution]. Every nonzero constant-coefficient scalar linear differential operator on $\mathbb R^d$ has a distributional fundamental solution. If $P(D)E=\delta_0$ and $v$ has compact support, $E*v$ is a distributional solution of $P(D)u=v$.

Sobolev norm and negative spaces [fa2:p4:sobolev-definition]. For open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, integer $m\ge0$, and $1\le p\le\infty$, let $W^{m,p}(\Omega)$ consist of $L^p$ functions whose distribution derivatives through order $m$ lie in $L^p$.
