Use the norm $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\pfnorm{\partial^\alpha u}_p$; the equivalent Euclidean product norm is used for its Hilbert structure when $p=2$. For $p<\infty$, $W^{m,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty$. No corresponding closure characterization is silently asserted at $p=\infty$.

For every open Omega subset R^d, integer m>=0 and 1<=p<=infinity, with W^{m,p} and W_0^{m,p} as defined at 17730–17740: Completeness, local smoothing, and calculus [fa2:p4:sobolev-calculus]. $W^{m,p}$ is Banach, reflexive for $1<p<\infty$, and separable for $p<\infty$. Smooth functions in $\Omega$ are dense for finite $p$. On every compact interior set, convolution smooths and converges with all the weak derivatives of order at most $m$ in $L^p$ for finite $p$. At $p=\infty$ it gives uniform derivative bounds, local $L^r$ convergence for finite $r$, and weak-star derivative convergence; $L^\infty$ norm convergence is not claimed. For $m=1$, the weak derivative criterion is equivalent to the existence of an almost-everywhere representative absolutely continuous on almost every coordinate line, with the classical line derivatives in $L^p$. Products of bounded $W^{1,p}$ functions obey the product rule. If $F\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ has bounded derivative, then $\nabla F(u)=F'(u)\nabla u$ whenever $F(u)\in L^p$; in particular $F(0)=0$ suffices. Real truncations and absolute values obey their almost-everywhere chain rules as well.

For a nonempty open interval I and 1<=p<=infinity (reciprocal infinity is zero): One-dimensional absolute continuity [fa2:p4:one-dimensional-sobolev]. On an interval $I$, each $u\in W^{1,p}(I)$ has a unique continuous representative, locally absolutely continuous, with $u(x)-u(y)=\int_y^xu'(t)\,dt$. It extends continuously to finite endpoints. For finite $I$, \[ \pfnorm u_\infty\le |I|^{-1/p}\pfnorm u_p +|I|^{1-1/p}\pfnorm{u'}_p. \] For $p>1$, $|u(x)-u(y)|\le\pfnorm{u'}_p|x-y|^{1-1/p}$. $W^{1,\infty}$ is exactly the essentially bounded functions with a Lipschitz representative, whose least Lipschitz constant is $\pfnorm{u'}_\infty$. The global $L^\infty$ condition matters on an unbounded interval.

Extension under the actual boundary hypotheses [fa2:p4:sobolev-extension]. On a half-space, or on a $C^1$ domain with compact boundary, there is a bounded linear extension $E:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ simultaneously for $1\le p\le\infty$. It may be chosen to map bounded domains to functions supported in one fixed bounded neighborhood. Consequently smooth functions up to the boundary are dense for finite $p$. The assertion here does not replace $C^1$ by Lipschitz without proving the additional chart theorem.

For 1<=p<=infinity in the forward implication: Translation characterization [fa2:p4:sobolev-translations]. On $\mathbb R^d$, $u\in W^{1,p}$ implies $\pfnorm{u(\cdot+h)-u}_p\le |h|\pfnorm{\nabla u}_p$, using a fixed Euclidean gradient norm. Conversely, for $1<p<\infty$, $u\in L^p$ with these differences bounded by $C|h|$ belongs to $W^{1,p}$, with each derivative norm at most $C$.
The $p=1$ Sobolev inequality [fa2:p4:sobolev-one]. If $d>1$ and $u\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^d)$, then $\pfnorm u_{d/(d-1)}\le C_d\sum_j\pfnorm{\partial_ju}_1$.

Sobolev and Morrey embeddings [fa2:p4:sobolev-embedding]. For $1\le p<d$, on $\mathbb R^d$, $\pfnorm u_{p^*}\le C\pfnorm{\nabla u}_p$ for $u\in C_c^\infty$, $p^*=dp/(d-p)$, and hence for $u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$. On bounded $C^1$ domains the same embedding holds with the full $W^{1,p}$ norm. For $p=d$ these domains admit all finite target exponents. For $p>d$ there is a continuous representative satisfying $|u(x)-u(y)|\le C\pfnorm{\nabla u}_p|x-y|^{1-d/p}$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the analogous full-norm estimate on an extension domain. Iteration gives the higher-order embeddings: if $mp<d$, $W^{m,p}\hookrightarrow L^{dp/(d-mp)}$; if $mp=d$, all finite exponents are allowed on bounded extension domains; if $mp>d$, the derivatives have the H\"older regularity obtained when their remaining Sobolev order exceeds $d/p$. In particular nonintegral $m-d/p=k+\alpha$ gives $C^{k,\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$; at a positive integer gap $k=m-d/p$, the conclusion is $C^{k-1,\alpha}$ for every $0<\alpha<1$, without claiming a Lipschitz endpoint for that last derivative.

Kolmogorov--Riesz and Rellich [fa2:p4:kolmogorov-riesz, fa2:p4:rellich]. For $1\le p<\infty$, a bounded family $\mathcal A\subset L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ is relatively norm compact exactly when it is uniformly tight in $L^p$ and $\sup_{f\in\mathcal A}\pfnorm{f(\cdot+h)-f}_p\to0$ as $h\to0$. The translation condition alone gives compactness after restriction to any bounded measurable region. On bounded $C^1$ domains, $W^{1,p}\hookrightarrow L^q$ is compact for $q<p^*$ if $p<d$, for every finite $q$ if $p=d$, and into $C(\overline\Omega)$ if $p>d$. For $W^{1,p}_0$ the subcritical $L^q$ conclusions hold on arbitrary bounded open sets.

Trace, its kernel, and Poincar\'e [fa2:p4:sobolev-trace, fa2:p4:poincare]. On a bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$, restriction of smooth functions extends to a bounded trace $\operatorname{Tr}:W^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^p(\partial\Omega)$. Its kernel is $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$, and a function is in that kernel exactly when its zero extension belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$. On arbitrary bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$, $\pfnorm u_p\le C\pfnorm{\nabla u}_p$ for $u\in W^{1,p}_0$. The same inequality holds trivially on $\Omega=\varnothing$ in every dimension. On an interval these trace values are its two endpoint values.

Negative Sobolev representation [fa2:p4:negative-sobolev]. For $1\le p<\infty$ and $q=p'$, every functional $F\in(W^{1,p}_0(\Omega))'$ has the representation \[ F(u)=\int f_0u+\sum_{j=1}^d\int f_j\partial_ju, \qquad f_j\in L^q, \qquad \pfnorm F=\max_{0\le j\le d}\pfnorm{f_j}_q, \] for the sum-component Sobolev norm used here and on the present Lebesgue measure space. With the distribution convention this is $F=f_0-\sum\partial_jf_j$. On bounded domains with $d\ge1$, and trivially on $\Omega=\varnothing$ in every dimension, $f_0$ can be omitted with a constant depending on Poincar\'e; norm equality then refers to the derivative norm, not automatically the original full norm.

For arbitrary real s,t, using the actual Fourier transform of tempered distributions with the 2pi convention: The Fourier Sobolev scale [fa2:p4:sobolev-hilbert]. For real $s$ define $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ by $\pfnorm u_{H^s}^2=\int(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^s|\widehat u(\xi)|^2d\xi$. It is a Hilbert space of tempered distributions. Its linear dual is $H^{-s}$ under the bilinear distribution pairing \[ (u,v)\longmapsto\int\widehat u(\xi)\widehat v(-\xi)d\xi, \] which extends $\int uv$ on smooth functions, and $(I-\Delta)^{t/2}:H^s\to H^{s-t}$ is an isometric isomorphism. For nonnegative integer $m$, $H^m=W^{m,2}$ with equivalent norms. Compactly supported distributions belong to $H^{-N}$ for some $N$. Multiplication by a compactly supported smooth function is bounded on every $H^s$; derivatives lower the index by their order. If $s>k+d/2$, $H^s\subset C^k$ with bounded continuous derivatives.

For every real s, circle H^s is realized by periodic distributions, with their actual distributional Fourier coefficients; its derivative is the distributional derivative, and its dual pairing is the scalar-linear bilinear distribution pairing. Periodic and smooth-curve Hilbert scales [fa2:p4:periodic-sobolev]. On the circle, $H^s=\{u:\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(1+4\pi^2n^2)^s|\widehat u(n)|^2<\infty\}$. Its dual is $H^{-s}$, derivatives lower order, and $H^{s+\varepsilon}\hookrightarrow H^s$ is compact for $\varepsilon>0$. On a compact smooth curve, a finite smooth atlas and partition of unity define equivalent $H^s$ norms independently of atlas. A $C^\infty$ reparametrization is an isomorphism of these spaces; the scalar-density Jacobian is included in the dual pairing.

Constant-coefficient elliptic parametrix and local regularity [fa2:p4:elliptic-parametrix]. Let $L=P(D)$ have order $m$ and elliptic principal symbol. There is a tempered distribution $Q$, smooth off zero, with $LQ=\delta+r$, $r\in\pfS$. A parametrix supported in any prescribed ball about zero can be chosen with a smooth remainder. If $Lu$ is smooth on an open set, then $u$ is smooth there.

Three lines [fa2:p4:three-lines]. If $F$ is bounded and continuous on $0\le\operatorname{Re}z\le1$ and holomorphic inside, with $|F(j+it)|\le M_j$, then $|F(\theta)|\le M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta$, $0<\theta<1$.

Riesz--Thorin, with common-domain compatibility [fa2:p4:riesz-thorin]. On $\sigma$-finite measure spaces let one complex-linear operator on the complex space $L^{p_0}+L^{p_1}$ have compatible bounds $L^{p_j}\to L^{q_j}$ with norms $M_j$, $1\le p_j,q_j\le\infty$. For $0<\theta<1$ set $p^{-1}=(1-\theta)p_0^{-1}+\theta p_1^{-1}$ and similarly $q$. Then $\pvnorm{Tf}_q\le M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta\pvnorm f_p$. In particular the finite-measure $L^1/L^\infty$ self-map form has $M_p\le M_1^{1/p}M_\infty^{1/p'}$; that special self-map bound also holds for real operators, by the norm-preserving endpoint complexification proved in Proposition~\ref{fa2:p2:endpoint-interpolation-bridge}.

Marcinkiewicz interpolation [fa2:p4:marcinkiewicz]. A sublinear operator with weak $(p_0,p_0)$ and weak $(p_1,p_1)$ bounds, $1\le p_0<p_1\le\infty$, is strongly bounded on $L^p$ for $p_0<p<p_1$. The infinity endpoint here means a strong supremum bound. The result applies to the modulus of a linear operator defined first on a dense intersection.

Hardy--Littlewood maximal bounds [fa2:p4:maximal]. Define \[ Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)}|f|. \] Then $\mu\{Mf>\lambda\}\le C_d\pvnorm f_1/\lambda$. It is bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p\le\infty$, and if d>=1 it is not bounded on $L^1$. Every locally integrable function has almost every point as a Lebesgue point. Authorized correction: all affirmative estimates and Lebesgue differentiation hold for every d>=0; only failure of strong L^1 boundedness requires d>=1 (AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA.txt, maximal correction). The weak estimate is for f in L^1 and every lambda>0; local differentiation is for every locally integrable f.

For d>=1, as required by AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA.txt correction 1: Calder\'on--Zygmund decomposition [fa2:p4:cz-decomposition]. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ and $\lambda>0$, there are disjoint dyadic cubes $Q_j$, $f=g+\sum b_j$, with \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum|Q_j|\le\pvnorm f_1/\lambda,\qquad \pvnorm g_\infty\le2^d\lambda,\qquad \pvnorm g_1\le\pvnorm f_1,\\ &\int b_j=0,\qquad \sum\pvnorm{b_j}_1\le2\pvnorm f_1,\qquad \pfsupp b_j\subset Q_j. \end{aligned} \] If $f\in L^2$, also $g,b_j\in L^2$ and the sum converges in $L^2$ as well as in $L^1$.

For Euclidean dimension d>=0, retain the stated all-dimensional affirmative operator theorem; the d>=1 qualification of the decomposition does not restrict this theorem. Standard convolution Calder\'on--Zygmund theorem [fa2:p4:calderon-zygmund]. Let $T$ be an $L^2$-bounded translation-invariant operator whose distribution kernel agrees off zero with a $C^1$ function $k$, where $|k(x)|\le C|x|^{-d}$ and $|\nabla k(x)|\le C|x|^{-d-1}$. Then $T$ is weak $(1,1)$ and bounded on every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$, with compatible extensions. This is a theorem about standard convolution kernels; a general variable-kernel theory is not being claimed from it.

The standard smooth-kernel multiplier equivalence [fa2:p4:cz-multiplier]. For a distribution $K$ smooth off zero with $|\partial^\alpha k(x)|\le C_\alpha|x|^{-d-|\alpha|}$, the following equivalent conditions specify a Calder\'on--Zygmund distribution: uniformly bounded pairings with all dilations of normalized compactly supported $C^N$ bumps, for one sufficiently large fixed $N$; or $\widehat K=m$ bounded, smooth off zero, with $|\partial^\alpha m(\xi)|\le C_\alpha|\xi|^{-|\alpha|}$. Equivalently, in the presence of all the displayed kernel bounds, it suffices that $\widehat K$ be a bounded function. Here the bump condition means sup_{s>0,phi}|K(phi(./s))|<infinity, for smooth phi supported in the unit ball with ||phi||_{C^N}<=1 and one sufficiently large fixed N; it is a uniform bound over the entire normalized bump family and all positive dilations.

Principal value, boundary values, and Hilbert transform [fa2:p4:hilbert-transform, fa2:p4:principal-value]. On $\mathbb R$, $\operatorname{pv}(1/x)$ is tempered, $(\log|x|)'=\operatorname{pv}(1/x)$, and \[ (x\pm i0)^{-1}=\operatorname{pv}(1/x)\mp i\pi\delta_0, \qquad \widehat{\operatorname{pv}(1/x)}=-i\pi\operatorname{sgn}\xi. \] The Hilbert transform has multiplier $-i\operatorname{sgn}\xi$, is an isometry of $L^2$ with $H^2=-I$, and is bounded on $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$ and weak $(1,1)$. It has neither a strong $L^1$ nor a strong $L^\infty$ bound. Its symmetric truncated integrals converge in $L^2$ to the multiplier definition.

The atom sums converge in L^1 and identify the actual completed atomic Hardy space as an L^1 subspace; all Euclidean dimensions d>=0 are included. Atomic $H^1$, its completeness, and the endpoint bound [fa2:p4:hardy-atomic]. An atom is supported in a ball $B$, has integral zero, and has supremum norm at most $|B|^{-1}$. The sums $f=\sum\lambda_ja_j$, $\sum|\lambda_j|<\infty$, form a Banach space $H^1_{\rm at}$ with norm the infimum of coefficient sums. It embeds continuously in $L^1$, all its members have integral zero, and every standard convolution CZ operator is bounded $H^1_{\rm at}\to L^1$.

BMO [fa2:p4:bmo], for every d>=0: locally integrable real or complex functions on R^d modulo constants and almost-everywhere equality, with seminorm sup over positive-radius balls B of |B|^(-1) integral_B |b-b_B|, where b_B=|B|^(-1)integral_B b; BMO consists of those functions for which this is finite. Authorized correction 2 retains the all-dimensional definition.

For every d>=0, BMO(R^d) modulo constants and almost-everywhere equality is complete in its quotient norm, hence Banach, and every bounded measurable scalar function belongs to BMO. Only the separate unbounded logarithm example is dimension-qualified by AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA correction 2.

For d>=1, the function log|x| on R^d, assigned value zero at x=0, is locally integrable including the origin, is an unbounded BMO function, and has uniformly bounded mean oscillation over all balls. This is the precise dimensional correction in AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA correction 2; no unboundedness is asserted in d=0.

For the completed atomic H^1(R^d) defined at 18503–18512, with no positive-dimension restriction: $p$-atoms and compactly supported mean-zero functions [fa2:p4:hardy-p-atoms]. For every $1<p<\infty$, a function supported in a ball $B$, with integral zero and $\pfnorm a_p\le|B|^{1/p-1}$, belongs to $H^1_{\rm at}$ with norm at most a constant depending only on $p,d$. Thus $L^\infty$ atoms can be replaced by these $p$-atoms with an equivalent norm. Every compactly supported $L^p$ function of integral zero belongs to $H^1$.

For the actual completed atomic H^1(R^d), and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t): Smooth maximal bound and truncated Hilbert convergence [fa2:p4:hardy-maximal-forward]. For $\Phi\in C_c^1(\mathbb R^d)$, $M_\Phi f=\sup_{t>0}|\Phi_t*f|$ satisfies $\pfnorm{M_\Phi f}_1\le C_\Phi\pfnorm f_{H^1}$. The bound is uniform over bumps supported in the unit ball with uniformly bounded $C^1$ norm. On the real line symmetric Hilbert truncations converge in $L^1$ for every $H^1$ function, and their norms $H^1\to L^1$ are bounded independently of the truncation parameter.

For real or complex scalars, with scalar-linear pairing and the actual completed atomic H^1 and BMO modulo constants and almost-everywhere equality: The dual of atomic $H^1$ [fa2:p4:hardy-bmo-dual]. Every continuous linear functional on $H^1_{\rm at}(\mathbb R^d)$ is pairing with a BMO function, unique modulo constants. Its norm and the BMO seminorm are equivalent with dimension constants. Pairing is first the integral on finite atom sums and then its continuous extension; an absolutely convergent Lebesgue integral $\int fg$ for every pair is not asserted.

Herglotz--Riesz and positive harmonic representation [fa2:p4:herglotz]. If $F$ is holomorphic in the disk and $\operatorname{Re}F\ge0$, there are a unique positive finite measure $\mu$ on the circle and a unique real $c$ such that \[ F(z)=ic+\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,d\mu(\zeta). \] Here $c=\operatorname{Im}F(0)$ and $\mu(\mathbb T)=\operatorname{Re}F(0)$. Every positive harmonic function is the Poisson integral of a unique positive finite measure.

Carath\'eodory's circle moment theorem [fa2:p4:circle-moment]. A two-sided sequence with $c_{-n}=\overline{c_n}$ is the moment sequence $c_n=\int\zeta^n d\mu$ of a finite positive circle measure exactly when all Toeplitz quadratic forms $\sum_{j,k}\overline a_ja_kc_{k-j}$ are nonnegative.

Positive definiteness includes Hermitian symmetry phi(-x)=conj(phi(x)), as required by the authorized real/complex convention. Bochner's positive-definite representation [fa2:p4:bochner-positive]. A continuous positive-definite function $\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^d$ is the Fourier transform, with the sign changed if desired, of a unique finite positive measure; its mass is $\varphi(0)$. Positive definiteness means $\sum\overline a_ja_k\varphi(x_k-x_j)\ge0$ for all finite choices. Continuity at zero alone suffices and implies uniform continuity everywhere.

Poisson summation [fa2:p4:poisson-summation]. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}f(n)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\widehat f(n)$, with absolute convergence. For an invertible real matrix $A$, \[ \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}f(An) =|\det A|^{-1}\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d} \widehat f(A^{-\mathsf T}n). \]

Local Fourier flattening [fa2:p4:wiener-local]. For $f\in L^1$, a frequency $\xi_0$, and $\varepsilon>0$, there is $h\in L^1$ with $\pvnorm h_1<\varepsilon$ and $\widehat h(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi_0)-\widehat f(\xi)$ on a neighborhood of $\xi_0$.

Wiener's translation-density and Tauberian theorem [fa2:p4:wiener-tauberian]. A closed translation-invariant subspace $Y\subset L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ equals $L^1$ if its members' transforms have no common zero. In particular translates of $K\in L^1$ span densely exactly when $\widehat K$ vanishes nowhere. If $\phi\in L^\infty$ and $K*\phi(x)\to a\int K$ as $|x|\to\infty$, with such a $K$, then $f*\phi(x)\to a\int f$ for every $f\in L^1$. If in addition $\phi$ is slowly oscillating at infinity, it itself tends to $a$. The analogous one-sided statement on $\mathbb R$ holds with $x\to+\infty$. Here slow oscillation means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $\delta,R>0$ with $|\phi(x-h)-\phi(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|h|<\delta$ and $|x|>R$ (respectively $x>R$).

The analytic Hilbert space [fa2:p4:hardy-disk]. $H^2(\mathbb D)$ consists of $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nz^n$ with $\sum|a_n|^2<\infty$. Its boundary function is the $L^2$ Fourier sum of those coefficients, and radial values are its Poisson extension. An inner function is bounded holomorphic with boundary modulus one almost everywhere. An outer function is a cyclic vector for multiplication by $z$ in $H^2$.

Beurling's theorem [fa2:p4:beurling]. Every nonzero closed subspace of $H^2$ invariant under multiplication by $z$ is $\vartheta H^2$ for an inner $\vartheta$, unique up to a unimodular constant. Invariance under all bounded analytic multipliers is equivalent to this shift invariance.

Use normalized circle Haar measure m and radial L^2 boundary function f*. The constant c in the outer formula has modulus one. Inner--outer factorization and the singular measure [fa2:p4:hardy-factorization]. Every nonzero $f\in H^2$ factors into an inner and an outer function, uniquely up to opposite unimodular constants. Its outer factor can be written \[ O(z)=c\exp\!\left(\int_{\mathbb T} \frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\log|f^*(\zeta)|dm(\zeta)\right). \] An inner function is a Blaschke product times $c\exp(-\int(\zeta+z)/(\zeta-z)d\sigma(\zeta))$, where $\sigma$ is a finite positive singular circle measure. Its zeros and this singular measure are unique.

Half-plane Hardy functions and a causal support [fa2:p4:hardy-halfplane]. An analytic function $F$ in the upper half-plane satisfies $\sup_{y>0}\int_{\mathbb R}|F(x+iy)|^2dx<\infty$ exactly when \[ F(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{2\pi izt}f(t)dt \quad\text{for some }f\in L^2(0,\infty). \] The integral is absolutely convergent at $y>0$ and has boundary values in $L^2$. The Cayley transform $z=i(1+w)/(1-w)$ gives the isometry to disk $H^2$ by $F\mapsto2\sqrt\pi\,F(i(1+w)/(1-w))/(1-w)$. Under this correspondence its inner factor has a distinguished factor $e^{iaz}$, $a\ge0$, arising from the atom at $w=1$ in the singular measure. If $F_1,F_2,F_1F_2$ all belong to the half-plane $H^2$, these coefficients add under multiplication.

Titchmarsh convolution support theorem [fa2:p4:titchmarsh]. For nonzero compactly supported distributions $u,v$ on the real line, let $a_u,b_u$ be the left and right endpoints of their supports. Then $a_{u*v}=a_u+a_v$ and $b_{u*v}=b_u+b_v$. In particular a convolution cannot acquire an initial open interval of zeros by cancellation beyond the sum of the two initial support intervals. This is stronger than support inclusion.

The source half-line $L^1$ version [fa2:p4:titchmarsh-halfline]. For nonzero $f,g\in L^1(0,\infty)$ the lower support endpoints add under convolution. If $F(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{2\pi izt}f(t)dt$, then $f=0$ on $(0,c)$ if and only if $e^{-2\pi icz}F(z)$ is bounded on the upper half-plane.

Here divides in H^infinity means b=O h or b=vartheta h for some h in H^infinity, as appropriate. Hardy multipliers and divisibility [fa2:p4:hardy-divisibility]. Every bounded operator on disk $H^2$ commuting with the shift is multiplication by a unique $b\in H^\infty$, with operator norm $\pfnorm b_\infty$. For bounded analytic functions, an inner $\vartheta$ divides $b$ in $H^\infty$ exactly when $bH^2\subset\vartheta H^2$. An outer $O\in H^\infty$ divides a bounded analytic $b$ exactly when the boundary quotient $b^*/O^*$ is essentially bounded. If $b,c$ are not both zero, their greatest common inner divisor, up to a unimodular constant, is the Beurling generator of $\overline{bH^2+cH^2}$. If $b=c=0$, this closed sum is $\{0\}$ and has no inner Beurling generator; there is no greatest common inner divisor within the class of inner functions.

Fractional difference norm [fa2:p4:fractional-sobolev]. For $0<s<1$ and $1\le p<\infty$, set \[ [g]_{s,p}^p=\int_{\mathbb R^n} \frac{\pfnorm{g(\cdot+h)-g}_p^p}{|h|^{n+sp}}dh, \qquad W^{s,p}=\{g\in L^p:[g]_{s,p}<\infty\}. \] The difference integrand is assigned value zero at $h=0$. For $1<s<2$ require first derivatives in $W^{s-1,p}$ as well. For $0<s<1$, bi-Lipschitz changes of variables with their usual almost-everywhere Jacobian bounds give equivalent order-$s$ norms. Multiplication by a bounded globally Lipschitz scalar function is bounded on $W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^n)$. In particular, smooth bounded multipliers with bounded first derivatives have this property; smoothness and boundedness alone are insufficient on the whole space. For $0<s<1$ these coordinate and multiplier statements define the corresponding spaces on a compact $C^1$ boundary by a finite atlas and bounded Lipschitz cutoffs, with equivalent norms on overlaps.

For 0<s<1, 1<=p<infinity, g in W^{s,p}(R^n), and a bounded globally Lipschitz scalar multiplier with M=||a||_infinity and global Lipschitz constant L, ||ag||_p<=M||g||_p and [ag]_{s,p}^p<=2^{p-1}(M^p[g]_{s,p}^p+||g||_p^p integral_{R^n} min(L|h|,2M)^p/|h|^{n+sp} dh). For n>=1 the latter integral is <=|S^{n-1}|(L^p/(p(1-s))+(2M)^p/(sp)). For n=0 the difference seminorm is zero and only the L^p bound is needed. Smooth bounded functions with bounded first derivatives have such a Lipschitz constant. The bounded-Lipschitz quantitative estimate is the authorized multiplier correction; no global conclusion is asserted from smoothness and boundedness alone.

Sharp first trace, including its endpoint boundary [fa2:p4:sharp-trace]. For $1<p<\infty$ and $s=1-1/p$, the trace on a half-space is a bounded surjection $W^{1,p}\to W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{d-1})$ with a bounded linear right inverse. The same holds on bounded $C^1$ domains. At $p=1$ its range is all $L^1$ of the boundary; surjectivity here is proved without asserting a bounded linear right inverse. Its kernel in all these cases is the $W^{1,p}_0$ already identified above.

The boundary jet map has domain W^{2,p}(Omega). Two boundary jets and Green's formula [fa2:p4:second-trace]. On a bounded $C^2$ domain and $1<p<\infty$, the map $u\mapsto(\operatorname{Tr}u,\operatorname{Tr}\partial_
u u)$ is bounded and onto $W^{2-1/p,p}(\partial\Omega)	imes W^{1-1/p,p}(\partial\Omega)$. For $u,v\in H^1$ the first-order integration-by-parts formula holds with their $L^2$ traces: \[ \int_\Omega(u\partial_j\overline v+ \partial_ju\,\overline v) =\int_{\partial\Omega}\operatorname{Tr}u\, \overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\,
u_j. \] For $u\in H^2$, $v\in H^1$, \[ -\int_\Omega\Delta u\,\overline v =\int_\Omega
abla u\cdot\overline{
abla v} -\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_
u u\,\overline v. \] The stated second-jet surjectivity does not include the integer fractional-order endpoint $p=1$ without a separate trace-space analysis.
Zero area with a unit segment in every direction [fa2:p4:besicovitch]. There is a compact planar set of Lebesgue measure zero containing a line segment of length one in every unoriented direction.

Homogeneous extension, residues, and the critical obstruction [fa2:p4:homogeneous-extension]. Let $k\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\})$ satisfy $k(rx)=r^\lambda k(x)$ for $r>0$, where $\lambda\in\mathbb C$. If $\lambda\notin\{-d,-d-1,\ldots\}$, there is a unique homogeneous distribution of degree $\lambda$ agreeing with $k$ off zero. For $\lambda=-d-m$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, such an extension exists if and only if \[ \int_{S^{d-1}}k(\theta)\theta^\alpha\,d\sigma(\theta)=0 \quad (|\alpha|=m). \] When it exists, the ambiguity is exactly $\sum_{|\alpha|=m}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_0$. In general there is a tempered finite-part extension $F$ with \[ F_a=a^{-d-m}(F+(\log a)R_m),\qquad R_m=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\frac{(-1)^m}{\alpha!} \left(\int_{S^{d-1}}k(\theta)\theta^\alpha d\sigma\right) \partial^\alpha\delta_0. \] Here $u_a(\phi)=a^{-d}u(\phi(\cdot/a))$ is the dilation whose action on functions is $u_a(x)=u(ax)$.

Fourier degrees and the Riesz-kernel constant [fa2:p4:homogeneous-fourier]. Every homogeneous distribution is tempered. Fourier transform changes degree $\lambda$ to degree $-d-\lambda$. If the original distribution is smooth away from zero, so is its Fourier transform. In particular, for $0<a<d$, \[ \mathcal F(|x|^{-a})(\xi)= \pi^{a-d/2}\frac{\Gamma((d-a)/2)}{\Gamma(a/2)}|\xi|^{a-d}. \]

Laplacian and causal heat fundamental solutions [fa2:p4:laplace-heat-fundamental]. Write $\omega_{d-1}=|S^{d-1}|$. Fundamental solutions for $\Delta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ are \[ \Phi_d(x)=\frac{|x|^{2-d}}{(2-d)\omega_{d-1}}\ (d\ge3), \quad \Phi_2(x)=\frac{\log|x|}{2\pi},\quad \Phi_1(x)=\frac{|x|}{2}. \] A fundamental solution of $\partial_t-\Delta_x$ on space-time is \[ E(t,x)=1_{t>0}(4\pi t)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}. \] All formulas are distribution identities including the delta source.

Fourier divergence and nonsurjectivity of coefficients [fa2:p4:fourier-failures]. There is a continuous function on the circle whose symmetric Fourier partial sums are unbounded at a prescribed point. The injective bounded coefficient map $L^1(\mathbb T)\to c_0(\mathbb Z)$ is not onto. There are also $L^1$ functions whose symmetric Fourier partial sums do not converge in $L^1$. Normalized Haar measure is used here.

Over the real or complex scalar field; for p<1 use the complete L^p quasi-norm topology, not an assumed norm. Grothendieck's bounded-function subspace theorem [fa2:p4:grothendieck-lp]. Let $\mu(X)<\infty$, $0<p<\infty$, and let $E$ be a closed linear subspace of $L^p(\mu)$ whose every element belongs to $L^\infty(\mu)$. Then $E$ is finite dimensional.

Hausdorff--Young [fa2:p4:hausdorff-young]. For $1\le p\le2$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$, $\pfnorm{\widehat f}_{p'}\le\pfnorm f_p$ on $\mathbb R^d$, with the compatible extended Fourier transform. On the circle, $\pfnorm{(\widehat f(n))}_{\ell^{p'}}\le\pfnorm f_p$.

Laplace and Hilbert--Hankel transforms [fa2:p4:laplace-hankel]. On the positive half-line, $Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)dt$ extends to a bounded self-adjoint operator on $L^2$ with norm $\sqrt\pi$. Its square is the Hilbert--Hankel (Carleman) operator \[ Hf(s)=\int_0^\infty\frac{f(t)}{s+t}dt. \] For $1<p<\infty$, $H$ has exact $L^p$ norm $\pi/\sin(\pi/p)$. It has neither strong endpoint bound. The Laplace transform $L:L^p\to L^p$ is unbounded for $p\ne2$, $1\le p\le\infty$.

For every Euclidean dimension d>=0 and every ball B; standard convolution CZ means the L^2-bounded translation-invariant operators with standard off-zero kernel estimates specified at 18366–18376. John--Nirenberg integrability and the BMO endpoint [fa2:p4:john-nirenberg]. For every BMO function $g$ and $1\le q<\infty$, \[ \left(\frac1{|B|}\int_B|g-g_B|^q\right)^{1/q} \le C_dq\pfnorm g_{\rm BMO}. \] There are dimension constants $c,C>0$ such that \[ \frac1{|B|}\int_B \exp\left(\frac{c|g-g_B|}{\pfnorm g_{\rm BMO}}\right)\le C \] when the denominator is nonzero. Standard convolution CZ operators extend by transposition to $L^\infty\to\mathrm{BMO}/\mathbb C$; in particular the Hilbert transform has this endpoint interpretation.

An atomic Fourier improvement over $L^1$ [fa2:p4:hardy-fourier]. For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R^d)$, \[ \int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{|\widehat f(\xi)|}{|\xi|^d}d\xi \le C_d\pfnorm f_{H^1}. \]  This bound is for the actual completed atomic H^1(R^d), its L^1 Fourier transform, and every d>=0. The d=0 convention is |0|^0=1. AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA correction 3 restricts only the separate necessity assertion.

For d>=1, the cancellation condition integral a=0 in the definition of atoms is essential to the weighted Fourier inequality integral_{R^d}|hat f(xi)|/|xi|^d dxi<=C_d ||f||_{H^1}. The negative necessity assertion is not made in d=0 (AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA correction 3). The printed proof-internal universal nonzero-mean divergence calculation is not an extra independent target.

The same sequence works for all finite p; normalized Haar measure is used. A common lacunary Hilbert subspace in every finite $L^p$ [fa2:p4:lacunary-subspace]. There is a fixed increasing integer sequence $(n_j)$ such that, for every $1\le p<\infty$, the closed span of $e^{in_jt}$ in $L^p(\mathbb T)$ is isomorphic to $\ell^2$, with equivalent coefficient and $L^p$ norms. These infinite-dimensional closed spaces contain unbounded functions, in agreement with Theorem~\ref{fa2:p4:grothendieck-lp}.

Setwise convergence and Hahn--Vitali--Saks [fa2:p4:hahn-vitali-saks]. On a $\sigma$-finite measure space, let $f_n\in L^1$ and suppose $\int_Af_n$ converges to a finite scalar for every measurable set $A$. Then $(f_n)$ is bounded and uniformly integrable with finite-measure tail control, and converges weakly in $L^1$ to some $f\in L^1$. In particular $L^1$ is weakly sequentially complete. Weak convergence together with almost-everywhere convergence implies $L^1$ norm convergence.

De la Vall\'ee--Poussin's criterion [fa2:p4:de-la-vallee-poussin]. If $\mu(X)<\infty$, a family $F\subset L^1$ is bounded and uniformly integrable if and only if there is a continuous increasing convex $G:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $G(t)/t\to\infty$ and $\sup_{f\in F}\int G(|f|)<\infty$.

For real or complex measures, with no exclusion of the empty or zero-dimensional Euclidean case (AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA, correction 5): Norm-preserving weak-star approximation of measures [fa2:p4:measure-approximation]. On a compact metric space every finite scalar Radon measure is a sequential weak-star limit of finitely supported measures of exactly the same variation norm. Probabilities may be approximated by finitely supported probabilities. If $K=\overline\Omega$ for a bounded open Euclidean set, the approximants may instead be $u_n\,dx$, with $u_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $\pfnorm{u_n}_1=\pfnorm\mu$; for a positive measure they can be nonnegative. The same assertion holds for $C_0(\Omega)'$.

For every bounded open Euclidean Omega, including Omega empty and d=0, the scalar-linear density map L^1(Omega)->M(closure Omega)=C(closure Omega)', u |-> u dx (extended by zero), is an isometric embedding, ||u dx||=||u||_1, for real or complex scalars. The C_0(Omega) dual version is likewise isometric by measure variation. This retained bridge is explicitly required by AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA correction 5. The unrelated false unconditional point-mass norm-additivity calculation at 20041–20042 is proof-internal and is superseded by that correction, not a new target.

Sharp interval Poincar\'e--Wirtinger constants [fa2:p4:sharp-interval-poincare]. On $I=(0,1)$, writing $\bar u=\int_Iu$, one has \[ \pfnorm{u-\bar u}_\infty\le\pfnorm{u'}_1,\qquad \pfnorm u_\infty\le\tfrac12\pfnorm{u'}_1 \quad(u\in W^{1,1}_0), \] and $\pfnorm{u-\bar u}_1\le\tfrac12\pfnorm{u'}_1$. All constants are sharp. The first and third are not attained by nonconstant functions; the second is attained by any nonzero nonnegative unimodal absolutely continuous tent with zero endpoints. In $H^1$, $\pfnorm{u-\bar u}_2\le\pi^{-1}\pfnorm{u'}_2$, with equality precisely for a constant plus a multiple of $\cos\pi x$. In $H^1_0$, the sharp constant is also $1/\pi$, with optimizers the multiples of $\sin\pi x$. For $1<p\le\infty$ and $1\le q\le\infty$, the best constants in the corresponding mean-zero and zero-trace $\pfnorm u_q\le C\pfnorm{u'}_p$ inequalities are attained.

Throughout this chapter d>=1 and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t). Fix Phi in C^infinity(R^d) with c=integral Phi nonzero, and for every multi-index alpha, |partial^alpha Phi(x)|<=C_alpha(1+|x|)^(-d-1-|alpha|). Fixed radial maximal characterization [fa2:p4:hardy-fixed-maximal]. Suppose $\Phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, $c=\int\Phi\ne0$, and for every multi-index $\alpha$, \[ |\partial^\alpha\Phi(x)|\le C_\alpha (1+|x|)^{-d-1-|\alpha|}. \] For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ put $F_\Phi f(x)=\sup_{t>0}|\Phi_t*f(x)|$. Then $f\in H^1_{\rm at}$ if and only if $F_\Phi f\in L^1$, and \[ C^{-1}\|f\|_{H^1_{\rm at}}\le\|F_\Phi f\|_1 \le C\|f\|_{H^1_{\rm at}}, \] with constants depending on $\Phi,d$. In particular this holds for a Schwartz kernel of nonzero integral, for the Gaussian heat kernel, and for the Poisson kernel $C_d(1+|x|^2)^{-(d+1)/2}$ of integral one. If $\Phi$ is Schwartz, the hypothesis $f\in L^1$ can be replaced by $f\in\mathcal S'$ together with $F_\Phi f\in L^1$; that latter condition itself recovers an $L^1$ representative.

Proof-development-only passages: weighted convolution norm calculation 20150–20159, shifted averaging estimate 20210–20222, and annular test expansion/radial-transfer estimates 20296–20312 serve the chosen proof of the fixed-kernel theorem. Their particular estimates and witnesses are not extra mandatory deliverables. The separately stated named lemmas in this chapter and the maximal-function definitions needed to state them are independently inventoried mathematical obligations.

Throughout this chapter d>=1 and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t). Fix Phi in C^infinity(R^d) with c=integral Phi nonzero, and for every multi-index alpha, |partial^alpha Phi(x)|<=C_alpha(1+|x|)^(-d-1-|alpha|). An integrable inverse on a small frequency ball [fa2:p4:hardy-lowpass-inverse]. There is a Schwartz function $\eta$ with $\widehat\eta=1$ near zero and compactly supported smooth Fourier transform, and a kernel $\Psi$ with \[ \eta=\Psi*\Phi,\qquad |\Psi(x)|\le C(1+|x|)^{-d-1/2}. \] The Fourier cutoff can be chosen with $\operatorname{supp}\widehat\eta\subset B(0,2/R)$ and $\widehat\eta=1$ on $B(0,1/R)$ for some fixed $R$.

In dimension d>=1, set epsilon=1/2, A=d+1, r=1-[4(d+1)]^(-1), so Ar>d and A(1-r)=1/4<epsilon, and choose an integer N>2A+d+4. Let B_N be the smooth functions supported in the unit ball with ||partial^alpha psi||_infinity<=1 for |alpha|<=N. For f in L^1 and eta the fixed Schwartz low-pass kernel supplied by the inverse lemma, define G_N f(x)=sup_{t>0,psi in B_N}|psi_t*f(x)| and P(x)=sup_{j in Z,y in R^d}|eta_{2^(-j)}*f(y)|/(1+2^j|x-y|)^A. Both functions are measurable (lower semicontinuous); P has the same supremum if y is restricted to a countable dense subset.

Use eta, P, A and N defined at 20226–20240, with eta supplied by the low-frequency inverse lemma. Throughout this chapter d>=1 and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t). Fix Phi in C^infinity(R^d) with c=integral Phi nonzero, and for every multi-index alpha, |partial^alpha Phi(x)|<=C_alpha(1+|x|)^(-d-1-|alpha|). The compact-test transfer estimate [fa2:p4:hardy-compact-transfer]. For $f\in L^1$ and $P(x)<\infty$, \[ |\psi_t*f(z)|\le C P(x)(1+|x-z|/t)^A \quad(\psi\in\mathcal B_N,t>0). \] The same bound holds for any fixed uniformly bounded family of compactly supported smooth tests with bounded $C^N$ norm and one common support radius. In particular $\mathcal G_Nf\le CP$.

Let f in L^1(R^d); use eta, P, G_N, r, A and N as defined at 20226–20240, and let M be the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator. Throughout this chapter d>=1 and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t). Fix Phi in C^infinity(R^d) with c=integral Phi nonzero, and for every multi-index alpha, |partial^alpha Phi(x)|<=C_alpha(1+|x|)^(-d-1-|alpha|). The nonlinear maximal estimate [fa2:p4:hardy-peetre]. If $F=F_\Phi f\in L^1$, then \[ P(x)\le C\{M(F^r)(x)\}^{1/r}\quad\hbox{a.e.},\qquad \|\mathcal G_Nf\|_1\le C\|F\|_1. \]

Throughout this chapter d>=1 and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t). Smooth Whitney partitions, including nested levels [fa2:p4:hardy-whitney]. If $\Omega$ is a nonempty open set of finite measure, there are dyadic cubes $Q_i$ with disjoint interiors covering $\Omega$, and smooth $\eta_i\ge0$, such that $\sum_i\eta_i=1$ on $\Omega$, each $\eta_i$ is supported in $Q_i^*=(9/8)Q_i\Subset\Omega$, $\int\eta_i\ge c|Q_i|$, and $|\partial^\alpha\eta_i|\le C_\alpha\ell_i^{-|\alpha|}$. The enlarged cubes have bounded overlap and neighboring sides are comparable. If $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ has its analogous cubes $Q_j'$, then intersection of $Q_j'^*$ and $Q_i^*$ implies $\ell_j'\le C\ell_i$ and $Q_j'^*\subset C Q_i$. Each fixed $Q_j'^*$ meets at most a fixed number of the $Q_i^*$.

Use N and G_N as defined at 20226–20240. Throughout this chapter d>=1 and Phi_t(x)=t^(-d)Phi(x/t). Grand maximal function gives atoms [fa2:p4:hardy-grand-atomic]. If $f\in L^1$ and $G=\mathcal G_N f\in L^1$, then $f\in H^1_{\rm at}$ and $\|f\|_{H^1_{\rm at}}\le C\|G\|_1$.

A primitive of every distribution on the line [fa2:p4:distribution-primitive]. Every $u\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$ has a primitive $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$, and any two primitives differ by a constant distribution. The same assertion holds on an open interval.

Positive distributions are locally finite measures [fa2:p4:positive-distribution-measure]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. A scalar-linear distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ is nonnegative on nonnegative real tests if and only if it is integration against a unique positive locally finite Radon measure on $\Omega$. No finite total-mass assertion is implicit.

Convexity and the distribution Hessian [fa2:p4:convex-distribution-hessian]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. It is convex if and only if for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$ the distribution $\partial_a^2f=\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\partial_i\partial_j f$ is positive. In one dimension this says exactly that $f''$ is a positive locally finite measure. The matrix of distribution second derivatives thus has the precise positive-semidefinite meaning given by all of these scalar tests.

Periodic distributions and polynomial Fourier growth [fa2:p4:periodic-distributions]. Write $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ with normalized Haar measure. Distributions on $\mathbb R^d$ invariant under every integer translation are canonically the continuous linear functionals on $C^\infty(\mathbb T^d)$. Their Fourier coefficients \[ c_n=U(e^{-2\pi i n\cdot x}),\qquad n\in\mathbb Z^d, \] have polynomial growth. Conversely every sequence with $|c_n|\le C(1+|n|)^N$ defines exactly one such distribution, by \[ U(\phi)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}c_n\widehat\phi(-n). \] The series converges absolutely on every smooth test, and its finite Fourier sums converge in the distribution sense.

For the completed atomic H^1(R^d), A>=0; the integral-zero hypothesis includes ordinary integrability of g (also follows from the L^2 and tail bounds). An elementary summable molecule decomposition [fa2:p4:hardy-decaying-molecule]. Suppose $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ has integral zero, $\|g\|_2\le A$, and $|g(x)|\le A|x|^{-d-1}$ for $|x|\ge2$. Then $g\in H^1_{\rm at}$ and $\|g\|_{H^1}\le C_d A$. The translated and dilated version has the same bound with the correspondingly normalized $L^2$ size and tail.

For the actual completed atomic H^1 and the compatible standard convolution CZ operator specified earlier; retain all Euclidean dimensions d>=0. Convolution singular integrals preserve $H^1$ [fa2:p4:cz-hardy-invariance]. Every standard convolution Calder\'on--Zygmund operator of Part IV is bounded $H^1_{\rm at}(\mathbb R^d)\to H^1_{\rm at}(\mathbb R^d)$. In particular this is stronger than the previously proved $H^1\to L^1$ endpoint estimate.

The annular cancellation criterion [fa2:p4:cz-annular-criterion]. Let $k\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\})$ satisfy $|\partial^\alpha k(x)|\le C_\alpha|x|^{-d-|\alpha|}$. There exists a Calder\'on--Zygmund distribution $K$ agreeing with $k$ off zero if and only if \[ \sup_{0<r<R<\infty} \left|\int_{r<|x|<R}k(x)\,dx\right|<\infty. \] Here the integrals are ordinary integrals on finite annuli. Such an extension is unique modulo a scalar multiple of $\delta_0$.

Fourier divergence on a residual set of points [fa2:p4:generic-fourier-divergence]. There is a residual subset of $C(\mathbb T)$ such that, for each of its functions $f$, the set \[ \{x\in\mathbb T:\sup_N|S_Nf(x)|=\infty\} \] is residual in $\mathbb T$. Here $S_N$ denotes the symmetric Fourier partial sum, and residual means the complement of a set of first category.

For a measurable space (X,Sigma) and Banach space Y, a vector measure m:Sigma->Y is countably additive in norm. Its variation is |m|(A)=sup{sum_{j=1}^r ||m(A_j)|| : A is the disjoint union of the finite measurable partition (A_j)}.

For a norm-countably-additive Banach-valued vector measure m, if |m|(X)<infinity then its variation |m| is a finite positive countably additive measure. For every positive measure mu, m absolutely continuous with respect to mu implies |m| absolutely continuous with respect to mu.

A compact range before any density is assumed [fa2:p4:reflexive-measure-range]. A finite-variation vector measure taking values in a reflexive Banach space has relatively norm compact range.  Consequently the closed linear span of its range is a separable reflexive Banach space.

Radon--Nikodym for reflexive range, including nonseparable range [fa2:p4:vector-radon-nikodym]. Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite positive measure space and $Y$ a reflexive Banach space.  If $m:\Sigma\to Y$ is norm countably additive, has finite variation, and $m\ll\mu$, then there is a unique Bochner integrable $g:X\to Y$, up to null sets, such that \[ m(A)=\int_Ag\,d\mu\quad(A\in\Sigma),\qquad |m|(A)=\int_A\|g\|\,d\mu. \] In particular no separability assumption on $Y$ is needed.

Take the real or complex Banach range L^1[0,1]. The range condition cannot be discarded [fa2:p4:vector-rn-failure]. On $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure let $m(A)=1_A$ with values in $Y=L^1[0,1]$.  This is norm countably additive and $|m|(A)=\mu(A)$.  It has no Bochner density.  Indeed a measure with Bochner density has relatively norm compact range: approximate that density in $L^1$ by finite-valued simple functions; the ranges of their integrals over arbitrary sets lie in compact finite dimensional boxes and approximate the range uniformly.  But the indicators of independent dyadic half-sets have pairwise $L^1$ distance $1/2$.  Thus the range here is not relatively norm compact.  Reflexivity is a sufficient range hypothesis in the theorem, not a property of all Banach spaces.

Full Bochner $L^p$ duality for reflexive $E$ [fa2:p4:vector-lp-dual]. Let $\mu$ be sigma-finite and $E$ a reflexive real or complex Banach space, without a separability assumption.  If $1\le p<\infty$ and $1/p+1/q=1$, with $q=\infty$ for $p=1$, then \[ L^q(\mu;E')\longrightarrow L^p(\mu;E)',\qquad g\longmapsto\left[f\longmapsto\int_Xg(t)(f(t))\,d\mu(t)\right] \] is a surjective linear isometry.  Both vector-valued spaces consist of strongly measurable functions, modulo almost-everywhere equality.  The pairing is bilinear, with no Hilbert conjugation.

For the same real or complex Bochner spaces; the converse is for 1<p<infinity as in the forward assertion. Bochner reflexivity without a separability restriction [fa2:p4:vector-lp-reflexive]. If $1<p<\infty$, $\mu$ is sigma-finite, and $E$ is reflexive, then $L^p(\mu;E)$ is reflexive.  Conversely, if $\mu$ has a set of positive finite measure and $L^p(\mu;E)$ is reflexive, then $E$ is reflexive.  No analogous unconditional reflexivity assertion holds for $p=1$ or $p=\infty$.

For every a>0, p(s)=cosh(as) is continuous, real and even, is nonnegative on all real even continuous compactly supported tests in the quadratic form double integral p(s-t)f(s)f(t) ds dt, and is unbounded. Thus even-test positivity is strictly weaker than ordinary positive definiteness, which tests all functions.

For every lambda in R and t in R define C_lambda(t)=cos(sqrt(-lambda)t) if lambda<0, 1 if lambda=0, and cosh(sqrt(lambda)t) if lambda>0; define S_lambda(t)=sin(sqrt(-lambda)t)/sqrt(-lambda) if lambda<0, t if lambda=0, and sinh(sqrt(lambda)t)/sqrt(lambda) if lambda>0. These are the real even and odd scalar solution families used by the Krein representations.

For every real lambda, C_lambda and S_lambda solve w''=lambda w with initial data (w(0),w'(0))=(1,0) and (0,1), respectively. For all real s,t, C_lambda(s-t)+C_lambda(s+t)=2 C_lambda(s) C_lambda(t) and C_lambda(s-t)-C_lambda(s+t)=-2 lambda S_lambda(s) S_lambda(t), including lambda=0.

For C_lambda and S_lambda defined at 21197–21215, and positive definite meaning Hermitian symmetric with nonnegative finite scalar quadratic forms: A continuous kernel satisfying the wave identity [fa2:p4:krein-kernel]. Let $F$ be continuous, real and even on $\mathbb R$. If $K_+(s,t)=(F(s-t)+F(s+t))/2$ is positive definite, there is a positive finite Borel measure $
u$ on $\mathbb R$ with \[ F(s)=\int C_\lambda(s)\,d
u(\lambda),\qquad 
u(\mathbb R)=F(0),\qquad \int_{\lambda>0}\cosh(R\sqrt\lambda)\,d
u<\infty\quad(R>0). \] If instead $K_-(s,t)=(F(s-t)-F(s+t))/2$ is positive definite, there is a positive locally finite measure $
u$ for which \[ F(s)=F(0)+\int rac{1-C_\lambda(s)}{\lambda}\,d
u(\lambda), \] where the integrand at $\lambda=0$ is $-s^2/2$. Its integrals are absolutely convergent, uniformly dominated on compact $s$-intervals.

Krein's even-test representation and extreme functions [fa2:p4:krein-even]. A continuous real even $p$ satisfies \[ \iint p(s-t)f(s)f(t)\,dsdt\ge0 \quad\text{for every real even continuous compactly supported }f \] if and only if it has a positive measure representation $p(s)=\int C_\lambda(s)d\nu(\lambda)$ with the finite mass and exponential integrability stated in the preceding lemma. Equivalently it is a positive cosine mixture plus a positive cosh mixture; the zero atom may be assigned only to the cosine part to avoid duplicating the constant function. The normalized convex set $p(0)=1$ has extreme points exactly $\cos(as)$, $a\ge0$, and $\cosh(bs)$, $b>0$ (the constant is already the case $a=0$). Explicitly the representing positive finite Borel measure has nu(R)=p(0), and integral_{lambda>0} cosh(R sqrt(lambda)) dnu<infinity for every R>0. General representation uniqueness is not asserted.

The measure need not be unique [fa2:p4:krein-nonunique]. General continuous even-test-positive functions can have different positive cosine--cosh representations, even after removing the duplicate zero atom.

The correct compensated odd-test form [fa2:p4:krein-odd]. A continuous real even $q$ is nonnegative on all odd real compactly supported tests in the analogous quadratic integral if and only if it has the compensated representation of the kernel lemma, for a positive locally finite measure with compact-interval domination. Its constant $q(0)$ is unrestricted. In particular $q(s)=-s^2$ has this positivity, although it has no representation as a finite positive cosine mixture minus a finite positive cosh mixture. Explicitly the quadratic integral is double integral q(s-t)f(s)f(t) ds dt>=0 for every real odd continuous compactly supported f, and the representation is q(s)=q(0)+integral (1-C_lambda(s))/lambda dnu(lambda), integrand -s^2/2 at lambda=0. All integrals converge absolutely and admit one integrable majorant on every compact s-interval; no finite total-mass assumption on nu is imposed.

All spaces and functions in these convex assertions are real. In the first equivalence f is any member of X', M^perp is its annihilator, and the closure is in norm. In the L^p specialization f belongs to L^{p'} and the measure may be any positive measure. Support inequalities and constrained extensions [fa2:p4:constrained-support]. Let $X$ be reflexive, $M\subset X$ a closed subspace, and $C\subset X'$ nonempty and convex. Then \[ f(u)\leq\sup_{g\in C}g(u)\ (u\in M) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\in\overline{M^\perp+C}. \] If $C$ is also closed and bounded the sum is already closed. In particular, for $1<p<\infty$, $j,k\in L^{p'}$, $k\geq0$, and $M=\{u\in L^p:\int ju=0\}$, the inequality $\int fu\leq\int k|u|$ on $M$ is equivalent to $f=\lambda j+g$ for some real $\lambda$ and $|g|\leq k$ a.e. For a sigma-finite measure space, $M$ any linear subspace of $L^1$ and $a,b\in L^\infty$ with $a\leq b$, there is $h\in M^\perp\cap L^\infty$ with $a\leq h\leq b$ iff \[ \int(a u^+-b u^-)\leq0\quad(u\in M). \] On measures without a scalar $L^1$ dual representation the Hahn--Banach conclusion is instead a dominated continuous dual functional; a global $L^\infty$ representative is not presumed.

All functions are real valued, and p'=p/(p-1). Weak convergence with convergence of convex energy [fa2:p4:nemytskii-energy]. Let $\mu(\Omega)<\infty$, $1<p<\infty$, and let $g:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ be continuous nondecreasing with $|g(t)|\leq C(1+|t|^{p-1})$. Put $G(t)=\int_0^t g(s)ds$. If $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ in $L^p$ and $\limsup\int G(u_n)\leq\int G(u)$, then $g(u_n)\to g(u)$ in every $L^q$, $1\leq q<p'$. If $g$ is strictly increasing, $u_n\to u$ in every $L^q$, $1\leq q<p$. If also $|g(t)|\geq\alpha|t|^{p-1}-C$ for some $\alpha>0$, the respective conclusions hold in $L^{p'}$ and, in the strict case, in $L^p$. These endpoint conclusions can fail without that lower growth assumption, even for strictly increasing $g$.

The feasible functions are u in E, with u>=0 almost everywhere and integral u<=1. A minimizer in a nonreflexive intersection space [fa2:p4:singular-weight-minimizer]. The Banach space $E=L^1(\mathbb R)\cap L^2(\mathbb R)$ with sum norm is not reflexive. For $0<\alpha<1/2$, however, \[ \inf_{u\geq0,\ \int u\leq1} \left(\|u\|_2^2-\int |x|^{-\alpha}u(x)dx\right) \] has a unique minimizer in $E$.

For real or complex measurable functions modulo almost-everywhere equality on an arbitrary finite positive measure space; zero-norm and zero-measure cases are included, with suprema over empty collections interpreted as zero. Distribution functions and a Banach norm for weak $L^p$ [fa2:p4:marcinkiewicz-space]. On a finite measure space write $\alpha_f(t)=\mu\{|f|>t\}$. It is nonincreasing and right continuous. If $f_n\to f$ a.e., then for $t>0$ \[ \alpha_f(t)\leq\liminf\alpha_{f_n}(t) \leq\limsup\alpha_{f_n}(t)\leq\alpha_f(t-). \] For $1<p<\infty$ put \[ Q_p(f)=\sup_{t>0}t\alpha_f(t)^{1/p},\qquad N_p(f)=\sup_{\mu(A)>0}\mu(A)^{-1/p'}\int_A|f|. \] Then $Q_p\leq N_p\leq p'Q_p$, and the a.e. quotient of functions with finite $N_p$ is Banach in that norm. One has $N_p(f)\leq\|f\|_p$, $N_q(f)\leq\mu(\Omega)^{1/q-1/p}N_p(f)$ for $1<q\leq p$, and \[ \|f\|_q\leq (p/(p-q))^{1/q} \mu(\Omega)^{1/q-1/p}Q_p(f)\quad(1\leq q<p). \] If $1<q<p<r<\infty$ and $1/p=\theta/q+(1-\theta)/r$, then $\|f\|_p\leq C_{p,q,r}N_q(f)^\theta N_r(f)^{1-\theta}$. For d>=1 only, the inclusion of $L^p$ is strict on the Euclidean unit ball: $|x|^{-d/p}$ belongs to weak $L^p$ there but not to $L^p$. This local dimensional qualification follows AUTHORIZED_SOURCE_ERRATA correction 4 and does not restrict any general finite-measure statement above.

Scope conventions: the C(K), L2 and measure realizations of a kernel require their own bridges; Banach transposes are scalar-linear, and Hilbert adjoints use the conjugate-first inner product. The mathematical bridge conclusions are inventoried separately.

Arzel\`a--Ascoli on a compact Hausdorff space: A uniformly bounded equicontinuous subset of $C(X)$, $X$ compact
Hausdorff, is relatively compact in the uniform norm. Conversely,
a relatively compact family has these properties.

Continuous kernels and their transpose: Let $X,Y$ be compact Hausdorff, $\nu$ a finite positive Radon
measure on $Y$, and $k\in C(X\times Y)$.
Then $Ku(x)=\int_Yk(x,y)u(y)\,d\nu(y)$ is a bounded compact map
$C(Y)\to C(X)$, with
$\pvnorm K\le\nu(Y)\pvnorm k_\infty$.
Under the linear Riesz--Markov identification,
$K'\eta=h\nu$, where $h(y)=\int_Xk(x,y)\,d\eta(x)$.
No conjugation occurs in this formula.

$L^2$ kernels and the continuous-to-$L^2$ bridge: On $\sigma$-finite measure spaces $(X,\mu),(Y,\nu)$, a kernel
$k\in L^2(\mu\otimes\nu)$ defines a.e. a bounded compact map
$K:L^2(\nu)\to L^2(\mu)$, with
$\pvnorm K\le\pvnorm k_2$ and
\[
 K^*v(y)=\int_X\overline{k(x,y)}v(x)\,d\mu(x).
\]
It is Hilbert--Schmidt with squared Hilbert--Schmidt norm
$\int|k|^2$. For compact $X,Y$ with finite Radon measures and
continuous $k$, the two definitions agree on continuous functions;
their $L^2$ extensions agree by density. A Hermitian kernel on
one space gives a compact self-adjoint map.

Schur's weighted kernel test: On $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, suppose a product-measurable kernel
and positive measurable weights $a(x),b(y)$
satisfy
\[
 \int|k(x,y)|b(y)\,d\nu(y)\le A a(x),\qquad
 \int|k(x,y)|a(x)\,d\mu(x)\le B b(y).
\]
Then $K:L^2(\nu)\to L^2(\mu)$ is bounded with
$\pvnorm K\le\sqrt{AB}$, whenever the weights are positive and
finite a.e. The unweighted row and column bounds also give
$\pvnorm K_{L^p\to L^p}\le A^{1-1/p}B^{1/p}$ for
$1\le p\le\infty$.

Weakly singular kernels: Let $G\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact and let $k$ be continuous off
the diagonal with $|k(x,y)|\le C|x-y|^{\alpha-d}$ for some
$\alpha>0$ (a bounded kernel can be added). Its integral map is
compact on $C(G)$ and on every $L^p(G)$, $1\le p\le\infty$.
The same assertion holds on a compact $n$-dimensional $C^1$
surface with surface measure and singularity $|x-y|^{\alpha-n}$.

Here a_j∈X and ℓ_j∈X′, and c_i=ℓ_i(u). Exact finite-rank reduction: For $Ku=\sum_{j=1}^ma_j\ell_j(u)$ on a Banach space,
$u-\lambda Ku=f$ is equivalent to
\[
 c_i-\lambda\sum_j\ell_i(a_j)c_j=\ell_i(f),\qquad
 u=f+\lambda\sum_ja_jc_j.
\]
No independence of the $a_j$ or $\ell_j$ is required.

Fredholm kernel equations: For any of the compact kernel maps above acting on the same Banach
space, $u-\lambda Ku=f$, $\lambda\ne0$, is uniquely solvable for
all data if and only if $\lambda^{-1}$ is not an eigenvalue of $K$.
Otherwise it is solvable exactly when every member of
$\ker(I-\lambda K)'$ annihilates $f$; the solution set is a
translate of the finite-dimensional homogeneous kernel.
In Hilbert space the condition is
$f\perp\ker(I-\overline\lambda K^*)$.

Picard criterion and instability: Let $K:H\to G$ be compact with positive singular system
$(\sigma_j,e_j,f_j)$. Then $Ku=g$ is solvable exactly when
\[
 g\perp\ker K^*,\qquad
 \sum_j\frac{|\langle f_j,g\rangle|^2}{\sigma_j^2}<\infty.
\]
The series $u^\dagger=\sum_j\sigma_j^{-1}\langle f_j,g\rangle e_j$
is the unique minimum-norm solution, and all solutions are
$u^\dagger+\ker K$. An infinite-rank compact operator cannot
have a bounded inverse on its range when that range carries the
ambient norm.

Factorial bounds and full-interval resolvent: Let $I=[0,T]$, $E$ Banach, and $k(t,s)\in\mathcal L(E)$ be
operator-norm continuous on $0\le s\le t\le T$, with bound $M$.
For $Vu(t)=\int_0^tk(t,s)u(s)\,ds$,
\[
 \pvnorm{V^n}\le M^nT^n/n!,\qquad
 (I-\lambda V)^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\lambda^nV^n,
 \qquad \pvnorm{(I-\lambda V)^{-1}}\le e^{|\lambda|MT}.
\]
For every parameter and continuous datum the equation has a unique
solution on the entire finite interval. In a nonzero complex
state space its spectrum is $\{0\}$ when $T>0$; the zero interval
is treated as the zero integral operator. Iterated kernels give a
continuous resolvent kernel. Picard iterates from any initial
continuous function converge uniformly to the solution.

Gronwall and a comparison principle: If $a,M\ge0$ and a nonnegative continuous $z$ satisfies
$z(t)\le a+M\int_0^tz(s)ds$, then $z(t)\le ae^{Mt}$.
For nonnegative continuous Volterra kernels and $\lambda\ge0$,
successive iteration preserves order and gives the corresponding
resolvent comparison for $I-\lambda V$.

Smoothness, first-kind equations, and ODEs: For a scalar kernel $k\in C^m$ on a neighborhood of the triangle
and $f\in C^m(I)$, the second-kind solution is $C^m$.
In the $C^1$ case,
$u'=f'+\lambda k(t,t)u+\lambda\int_0^t\partial_tk(t,s)u(s)ds$.
If $T>0$, $k\in C^1$ and $k(t,t)\ne0$ everywhere, the first-kind
equation $\int_0^tk(t,s)u(s)ds=g(t)$ has a continuous solution
exactly when $g(0)=0$, for $g\in C^1$; that solution is unique.
If $T=0$, it has a solution exactly when $g(0)=0$, and then every
scalar-valued function on $\{0\}$ is a solution, so uniqueness fails.
For operator-norm continuous $A:I\to\mathcal L(E)$ and continuous
$b:I\to E$, the equation
$u(t)=u_0+\int_0^t(A(s)u(s)+b(s))ds$ is equivalent to
$u'=Au+b$, $u(0)=u_0$, and is uniquely solvable on $I$.

Fractional integrals: For $\alpha>0$ put
$J_\alpha f(t)=\Gamma(\alpha)^{-1}\int_0^t(t-s)^{\alpha-1}f(s)ds$.
This normalization is explicit. Brunner's power-kernel operator
has no Gamma factor, and his parameter $\alpha=0$ denotes a
separate logarithmic kernel, not the nonintegrable power $r^{-1}$.

Let I=[0,T] with 0≤T<∞ and α,β>0; these operators act on C(I) or the indicated Lᵖ(0,T). Beta convolution and weakly singular Volterra: $J_\alpha J_\beta=J_{\alpha+\beta}$ on continuous functions and
on $L^p(0,T)$, $1\le p\le\infty$.
If $|k(t,s)|\le M$ and $k$ is continuous on the triangle, then
$V_\alpha f=\int_0^t(t-s)^{\alpha-1}k(t,s)f(s)ds$ is compact
on $C(I)$ and on each $L^p(0,T)$, and
\[
 \pvnorm{V_\alpha^n}\le
 \frac{M^n\Gamma(\alpha)^nT^{n\alpha}}{\Gamma(n\alpha+1)}.
\]
It is quasinilpotent and $I-\lambda V_\alpha$ is invertible for
every $\lambda$. The resolvent kernel has the same leading weak
singularity. These conclusions also hold for
$\int_0^t\log(t-s)k(t,s)f(s)ds$.
For constant $k=1$ and constant datum the normalized equation
$u=1+\lambda J_\alpha u$ has solution
$E_\alpha(\lambda t^\alpha)=\sum_{n\ge0}\lambda^nt^{n\alpha}/\Gamma(n\alpha+1)$. The same-leading-singularity conclusion means a resolvent kernel with continuous amplitude times (t−s)^{α−1}; for the logarithmic kernel its leading term is λk(t,s)log(t−s), with a remainder O((t−s)^{1−2ε}) for any fixed 0<ε<1/2 near the diagonal.

Abel inversion and the weakly singular first kind: Let $T>0$. For $0<\alpha<1$, $J_\alpha u=g$ on $(0,T]$ (equivalently a.e.)
with $g\in C^1[0,T]$ has a unique $L^1$ solution,
\[
 u(t)=\frac{g(0)t^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}+J_{1-\alpha}g'(t).
\]
It is continuous at zero exactly when $g(0)=0$; in that case its
value there is zero and the equation holds also at zero. If
$g(0)\ne0$, the integral convention at zero gives zero and is
not claimed to equal the nonzero datum there.
For a $C^1$ amplitude $k$ with nonvanishing
diagonal, the equation
$\int_0^t(t-s)^{\alpha-1}k(t,s)u(s)ds=g(t)$ with
$g\in C^1$, $g(0)=0$, has a unique continuous solution.
For $T=0$, the equation on $(0,T]$ is vacuous and $L^1[0,T]$
has only its zero equivalence class. For continuous functions,
either first-kind equation imposed also at zero is solvable
exactly when $g(0)=0$; every singleton value is then a solution.
The positive-length continuity and endpoint-reconstruction
claims are not asserted for that degenerate interval.

A valid H\"older gain and the source counterexample: Let $0<\alpha,\beta<1$ and $\gamma=\alpha+\beta<1$.
If $f\in C^\beta[0,T]$ and $f(0)=0$, then
$J_\alpha f\in C^\gamma[0,T]$.
The same conclusion holds for an amplitude $k\in C^1$ on a
neighborhood of the closed triangle. Mere continuity of $k$ is
insufficient.

Weak singularity does not preserve smoothness: For smooth constant data, $u=1+\lambda J_\alpha u$ has
$u(t)=1+\lambda t^\alpha/\Gamma(1+\alpha)+O(t^{2\alpha})$.
For $T>0$, $0<\alpha<1$ and $\lambda\ne0$ it is not $C^1$ at zero.
For $T=0$ the solution is the singleton value $u(0)=1$, which
has a smooth constant extension.
Its derivatives of order $j$ on $(0,T]$ satisfy the weighted bound
$|u^{(j)}(t)|\le C_jt^{\alpha-j}$ near zero, after subtracting the
constant term, by termwise differentiation of the convergent
Mittag--Leffler series. Thus smooth-data regularity for bounded
kernels cannot be transferred to singular kernels.

Local nonlinear existence and a continuation criterion: For Banach $E$, suppose $f$ is continuous and $G(t,s,z)$ is
continuous on a triangular time cylinder and a closed ball about
$f(0)$, bounded there by $B$ and uniformly Lipschitz in $z$ with
constant $L$. On an interval $[0,h]$ on which
$\pvnorm{f-f(0)}_\infty+Bh\le R$, the equation
$u(t)=f(t)+\int_0^tG(t,s,u(s))ds$ has a unique solution in that
ball. Picard iterates converge uniformly. For weakly singular
factor $(t-s)^{\alpha-1}$ replace $Bh$ by $Bh^\alpha/\alpha$;
the same conclusions hold.
If these hypotheses hold on every bounded $z$-ball, with uniform
time continuity there, a maximal solution that stops before a
finite available endpoint has unbounded norm. In finite-dimensional
$E$ the required uniform time continuity follows from continuity
on compact cylinders.

Existence without uniqueness, blow-up, and a third kind: The equation $u(t)=\int_0^t2\sqrt{|u(s)|}\,ds$ has the solutions
$u_c(t)=0$ for $t\le c$ and $u_c(t)=(t-c)^2$ for $t\ge c$,
for any $c\ge0$. Direct substitution proves this and displays the
failure of Lipschitz uniqueness. The equation
$u(t)=1+\int_0^tu(s)^2ds$ has $u(t)=(1-t)^{-1}$ on $t<1$;
the ODE equivalence and uniqueness show that no bounded continuation
through one exists. For the third-kind equation
$t u(t)=\int_0^tu(s)ds$, every constant is a continuous solution.
For $tu(t)=t+\int_0^tu(s)ds$ on $[0,T]$ with $T>0$, no
continuous solution exists: divide by $t$ and let $t\downarrow0$,
obtaining $u(0)=1+u(0)$. On $[0,0]$ every scalar singleton
function is a continuous solution of this equation.
The vanishing leading coefficient is therefore a substantive change,
not a second-kind equation with a harmless parameter value.

One complete delay model: Let $\tau>0$, prescribe continuous history $\eta$ on $[-\tau,0]$,
and let $A,B$ be continuous scalar or bounded-operator coefficients.
Then
\[
 u(t)=\eta(0)+\int_0^t[A(s)u(s)+B(s)u(s-\tau)]ds,
 \qquad u=\eta\text{ on }[-\tau,0],
\]
has a unique continuous solution on every finite time interval and
is $C^1$ for positive times. At zero its derivative agrees with a
differentiable history exactly when the initial compatibility
condition holds; higher derivatives can acquire step-junction
discontinuities if the corresponding history compatibilities fail. For differentiable history, the initial compatibility is η′(0−)=A(0)η(0)+B(0)η(−τ).

Continuous nonlinear existence and extremal solutions: Let $G$ be continuous on the scalar compact triangular cylinder
$0\le s\le t\le T$, $|z|\le R$, and $f\in C[0,T]$.
If $\norm f_\infty+T\sup|G|\le R$, the nonlinear
Volterra map has a fixed point in that ball even without a
Lipschitz assumption. The same conclusion holds with factor
$(t-s)^{\alpha-1}$, $\alpha>0$, replacing $T$ by $T^\alpha/\alpha$.
For real data, suppose instead that $G(t,s,z)$ is nondecreasing
in $z$ and continuous between a continuous subsolution $\ell$
and supersolution $v$, with $\ell\le v$. Then there are least
and greatest solutions in this order interval; successive iteration
from $\ell$ and $v$ converges uniformly to them. Subsolution and supersolution mean ℓ≤𝒱ℓ and 𝒱v≤v for the displayed nonlinear Volterra map 𝒱.

Fractional comparison and weighted endpoint derivatives: If $a,b\ge0$ and $z\ge0$ is continuous with
$z\le a+bJ_\alpha z$, then
$z(t)\le aE_\alpha(bt^\alpha)$.
Let $0<\alpha<1$, $k\in C^m$ near the closed triangle and
$f\in C^m[0,T]$. The solution of
$u=f+\lambda\int_0^t(t-s)^{\alpha-1}k(t,s)u(s)ds$
is $C^m$ for positive time and satisfies, for $1\le j\le m$,
\[
 |(u-f)^{(j)}(t)|\le C_jt^{\alpha-j}\quad(0<t\le T).
\]
For $m\ge1$ its precise first endpoint term is
\[
 u(t)=f(t)+\frac{\lambda k(0,0)f(0)}{\alpha}t^\alpha
                                      +O(t^{2\alpha}).
\]
For $T>0$, a nonzero displayed coefficient obstructs $C^1$
regularity. For $T=0$ the solution is the singleton value
$u(0)=f(0)$ and has a smooth constant extension, irrespective
of that coefficient. If $f(0)=0$ and $m\ge1$, the solution is $C^1$
through zero and $u'(0)=f'(0)$.

Galerkin existence through weak compactness: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, with conjugate-first inner product,
and let $a$ be a bounded form, conjugate-linear first and linear
second, satisfying $\operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge c\pfnorm v^2$,
$c>0$. For every continuous conjugate-linear $F$ there is a
unique $u$ with $a(v,u)=F(v)$ for all $v\in H$.
It is the weak limit of the finite-dimensional Galerkin solutions;
along nested subspaces with dense union the convergence is strong.
The finite-dimensional spaces may be directed by inclusion, so
the existence argument requires no separability assumption.

Sobolev energy spaces and compact lower-order terms: On a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$,
or on $\Omega=\varnothing$ in any dimension, put
$H=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$ with gradient norm, and let $H^\#$ denote the Banach space of continuous
conjugate-linear functionals, with pointwise scalar operations.
A bounded coercive form on $H$ solves every $H^\#$ datum uniquely.
In particular
$a(v,u)=\int\overline{\nabla v}\cdot A\nabla u$ is such a
form when $A$ is a bounded measurable matrix with
$\operatorname{Re}(\overline\xi\cdot A(x)\xi)\ge c|\xi|^2$
almost everywhere. A bounded zeroth-order form
$b(v,u)=\int q\overline vu$, $q\in L^\infty$, is compact
as a map $H\to H^\#$; adding it gives the precise Fredholm
compatibility alternative against the adjoint nullspace. The Fredholm alternative asserts closed range, finite kernel and cokernel of equal dimension, and solvability precisely when the data annihilate the adjoint kernel.

Opial--Baillon nonlinear iteration and averages: Let $T:H\to H$ be nonexpansive on a Hilbert space and have a
fixed point. Put $u_n=T^nf$, $S=(I+T)/2$,
$\mu_n=S^nf$, and $\sigma_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}u_j$.
Both $\mu_n$ and $\sigma_n$ converge weakly to fixed points.
If $T$ is odd, both convergences are strong.

Hardy averaging: the spectrum depends on the space: Let $Qf(x)=x^{-1}\int_0^xf(t)dt$ for $0<x\le1$.
On $C[0,1]$ put $Qf(0)=f(0)$. On the complex spaces,
\[
 \sigma_{C}(Q)=\{\lambda:|\lambda-1/2|\le1/2\},\qquad
 \sigma_{L^p}(Q)=\{\lambda:|\lambda-p'/2|\le p'/2\}
 \quad(1<p<\infty).
\]
The respective eigenvalue sets are the open disks together
with $1$ in the continuous case, and the open disk alone in
the $L^p$ case. The norm is $1$ on $C$ and $p'$ on $L^p$.
On $C^1[0,1]$ the spectrum is
$\{1\}\cup\{\lambda:|\lambda-1/4|\le1/4\}$;
its eigenvalues are $1$, $1/2$, and the latter open disk.
None of these operators is compact. But
$Q:L^p\to L^q$ is compact when $1\le q<p<\infty$,
and $Q:C\to L^q$ is compact for every finite $q$.
The source's real spectral intervals are precisely the real
sections of these complex disks, rather than complex spectra.

An interior point that separates an open convex set: If $D$ is a nonempty open convex subset of a real Hilbert space
and $x_0\notin D$, some $w_0\in D$ satisfies
$\langle w_0-x_0,w-x_0\rangle>0$ for every $w\in D$.

Small perturbations of one-sided regularizers: Let $K:X\to Y$ and $R:Y\to X$ be bounded between Banach spaces,
and let $C:X\to Y$ be bounded with $\|R\|\|C\|<1$.
If $RK-I_X$ is compact, then
$\widetilde R=(I_X+RC)^{-1}R$ is a left regularizer of $K+C$.
If $KR-I_Y$ is compact, then
$\widetilde R=R(I_Y+CR)^{-1}$ is a right regularizer of $K+C$.

Dense least-squares trials can fail without regularization: There is a compact injective dense-range map on $\ell^2$ and
nested finite-dimensional trial spaces with dense union such that
the unique exact-data least-squares approximants have residuals
tending to zero but an unbounded subsequence of solution errors.

Cordial noncompact Volterra counterexample: Let $T>0$. On $C[0,T]$ define, for $t>0$,
$Vf(t)=\int_0^t(t^2-s^2)^{-1/2}f(s)ds$ and
$Vf(0)=(\pi/2)f(0)$. This is bounded with norm $\pi/2$.
For every $r\ge0$, $t^r$ is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue
$\lambda_r=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^r\theta\,d\theta
=\tfrac12 B((r+1)/2,1/2)$.
Consequently $V$ is neither compact nor quasinilpotent.

The singular system and power norm of integration: For $Vf(t)=\int_0^tf(s)ds$ on $L^2(0,T)$, $T>0$, a singular system is
\[
 e_j(t)=\sqrt{2/T}\cos((j-\tfrac12)\pi t/T),\quad
 f_j(t)=\sqrt{2/T}\sin((j-\tfrac12)\pi t/T),\quad
 \sigma_j=\frac{T}{(j-\tfrac12)\pi}.
\]
In particular $\pvnorm V=2T/\pi$ although its spectrum is $\{0\}$.
Moreover
$\pvnorm{V^n}\sim T^n/(2n!)$ as $n\to\infty$.

A genuine long-time convolution bridge: Let $k\in L^1(0,\infty)$ with $a=\pvnorm k_1<1$.
Then $r=\sum_{n\ge1}k^{*n}\in L^1$,
$\pvnorm r_1\le a/(1-a)$, and $u=f+r*f$ uniquely solves
$u=f+k*u$ in every $L^p$, $1\le p\le\infty$.
Its Laplace transform satisfies
$\mathcal Lr(z)=\mathcal Lk(z)/(1-\mathcal Lk(z))$ for
$\operatorname{Re}z\ge0$. If bounded $f(t)\to\ell$, then
$u(t)\to\ell/(1-\int k)$.
Neither finite-interval solvability nor $k\in L^1$ alone implies
long-time stability.

Uniform convergence on compact sets: If $T_n:X\to Y$ are uniformly bounded linear maps and converge
pointwise to $T$, then convergence is uniform on every compact
subset of $X$. If $X$ is Banach and pointwise convergence is given,
uniform boundedness of the sequence follows automatically.
If $A$ is an invertible bounded map between Banach spaces and
$\pvnorm{A^{-1}(A_n-A)}<1$, then $A_n$ is invertible, with the
usual Neumann inverse and quantitative inverse-difference bound. Explicitly, if ε_n=‖A⁻¹(A_n−A)‖<1, A_n⁻¹=∑_{j≥0}(−A⁻¹(A_n−A))^j A⁻¹, ‖A_n⁻¹‖≤‖A⁻¹‖/(1−ε_n), and ‖A_n⁻¹−A⁻¹‖≤ε_n‖A⁻¹‖/(1−ε_n).

Collectively compact stability: Let $K_n:X\to X$ on a Banach space be collectively compact:
the union of their images of the unit ball has compact closure.
Suppose $K_nx\to Kx$ for every $x$, and $I-K$ is injective.
Then $K$ is compact, $I-K$ is invertible, and for large $n$,
$I-K_n$ is invertible with uniformly bounded inverses.
If $u_n-K_nu_n=f_n$, $u-Ku=f$, then
\[
 \pvnorm{u_n-u}\le C\bigl(\pvnorm{(K_n-K)u}+
                                      \pvnorm{f_n-f}\bigr).
\]

The spectral-radius criterion for iteration: For bounded $T$ on a complex Banach space,
$r(T)<1$ is equivalent to $\pvnorm{T^n}\to0$ and to the existence
of $C<\infty$, $q<1$ with $\pvnorm{T^n}\le Cq^n$.
It gives uniform geometric convergence of $x_{n+1}=Tx_n+b$
to $(I-T)^{-1}b$. Pointwise convergence $T^nx\to0$ for every
$x$ is weaker and does not require $r(T)<1$.

Abstract projection criterion: Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and injective between Banach spaces.
Let finite-dimensional $X_n\subset X$, $Y_n\subset Y$ have the
same dimension, let $P_n:Y\to Y_n$ be bounded projections, and
assume $\operatorname{dist}(x,X_n)\to0$ for every $x$.
Suppose $P_nA|_{X_n}$ is invertible for all sufficiently large $n$.
Then the projection method converges for every exact datum $Ax$
if and only if
\[
 Q_n=(P_nA|_{X_n})^{-1}P_nA:X\to X_n
 \quad\hbox{have uniformly bounded norms}.
\]
In that case
$\pvnorm{Q_nx-x}\le(1+\sup\pvnorm{Q_n})\operatorname{dist}(x,X_n)$.
This does not assert stability for arbitrary noisy data unless the
maps $(P_nA|_{X_n})^{-1}P_n$ themselves are uniformly bounded.

Compact second-kind projection: If $K$ is compact, $I-K$ injective, and bounded projections
$P_n:X\to X_n$ converge strongly to $I$, then
$u_n-P_nKu_n=P_nf$ has a unique solution in $X_n$ for large $n$,
and $u_n\to u=(I-K)^{-1}f$.

Galerkin, C\'ea, and Ritz: Let $a(v,u)$ on a Hilbert space be conjugate-linear in $v$,
linear in $u$, bounded by $M\pvnorm v\pvnorm u$, and satisfy
$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\pvnorm u^2$, $\alpha>0$.
For continuous anti-linear data $F$, let $u$ be its Lax--Milgram
solution. On every closed trial subspace $H_n$ there is a unique
Galerkin solution, and
\[
 a(v_n,u-u_n)=0,
 \qquad \pvnorm{u-u_n}\le(M/\alpha)
                    \inf_{v_n\in H_n}\pvnorm{u-v_n}.
\]
If $a$ is Hermitian, $u_n$ is its energy orthogonal projection,
and the error is exactly the minimum energy distance. Approximation
of every vector by the trial spaces implies convergence; a dense
union alone is not sufficient without eventual approximation.

Tikhonov for every bounded Hilbert operator: Let $A:H\to G$ be bounded, $\alpha>0$, and $f\in G$.
The functional
$\pvnorm{Ax-f}^2+\alpha\pvnorm x^2$ has a unique minimizer
\[
 x_\alpha=R_\alpha f,
 \quad R_\alpha=(\alpha I+A^*A)^{-1}A^*,
 \quad \pvnorm{R_\alpha}\le\frac1{2\sqrt\alpha}.
\]
For exact solvable data $f=Ax^\dagger$, with
$x^\dagger\perp\ker A$, $x_\alpha\to x^\dagger$.
If $\pvnorm{f^\delta-f}\le\delta$, convergence remains true when
$\alpha(\delta)\to0$ and $\delta/\sqrt{\alpha(\delta)}\to0$.

For the bounded Hilbert operator A:H→G and Tikhonov solutions x_α=(αI+A* A)⁻¹A*f of the preceding theorem: A source condition and its converse: For exact data and $x^\dagger\perp\ker A$,
$x^\dagger\in\operatorname{ran}(A^*A)$ implies
$\pvnorm{x_\alpha-x^\dagger}\le\alpha\pvnorm w$ when
$x^\dagger=A^*Aw$. Conversely an $O(\alpha)$ exact-data error
implies that range condition.

Singular filters and cutoff: For compact $A$ with singular system, let
$R_\eta f=\sum_j\psi_\eta(\sigma_j)\langle f_j,f\rangle e_j$.
Assume for every parameter
$C_\eta=\sup_j|\psi_\eta(\sigma_j)|<\infty$,
$\sup_{\eta,j}|\sigma_j\psi_\eta(\sigma_j)|<\infty$, and
$\sigma_j\psi_\eta(\sigma_j)\to1$ for every fixed $j$.
Then $R_\eta Ax^\dagger\to x^\dagger$ for the minimum-norm
solution, and noisy convergence holds if
$\eta\to0$ and $\delta C_\eta\to0$.
For spectral cutoff $\psi_\varepsilon(\sigma)=\sigma^{-1}
1_{\{\sigma\ge\varepsilon\}}$, $C_\varepsilon\le1/\varepsilon$.

Moment projection as regularization: Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded between Hilbert spaces. Let $Y_n$ be
nested finite-dimensional subspaces with dense union
in $(\ker A^*)^\perp$, and put $X_n=A^*Y_n$.
For solvable $f=Ax^\dagger$, with $x^\dagger\perp\ker A$, the equations
$P_{Y_n}Ax_n=P_{Y_n}f$, $x_n\in X_n$, have a unique solution,
and $x_n=P_{X_n}x^\dagger\to x^\dagger$.
For noisy data the error is at most
$\operatorname{dist}(x^\dagger,X_n)+\delta/\beta_n$, where
$\beta_n>0$ is the smallest singular value of
$P_{Y_n}A|_{X_n}$ when $Y_n\ne0$. In zero-dimensional stages
the solution and the noise term are both zero, so no singular
value is needed (equivalently set $1/\beta_n=0$ there).
A choice $n(\delta)\to\infty$ with
$\delta/\beta_{n(\delta)}\to0$ is a regularization.

Let A:H→G be bounded between real or complex Hilbert spaces and f∈G. Quasi-solutions and discrepancy constraints: The residual has a minimizer on every closed Hilbert ball.
It is unique if $A$ is injective. Every nonempty discrepancy set
$\{x:\pvnorm{Ax-f}\le\delta\}$ has a unique minimum-norm member.
If $\operatorname{dist}(f,\overline{\operatorname{ran}A})<\delta<\pvnorm f$,
that member is a Tikhonov solution with a parameter chosen so that
its residual is $\delta$.

Reproducing kernels and integral-operator ranges: A Hilbert space of functions with bounded point evaluations has
unique vectors $k_x$ with $f(x)=\langle k_x,f\rangle$ and
kernel $K(x,y)=\langle k_x,k_y\rangle$.
Conversely every positive definite scalar kernel defines a unique
Hilbert space with this reproducing property.
If $Au(x)=\int k(x,z)u(z)dz$ is a bounded map from $L^2$ into
functions with $k(x,\cdot)\in L^2$, its range, with minimum-preimage
norm, is such a Hilbert space and
$K(x,y)=\int k(x,z)\overline{k(y,z)}dz$. Positive definite scalar kernel includes Hermitian symmetry K(y,x)=overline(K(x,y)) (symmetry for real scalars) and ∑_{i,j}overline(c_i)c_j K(x_i,x_j)≥0 for all finite point/scalar lists.

Positive extensions with a majorizing subspace: Let $E$ be a real ordered vector space and $M\subset E$ a subspace
such that every $x\in E$ is bounded above by some member of $M$.
Every positive linear functional $\ell$ on $M$ has a positive
linear extension to $E$. In particular this holds when $M$ contains
an order unit $e$. In the Archimedean order-unit norm the extension
is bounded with norm $\ell(e)$.

Kakutani's equicontinuous affine-group theorem: An equicontinuous group of affine homeomorphisms of a nonempty
compact convex subset $K$ of a Hausdorff locally convex space has
a common fixed point.

Commuting affine maps and invariant means: A commuting family of continuous affine self-maps of a nonempty
compact convex subset of a Hausdorff locally convex space has a
common fixed point. Every abelian group $G$ has a positive unital
translation-invariant functional on $\ell^\infty(G)$ and therefore
a translation-invariant finitely additive probability on its power set.

Normalized Haar measure on compact groups: Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique normalized left-invariant
regular Borel measure. It is also right invariant and invariant
under inversion. Every nonempty open set has positive mass.

Stone--Weierstrass and extreme scalar measures: A self-adjoint point-separating unital subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb C)$,
$K$ nonempty compact Hausdorff, is uniformly dense. The real form requires
no self-adjointness. On a locally compact Hausdorff space the
$C_0$ version replaces unitality by nonvanishing at every point.
The extreme probability measures on $K$ are exactly the Dirac
measures. The extreme points of the complex measure unit ball
are exactly $z\delta_x$, $|z|=1$ (real signs in the real case).

Lyapunov convexity by purification: The range of a finite-dimensional finite nonatomic real vector
measure is compact and convex. Here nonatomic means its total
variation has no atoms; equivalently one may dominate its
coordinate variations by a finite nonatomic positive measure.
The complex case is the corresponding real $2n$-dimensional case.

Let K be compact Hausdorff. Bishop's antisymmetric-set theorem: Let $\mathcal A$ be a closed subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb C)$.
A subset is $\mathcal A$-antisymmetric when every algebra member
real-valued there is constant there. If $g\in C(K)$ agrees on
each maximal antisymmetric set with some member of $\mathcal A$,
then $g\in\mathcal A$.

Let K be compact Hausdorff, using finite regular scalar measures to identify C(K)′. Bishop restriction interpolation: Let $Y$ be a closed subspace of $C(K)$ and $F\subset K$ compact.
If $|\mu|(F)=0$ for every $\mu\in Y^\perp$, then restriction
$R:Y\to C(F)$ maps its open unit ball onto the open unit ball.
In particular it is onto. The condition concerns total variation,
not merely the possibly cancelling scalar mass $\mu(F)$.

Finite Blaschke interpolation: Let the finitely many interpolation nodes $z_j$ lie in the open
unit disk. If prescribed values at them admit a holomorphic
solution of $|f|\le1$, they admit a finite Blaschke-product
solution, including a unimodular constant as degree zero.

Quantitative absolute synthesis: Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence in the unit ball of a Banach space.
If $\sup_n|\ell(x_n)|\ge\beta\pvnorm\ell$ for every $\ell\in X'$,
$\beta>0$, then for every $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there are
$a\in\ell^1$ with $x=\sum a_nx_n$ and
$\norm{a}_{\ell^1}<\beta^{-1}\pvnorm x+\varepsilon$.

For every ε>0 and normalized circle Haar measure: Absolute Poisson-kernel synthesis: Let $(z_n)$ in the disk be nontangentially dense at almost every
boundary point: for a.e. $\zeta$ some subsequence tends to
$\zeta$ in a fixed Stolz cone. Every $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ has
an absolutely convergent expansion $f=\sum a_nP_{z_n}$ with
$\sum|a_n|<\norm{f}_{L^1}+\varepsilon$.

Silverman--Toeplitz summability: For rows $(a_{nk})_k\in\ell^1$, the matrix transformation
$y_n=\sum_ka_{nk}x_k$ sends every convergent sequence to a
sequence with the same limit if and only if
\[
 \sup_n\sum_k|a_{nk}|<\infty,\qquad
 a_{nk}\to0\ (k\text{ fixed}),\qquad
 \sum_ka_{nk}\to1.
\]

Let K be compact Hausdorff and use finite regular scalar measures with total-variation norm. Quadrature is weak-star convergence: On compact $K$, scalar finite measures $\mu_n$ converge against
every $C(K)$ function exactly when their variations are uniformly
bounded and their integrals converge on a uniformly dense linear
subspace, to the restriction of one bounded functional.
For compact metric $K$ and a finite measure $\mu$, partitions of
mesh tending to zero with weights $\mu(A_j)$ and nodes in each
cell give weak-star convergent quadrature measures.

Positive Markov kernels and invariant probabilities: Let $K$ be nonempty compact Hausdorff. A positive unital linear map
$P:C(K)\to C(K)$ has an invariant regular
probability measure. If it is given by a continuous kernel with
respect to a probability $\nu$ and $k(x,y)\ge\varepsilon>0$,
then that probability is unique and the iterates converge uniformly
to its integral, geometrically in oscillation. Quantitatively, for real f, osc(Pⁿf)≤(1−ε)ⁿosc(f) and ‖Pⁿf−∫f dμ‖∞≤(1−ε)ⁿosc(f); for complex f apply these bounds to real and imaginary parts. The ε=1 case gives a constant after one step.

A continuous spectrum from an explicit multiplier: On $L^2(\mathbb R)$ the inverse of $I-\partial_x^2$, with its
Sobolev domain $H^2$, is the Fourier multiplier
$m(\xi)=(1+4\pi^2\xi^2)^{-1}$. It is bounded self-adjoint with
norm one and spectrum $[0,1]$, has no eigenvalues, and is not compact.
